Sports.title: Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide again
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen produced a remarkable drive to win a wild Las Vegas Grand Prix that saw him withstand extreme pressure from George Russell and Kimi Antonelli before a late Mercedes collapse.

Pole-sitter Verstappen retained the lead at the start but the enormous power of a slipstream on the long straights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit made it impossible for the Dutchman to pull clear, and resulted in 34 changes of the lead and well over 300 total overtakes in the 50-lap race.

First Russell, and then later newly crowned world champion Antonelli were each able to pass Verstappen on multiple occasions but the Red Bull driver calmly retook the lead within a few corners every time, expertly managing the deployment of his power.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell hits the barrier after a lock-up when trying to overtake team-mate Kimi Antonelli at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, much to the delight of rival Max Verstappen.

Russell, trying to pass his team-mate for second with three laps remaining, ran into a barrier after overshooting a corner and dropped down the order, before Antonelli made an error with his deployment at the start of the final lap that allowed Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri to snatch a double podium for McLaren.

"That was crazy. Really, really surreal and something I've never seen before in F1 myself," Verstappen said.

"I think we had it [deployment] set up well and it was a crazy amount of fighting, and the slipstream was so big that it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were following."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton spins after contact with Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc, which led to a 10-second penalty for the latter at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

There was more unwanted drama for Ferrari as team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collided again as they battled for sixth with 12 laps remaining, with the latter given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing the incident.

Pierre Gasly took fifth ahead of his team-mate Franco Colapinto to secure a major points haul for Alpine, with Hamilton recovering to seventh, having served a 10-second penalty himself earlier in the race for overtaking Norris off track.

Carlos Sainz snatched eighth from Russell on the run to the finish line to equal Williams' best result of the season, while Leclerc claimed the final point in 10th.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Red Bulla's Isack Hadjar was running in third place but was forced to pit after losing his front wing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The result all but secures second in the drivers' standings for Verstappen, who made it four wins in six races to pull 37 points clear of third-placed Hamilton with two rounds to go in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

McLaren's late gains enabled them to close within nine points of Red Bull in the battle for third in the constructors' standings, with Verstappen's team-mate Isack Hadjar unfortunate to finish outside the points after a front-wing failure - moments after a Safety Car stoppage that had bunched the field - dropped him from third to last.

Las Vegas GP Result: Top 10 1) Max Verstappen, Red Bull



2) Lando Norris, McLaren



3) Oscar Piastri, McLaren



4) Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes



5) Pierre Gasly, Alpine



6) Franco Colapinto, Alpine



7) Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari



8) Carlos Sainz, Williams



9) George Russell, Mercedes



10) Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

Verstappen has last laugh in Russell battle

Despite Antonelli and Mercedes having already closed out this year's championships, there was plenty of tension on the grid as Verstappen and Russell lined up on the front row following a renewal of a long-term spat between the pair earlier in the weekend.

Following a collision between the pair in final practice that resulted in Verstappen being given a warning by the stewards, Russell launched a scathing criticism of the Dutchman, echoing comments he made almost exactly two years ago as he said someone needed to "stand up" to the Red Bull driver.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The start of the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Despite those words, there was plenty of respect on show between the pair on track as they battled for much of the race after Verstappen had made a strong start to retain the lead.

Russell, who was already under constant pressure from Hadjar and then Norris, adjusted his deployment strategy to repeatedly find a way past Verstappen in the final sector. However, he could never find a way to keep the Red Bull behind him through the opening corners of the following lap.

The only real pause in the frantic action came on lap 19 when Cadillac's Sergio Perez and Haas' Rafael Camara collided as the former attempted an overtake.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell tussles with Max Verstappen and Isack Hadajr at the start of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The damage left Perez stranded on track, triggering the Safety Car. Its deployment was extended when Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, who was running fifth at the time, spun and also came to a stop on the circuit.

When the race resumed at the end of lap 25, Russell continued to put Verstappen under pressure, retaking the lead several times. He even reclaimed first place after briefly dropping behind Norris.

Russell made his final move into the lead at the end of lap 37, but Verstappen quickly reclaimed the position. For the first time in the race, Russell then dropped behind team-mate Antonelli, who had fought back from a five-place grid penalty despite securing pole position in qualifying.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes' George Russell insists he's got no regrets despite locking up and hitting the barrier late in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Russell was tyring to mount one last push for victory on lap 48, but his attempt to go up the inside of Antonelli at Turn 5 came unstuck as he locked up and nudged into the barrier.

Having seen the incident in his mirrors, Verstappen immediately came on team radio - apparently delighted at his rival's error - saying: "Haha. Well done! My god…"

Verstappen had already demonstrated his awareness midway through the race, opening discussions with his team over the radio about adjusting their deployment strategy to ensure Mercedes could not beat him in a drag race to the line on the final lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen had a choice few words for long-time foe George Russell after winning the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Ultimately, such tactics weren't necessary as Antonelli, by lifting off the throttle, triggered a loss in deployment that allowed both McLarens to overtake him and gave Verstappen a relatively stress-free final lap.

The four-time world champion wasn't finished taking a dig at Russell. Asked about the Brit during the post-race press conference, Verstappen added: "It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and saw what was happening. I was like, 'Fantastic, my day is only getting better.'"

"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Leclerc penalised for 'unacceptable' collision with Hamilton

With Antonelli and Mercedes dominating this year's championships, much of F1's drama in recent weeks has been provided by the repeated battles between Ferrari team-mates Hamilton and Leclerc.

Hamilton was left furious following the Mexico City Grand Prix at the start of the month when Leclerc launched an ambitious attempt to take the lead from him on the opening lap, resulting in a clash that cost the team a likely one-two and gifted Verstappen victory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton complain about each other's driving over the radio during the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Both drivers said the situation had been resolved following talks in Brazil the following week, but that didn't appear to be the case on Saturday night in Las Vegas.

Starting from 9th and 10th after a dismal qualifying, the pair made minor contact at the start, but far worse was to come.

Hamilton had driven impressively to fight his way back through the field after serving a 10-second penalty for going off track while passing Norris. He was ahead of Leclerc in the battle for sixth and pushing to retake the position from the McLaren when the pair came together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc react after they crashed into one another at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Having seen Hamilton fail to get past Norris, Leclerc attempted to capitalise, making an ambitious move up the inside at Turn 7.

The result was a collision that spun Hamilton and saw him drop back through the field, with the stewards deciding Leclerc was to blame as he had come from too far behind his team-mate, which meant Hamilton had no obligation to leave space on the inside.

Hamilton was measured in his comments both on the radio and after the race, but Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur took the notable action as he summoned Leclerc to speak to him immediately after the race, saying over the radio: "Charles, I want to see you after the race before everything."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari Team Principal has branded Charles Leclerc's driving as 'unacceptable' after his collided with Lewis Hamilton during the Las Vegas GP.

Vasseur later told Sky Sports F1: "We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you are passed by the others. It means that you have to do your race and Charles did clearly a mistake that's penalising the team a lot. It's completely unacceptable today."

While the latest episode of the Verstappen-Russell beef will perhaps be the biggest talking point ahead of Thursday's media day at the Qatar Grand Prix, a new chapter of Ferrari's internal battle and Vasseur's inability to control the situation will be met with similar anticipation.

Sports.title: Price sets up Grand Slam final showdown with Van Veen
Sports.content:
Gerwyn Price will take on Gian van Veen in the Grand Slam of Darts final, live on Sky Sports from 7.30pm on Sunday.

Gerwyn Price came up with a 16-13 win over Kevin Doets in the semi-finals on Sunday afternoon, while Van Veen defeated Michael van Gerwen 16-11.

Price is targeting a fourth Grand Slam title, adding to his triumphs in 2018, 2019 and 2021.

There is also a big move in the rankings on the line for the Welshman as, if he wins, he will become world No 3, dropping Luke Humphries to world No 4.

Meanwhile, provisional world No 2 Van Veen is searching for his maiden Grand Slam title.

Price came through a real battle to make it into another final. He is aiming to maintain his perfect finals record in Wolverhampton and believes that over the majors in 2026, he has been the most consistent performer.

"I am into another final and I am not playing great," Price told Sky Sports. "I have played okay in patches this tournament. I am in another final and I am happy.

"I have probably been the most consistent player this season as far as majors are concerned.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Price jokes he's a rugby player 'pinching a living' after reaching Grand Slam of Darts final

"I obviously want to win this and there are some big ranking points at stake but I am just happy to get to another final.

"I care - there is £100,000 at stake and if I don't care about that there is something wrong - but if I lose it is another final.

"It is not about trophies, it is about earning a living for my family.

"I am just a rugby player pinching a living!"

Grand Slam of Darts: Semi-final results Kevin Doets 13-16 Gerwyn Price Michael van Gerwen 11-16 Gian van Veen

How Price beat Doets

It was a tight opening session between the pair from which Price took a 3-2 lead, increasing that to 4-2 with his fourth leg in a row.

Doets battled back but a brilliant 137 checkout and then break of throw from the Welshman put him 6-4 ahead.

From there, Price went on a rampage. He reeled off six legs in a row to get to double figures. Doets stopped the rot with a break of throw but the 10-4 scoreline showed how everything was going the Welshman's way.

Despite Price's momentum, Doets dug deep and won five on the next six legs to move the score to 11-9 and eventually 14-12.

However, the key moment came in the 27th leg when Doets missed two chances to break Price's throw and instead of bringing the score to 14-13, he went 15-12 behind.

That gave Price enough breathing space to wait for his throw, then take out a big 171 to leave 94 which he checked out on tops for a 12-darter.

Part: Price the Grand Slam favourite

Sky Sports Darts' John Part:

"Price had control and did things at the right times.

"When he seems to have the most trouble in matches is when he has a big lead. Perhaps his focus gets away from a bit.

"Ultimately, the real clutch darts were Price's and now you have to say he is the favourite in the final."

How Van Veen beat MVG

It was expected to be a close contest between the two Dutch darting stars and early on it was just that with Van Gerwen and Van Veen matching each other in every department.

That saw the game levelled at 5-5 and it was clear someone was going to have to take control.

However, it was not necessarily that Van Veen took control. Some disastrous doubling for both players, but in particular Van Gerwen, proved to be the key factor.

As Van Veen improved, Van Gerwen continued to mess around on the outer ring which allowed his opponent to go from 7-6 down to 10-7 ahead.

Although Van Gerwen tried to get himself back into the contest, a burst of four legs in a row moved Van Veen one leg away from the Grand Slam final, a massive 124 checkout on the bullseye getting him there.

Van Gerwen did hold his throw but it was purely a consolation as the Dutch No 1 pinned 107 on D16 for his first Grand Slam final.

Share

37m ago 11.15 EST David Hytner Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all. For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll. Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them. This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United? Read more Share

They need to come away with something today.” I agree with you about the perils of a hiding, though I still think it’s broadly a free hit for Pochettino – certainly in comparison to most of United’s Anfield trips. 1h ago 10.47 EST Jonathan Wilson Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation. Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager. With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast. It’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve? We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.” Mauricio Pochettino calls for Manchester United to show no fear against Liverpool Read more Share Updated at 10.47 EST

Sports.title: McBurnie’s late double snatches shock win for Hull to crush 10-man Brighton
Sports.content:
Oli McBurnie’s injury-time brace helped Hull to a dramatic victory over Brighton but the Tigers had the heroics of their goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis to thank for a result which continued their unbeaten home start since returning to the Premier League.

Fabian Hürzeler’s side were much the stronger of the teams on an afternoon they largely dominated. However, a string of chances in both halves passed them by without the goal their play deserved, thanks largely to Tzolakis, with the Greek international producing a string of sensational saves in both halves.

But after Brighton’s João Costinha was sent off for a second yellow card in the final moments, Hull pressed forward for an unlikely winner which they ultimately found, as McBurnie bundled home before tapping in a second two minutes later. It was a damaging afternoon for Brighton’s title hopes, who missed the chance to close the gap to Arsenal to three points.

How they did not secure at least a point is anyone’s guess. The Seagulls should not only have been in front at half-time, but ahead by such a margin that the game could have been over inside the opening 45 minutes.

Tzolakis was called into action early on, with a superb point-blank save to deny Diego Gómez from converting Maxim De Cuyper’s low cross. Gómez, De Cuyper and Yasin Ayari were causing mayhem on a frequent basis, with Ayari then next to miss a gilt-edged opportunity to open the scoring – but he could only fire a tame shot at Tzolakis.

Hull’s keeper was called into action again two minutes later; another slick Brighton move led to Ayari hitting the crossbar and from the rebound, Tzolakis reacted fastest to deny Georginio Rutter from inside the box before Gómez was next to miss a clearcut chance, with Tzolakis making another wonderful save with his foot to keep it goalless.

View image in fullscreen Oli McBurnie adds his second goal to seal an unlikely win for Hull. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

Half-time did little change the flow of momentum. Pascal Gross’ shot produced another reflex save from Tzolakis before Gómez then fired wide from six yards out, when it appeared easier to hit the target. You began to wonder if those missed opportunities were going to become costly, with Hull starting to become a threat at the other end, too.

On two separate occasions they countered Brighton attacks with wonderful breaks, but Mohamed Belloumi fluffed his lines both times after initially doing well to work the space for shots. Bart Verbruggen, mostly on a watching brief to that point, saved one before breathing a sigh of relief as the second squirmed wide of his post.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Hürzeler had seen enough. Three substitutes were introduced to try and find the breakthrough and one of those, Charalampos Kostoulas, finally beat Tzolakis with a clever chip over the Hull goalkeeper, but Regan Slater was on hand to hack the ball off the line and keep the game level heading into the final 10 minutes.

And all those Tzolakis saves ultimately proved crucial. When Costinha was shown a second yellow for a foul on the impressive Sorba Thomas, Hull surged forward with belief they could perhaps find a winner.

McBurnie then scrambled the ball past Verbruggen after Lucas Gourna-Douath was set free before, two minutes later, the Hull striker repeated the trick to double the Tigers’ lead and seal an incredible victory for the hosts.

Sports.title: ‘Obviously it’s not good’: Arteta sweating over David Raya’s fitness after injury
Sports.content:
Arsenal were left sweating on the fitness of their goalkeeper David Raya after the Spaniard was forced off with a shoulder injury during the second half of the 2-2 draw at Newcastle on Saturday evening.

It left Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City at the top of the Premier League but Arsenal’s manager was more concerned about Raya following an accidental collision with Newcastle’s William Osula. The Spaniard was helped off in evident pain and looked close to tears.

“Obviously it’s not good David had to come off but at the moment I don’t know [the prognosis],” said Arteta, explaining that a keeper who kept seven clean sheets in the season’s opening 10 games will have the joint scanned on Sunday. “He will have an MRI tomorrow. We will have more information tomorrow. But we know how important David is to us.”

Arsenal were 1-0 up at half-time at St James’ Park thanks to a goal from Eberechi Eze during an opening 45 minutes dominated by the visitors. Newcastle, though, improved significantly after the break and took the lead thanks to goals from Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw before Noni Madueke equalised.

Quick Guide How do I 

“My feeling is we have lost two points,” said Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half but we needed to score three or four goals and we didn’t. We knew there’d be a response but the way we gave Newcastle’s first goal away was completely unacceptable. We came back and scored a second goal but we lacked the moment of magic to kill the game. I don’t think we switched off in the second half; sometimes you have to praise the opposition.”

Matthias Jaissle was left smiling after that second-half performance rescued a game watched by Newcastle’s chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan. He had flown in from Riyadh to witness his first match of the season and is believed to have complimented his head coach afterwards.

View image in fullscreen William Osula (left) battles with the Arsenal defender Gabriel. Photograph: Peter Powell/EPA

“What you saw in the second half was Newcastle’s DNA par excellence and that’s something we can build on,” said Jaissle. “But we’ve got to be humble and realistic. The first half was not good and the second half was excellent. I’ve got mixed feelings because a little more was possible but a point was probably fair.

“I was a bit frustrated at half-time but we encouraged the players to do the high press in the right way and adopt a front-foot approach. There was no hesitating, no doubting, just pure belief and we clicked. I knew we were able to do it, so I was really pleased. We felt unbelievable connections and synergy with the crowd.

“To get a team as good as Arsenal shaking in your stadium was unbelievable. I hope we can carry on this feeling.”

Sports.title: Blackburn earn derby draw for Mowbray and extend Burnley’s wait for home win
Sports.content:
Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.

In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break. But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn’s first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.

Burnley remain deep in relegation trouble, without a home league victory for 400 days, having once again failed to hold on to a lead. They have now dropped 25 points from winning positions in the Championship this season.

Blackburn wanted a victory not just for local pride, but to honour Mowbray, who turned 63 on Sunday, and for whom this was to be a 900th match in management before his announcement on Tuesday that he would be stepping back. Their players warmed up in T-shirts bearing the message “We’re with you, Tony” on the back and the number 900 on the front.

Coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge in Mowbray’s absence and had to reshuffle the defence when Tom Atcheson was concussed after receiving a boot to the face in the third minute.

Stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth sustained a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.

The on-loan Leeds winger cut in from the right and fired a shot that flew into the roof of the net right by Pears, who was too slow to react.

View image in fullscreen Todd Cantwell wears a T-shirt in support of Blackburn’s absent manager Tony Mowbray at Turf Moor. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

But Gudjohnsen equalised four minutes later, racing on to a Harry Pickering long ball that drifted over Burnley centre-back Max Alleyne, and steering a sweet shot beyond goalkeeper Max Weiß for his 12th goal of the season. The Icelander celebrated by grabbing a T-shirt paying tribute to Mowbray from a photographer and displaying it for the cameras.

Blackburn finished the first half strongly, with Cantwell firing over a good chance, before Banel restored Burnley’s lead six minutes into the second half, running unchallenged to place a shot into the far corner as defender Hayden Carter backed off.

The home side were fortunate to escape a strong penalty appeal just before the hour mark as Cantwell burst into the penalty area and saw two attempted crosses both strike the arm of Igor Julio.

Blackburn did get a penalty with 16 minutes left as Josh Laurent, attempting to clear a low cross, failed to spot Gudjohnsen darting in from behind him and caught the striker’s leg. Cantwell drove the penalty straight down the middle to make it 2-2.

Gudjohnsen thought he had given Blackburn the lead two minutes later, when he controlled and drove a low shot against the base of the post with Weiß a spectator, but neither side could find a winner.

Sports.title: César Azpilicueta: ‘At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe – if you can’t perform, you’re out’
Sports.content:
César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot.

It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. He’s completed an MBA, a sports directorship diploma and there are media offers, a life to live. Matches to play still: against his kids the needle is never far away, he says. And although he hasn’t found a seven-a-side team yet he will.

“I get up, take them to school, go to the gym. I do pilates some days. I walk the dogs, play golf, then it’s after-school activities. I read, try to learn new things. I haven’t yet thought: ‘I’m bored,’” Azpilicueta says, although you wonder how long that will last. “Over the last 12 months I could see it. The summer before I already ‘hit the post’ with retirement. It’s natural: a day comes … if only I could play for ever but it is what it is and you have to keep evolving. I’m enjoying it.”

Don’t get the wrong idea. “In terms of controlling your time, playing every three days, always waiting on the next message: ‘Meet at …,’ it’s a release. But it’s not a liberation because you’re delighted to pull your boots on. An important part of your life ends; you kick a ball almost from the moment you walk, live your passion. Even last season – when there were days everything hurt, when you think: ‘How can I get injured like that?’ – I would make demands of myself, my teammates. I always liked that.

“I never thought I’d be a professional. I couldn’t tell you the moment I thought: ‘I’m a footballer,’” Azpilicueta continues, but he can tell you the score on his debut, for Osasuna in 2007. “One-nil win, Getafe.” Celta de Vigo were the last opponents: a 1-0 loss in May for Sevilla. Between those, more than 800 matches, 508 for Chelsea. Only five players have played more for Chelsea; no foreigner has.

View image in fullscreen César Azpilicueta returns to Stamford Bridge for October’s match against Tottenham. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

“I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I,” Azpilicueta says, and there’s that laugh again.

It’s a long time since he stood before his new teammates and sang an Estopa track. He arrived in London with a labrador and a sausage dog; he left a legend and the captain, with three kids and every trophy, a European and world champion.

Asked to define his career in a word, Azpilicueta goes for: constancia. Perseverance, consistency, commitment. He talks about the cruciate tear with Marseille aged 21 as a lesson, something that “changed my perspective and made me value discipline, preparation … Out of something negative I grew.” About always adapting, always overcoming, becoming what managers need you to be. There’s a laugh at the little lies – of course I’ve played on the left, boss – and the hours spent alone practising, convincing coaches or teammates to stay behind with him and go over it again and again.

“I arrived at Chelsea late in the market [in 2012],” Azpilicueta says. “My representative said: ‘We’ve spoken to Michael Emenalo, the sporting director, and they’re signing younger players.’ Oscar, Eden Hazard, Victor Moses, Marko Marin, Paulo Ferreira. I was 22. Doubts? Pfff … Olympique needed the money. Chelsea had just won the Champions League and I …”

That laugh. “I hadn’t played for Spain. What did Emenalo see in me? It’s hard to work it out. Also, what you are and what you become is different. You think: ‘What’s it going to be like?’ Another country, another pace, but Juan Mata was there, Fernando Torres, Oriol [Romeu]. Doctor [Paco] Biosca, Ivan the physio. Petr Cech spoke Spanish. Hazard and I spoke French together. I could [communicate] with the Brazilians. But it wasn’t just them. I integrated fast, tried to speak English.

double quotation mark I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I

“Not long after arriving there was this audience with fans. Fernando, Juan, Oriol and I. A Q&A. One said: ‘Look, your name is very difficult. Can we just call you Dave?’ Juan translated. I said: ‘Yeah, sure,’ thinking that they meant for the evening. And it stuck. Going down the street: ‘Hey, Dave!’ There was the occasional ‘Dave’ in the dressing room but mostly it was fans. I felt the affection.

“You go with an open mind and bit by bit carve yourself a place. Every time a new coach comes you think: ‘Now what? Will I fit?’ I started as a winger in Pamplona. At Chelsea I played right-back, left-back, a line of three which I hadn’t played in my life … lots of systems, lots of coaches.”

Twelve coaches, in fact. Azpilicueta played under all of them. “You arrive at a historic club like Chelsea and just try to stay as long as you can. That machine makes demands of you every three days. What I really noticed was a hunger to win: either you have that culture or … forget it. At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe. You see teammates come and go. The reality is the reality. On the pitch, you have to do it. It’s hard? Yes. But you can’t be sunk by a bad game. If you win: very good, done, next. If you can’t perform, you’re out … You have to manage that pressure.

View image in fullscreen ‘Dave’ Azpilicueta took to life in England quickly after his move to Chelsea in 2012. Photograph: Gerry Penny/EPA

“I’ve had plenty of unpleasant days. I remember a 6-0 loss to Manchester City.” So then what? “For me, the first thing would be watch the video. Look at the data. But know that’s not everything. Sleep, get up, turn it round. Get into training first. And it’s not just about you; some days it’s about lifting up teammates too.”

Preparation, he says, was fundamental. “I analysed everything. I want to know if when the winger receives, he turns left. I needed that. Football’s not mathematical – ‘this equals that’ – but that information helps you have more control, feel readier. I don’t know if I was more [serious] than others, but I was very cuadriculado, square. Others hardly did anything and were fine.”

That sounds like Eden Hazard. Azpilicueta laughs. “He was more … more … relaxed. Not everyone has to be the same. I was very square, I prepared differently, I was like a robot.”

Besides, Hazard was the best; it is his name, not Lionel Messi or Ronaldo’s, that comes up when Azpilicueta is asked his toughest opponent. “I was fortunate to train with Eden. He didn’t train 100%, but he forced you to. I had to kick him sometimes, haha! Playing together, he would say: ‘Give me the ball.’ I would say: ‘Stay there, I’ll defend for you.’”

Azpilicueta defended them all. “The first time I was captain was an FA Cup semi-final against Tottenham [in 2017],” he recalls. “We arrived late, no one said anything. [Gary] Cahill, the captain, was injured. We walk in and, pam, the armband’s in my place. Steve Holland says: ‘Let’s go to the referees meeting.’ ‘Oh, OK’ … and that was it. I liked it. I don’t think you change much; you have your own personality. You don’t have to score two because you’re captain. Besides, that was a one-off until later. But you do feel a little extra responsibility.”

View image in fullscreen ‘He didn’t train at 100%, but he forced you to,’ Azpilicueta says of Eden Hazard. Photograph: Andrew Fosker/BPI/Shutterstock

New players found Azpilicueta waiting for them, leadership through empathy and example. “Quite a few stayed at my house,” he says. But if there is a portrait of his leadership perhaps it is him paying for the bus, covering petrol for the first team and youth team, when Chelsea’s assets were frozen after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And his reaction to that being put to him now. “Nah,” he says. “Well. No. All of us. I didn’t do anything anyone else didn’t. We did it together, which is how things should be done.

“There a feeling of: ‘We have this issue, we’re going to sort this out,’” Azpilicueta adds, fist hitting the desk. “That situation was strange. We had won the Club World Cup, been with [Roman Abramovich] there and suddenly … it was the uncertainty: players, staff. Many people work for Chelsea, depend on that.”

Underlying it all is the same basic principle, Azpilicueta says: “People. There are so many day-to-day who make it work. And sure, we’re good at football but what really fulfils you is see people there with their families all together when you win, when you lift the Champions League.”

View image in fullscreen Azpilicueta lifts the Champions League as Chelsea captain in 2021. Photograph: Carl Recine/Reuters

Have you got a photo of you lifting that cup? “At home? No. A friend gave me a very nice one framed but it’s half hidden. I don’t much like showing it off.” If someone came to your house could they tell a footballer lives there? “No.”

Twenty years on, a lifetime later, a footballer doesn’t. So now what? “I don’t know,” Azpilicueta says, laughing. “Maybe I’ll be here, playing off a better handicap. But I like football, being involved. I’ve done some co-commentating. I have the MBA, the diploma. Not because I necessarily want to be a sporting director tomorrow, but because it interests me, because it’s nice to learn. I enjoyed the classes, meeting people, doing course work.”

The practical experience is even better. “The last few contracts I negotiated myself. I’ve had various agents help over the years but a time came with Chelsea when I thought: ‘What for?’ I sit down with Marina [Granovskaia], then with Behdad [Eghbali] and Todd [Boehly]. As captain I had spoken to them about so many issues that when it came to my own I thought: ‘I can do this alone.’ I might have got a better deal, who knows, but I was comfortable that way. I was never looking for anything, I was happy, my family was happy, I felt loved and valued and that was it. I just wanted to go in to work every day.”

Sports.title: Lionel Messi at center of red-card controversy as Inter Miami face early MLS playoff exit
Sports.content:
Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.

Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.

Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois said afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.

“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”

Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.

“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.

Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.

The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.

The result means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, can eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in Game 2 of the best-of-three series in Ohio next Friday.

“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Miami coach Kily González said afterwards.

“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out.

“There’s no better challenge for us as a team than this. It’s a test of character, and I know my team has that character.”

FC Dallas 3-0 Portland Timbers

Joaquín Valiente scored twice in the space of two minutes as FC Dallas beat the Portland Timbers 3-0 in the opening game of their best-of-three Western Conference first-round series.

The 25-year-old Uruguayan midfielder broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, volleying home a rebound after Daniel Job’s shot was parried by Portland goalkeeper James Pantemis.

Valiente doubled the lead two minutes later, timing his run to meet another pass from Job before redirecting the ball between Pantemis’s legs.

Samuel Sarver completed the scoring in the fourth minute of stoppage time, finishing a cross from Logan Farrington on the counterattack.

Dallas goalkeeper Daniel de Sousa Britto, known simply as Daniel, made four saves, while Pantemis finished with five for Portland.

The Timbers also lost Ariel Lassiter to an apparent injury in the 33rd minute.

Second-seeded Dallas can advance to the Western Conference semi-finals with a victory in Portland next Saturday.

New England Revolution 2-0 Philadelphia Union

Teenager Peyton Miller scored one goal and helped create another as the New England Revolution beat the Philadelphia Union 2-0 in the opening game of their Eastern Conference first-round series.

The 19-year-old Miller became the fifth-youngest goalscorer in MLS Cup playoffs history when he volleyed home a cross from Jack Harrison in the 73rd minute, his effort bouncing off the crossbar and into the net.

New England had taken the lead in the 10th minute when Miller’s shot from the edge of the penalty area deflected off Philadelphia defender Nathan Harriel for an own goal.

Harrison, who came on as a substitute in the 62nd minute, was making his first appearance since 9 September after missing more than two months with a quadriceps injury.

Philadelphia nearly equalized in the 37th minute when Cavan Sullivan turned and fired a shot from outside the penalty area that struck the left post.

The Union fielded the youngest starting lineup in MLS Cup playoffs history, with an average age of 23 years and 207 days, breaking the record set by the New York Red Bulls in 2022.

Matt Turner made two saves to preserve the shutout for New England, who can advance to the Eastern Conference semi-finals with a victory in Philadelphia next Saturday.

Sports.title: Teenage ace Williams-Barnett puts Tottenham on path to win over Ipswich
Sports.content:
Not since the emergence of a certain Harry Kane has there been this much excitement about a player from Tottenham’s academy. On his first senior start, Luca Williams-Barnett showed just why as the 18-year-old became their youngest Premier League goalscorer since Gareth Bale in 2007 before teeing up Dominic Solanke with a mesmerising and match-winning assist against Ipswich.

That made it four league victories from their last five matches for Roberto De Zerbi’s side and the Italian could only have enjoyed the view from the stands as he served his one-match touchline ban. Tottenham have struggled to match their London rivals Arsenal and Chelsea’s record of producing homegrown players in recent years but they appear to have struck gold with Williams-Barnett.

Harry Winks was the last academy graduate to score on his debut more than a decade ago – a feat that Kane also achieved two years earlier against Sunderland. Yet after Spurs decided to allow the England Under-21s striker Will Lankshear to join Middlesbrough in the summer, there was no chance that Williams-Barnett would be allowed to follow him out of the door. He became the 900th player ever to represent Spurs when he made his debut last year and the teenager left the field here to a standing ovation that he will never forget.

“I told him to play like he plays in the park with his friends, with the same freedom,” said De Zerbi. “And to play and to work hard without the ball, like [Ousmane] Dembélé, like Raphinha, like [Lamine] Yamal. Luca is a special player. I’m not surprised because his talent is bigger than you think. He’s very young but at same time he’s very mature. He is older than his age.”

Asked whether his protege has the potential to be compared to the Barcelona sensation Lamine Yamal, De Zerbi added: “Yes, I think so. One of the best things in my career I’ve seen today on the bus to the stadium. He was watching [clips] on YouTube of Ronaldinho, Hazard. I think he’s a special guy, because if one hour before you are debuting in the Premier League, you are watching Ronaldinho, Hazard, Neymar, all these types of talent. Having the qualities is one thing but he has the passion for football, too.”

View image in fullscreen Dominic Solanke scores Tottenham’s second goal. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

After a promising start to the campaign, Ipswich’s momentum has stalled – they have now gone five games without a victory. But Gary O’Neil, who has already seen 16-year-old Max Dowman score twice for Arsenal against his side in the Carabao Cup, acknowledged that they had been second best throughout. “You need things to be perfect when we come to a place like this and we didn’t make things easy for ourselves,” he said.

De Zerbi dropped a huge hint that Williams-Barnett could be handed his opportunity to start after two impressive cameos against Crystal Palace and Leeds. “Maybe, maybe,” he said on Friday. It turned out that the decision was actually taken last week, although the absence of Sandro Tonali due to illness forced Spurs into a reshuffle in midfield as Mateus Fernandes was handed the holding role.

Solanke has struggled to fill the void left by Kane since joining from Bournemouth in 2024 but looked in determined mood and he was inches wide with a swivel and shot from inside the area. A driving run from Williams-Barnett had the home supporters off their feet, with Solanke again going close from the resulting corner. It then needed a timely block from the teenager to stop Ipswich breaking downfield.

His big moment arrived less than 60 seconds later. Porro’s ball to the back post should have been dealt with by Abdoul Ouattara, only for a moment’s hesitation to allow Williams-Barnett to muscle in front of him and apply the finish with his knee. “He’s one of our own,” sang the Tottenham fans in delight.

Mohammed Kudus was unfortunate to see his superb effort from a free-kick cannon off the inside of the post and away to safety. Williams-Barnett will be disappointed not to have scored his second when he miskicked inside the six-yard box with the goal gaping. James Maddison was then denied by a brilliant save from Christian Walton and Williams-Barnett left the field at half-time looking very pleased with himself as he waved to his family in the crowd.

His smile grew even broader after Darnell Furlong was left bamboozled by a direct run down the left flank before the youngster delivered the ball on a plate for Solanke to score his first goal here since March. The defeat could have been worse for Ipswich had it not been for Walton, and O’Neil will know they are in danger of being sucked into trouble if this winless run continues. There are no such concerns for Tottenham these days. Thanks to Williams-Barnett, their future looks much brighter than a few weeks ago.

Sports.title: Scott McTominay and girlfriend Cam Reading announce pregnancy: Ex-Man United star celebrates 'precious gift' months after having heart surgery
Sports.content:
Scott McTominay and girlfriend Cam Reading announce pregnancy: Ex-Man United star celebrates 'precious gift' months after having heart surgery

Napoli star Scott McTominay and his girlfriend Cam Reading have announced they're expecting their first child together.

The couple shared a joint post on Instagram with one picture of them holding up an ultrasound image, another of Reading reclining in a bikini and a third of the pregnancy test itself.

They revealed the news on the same day McTominay broke Napoli's three-game losing streak, scoring the winner in a 1-0 victory over Torino.

The couple wrote: 'The most precious gift, a lifetime of love.' McTominay, 29, and Reading have settled into life in Italy after he joined from Man United and revived his career, winning the Scudetto and earning Player of the Year honours.

It remains to be seen whether the baby will be born in Italy or back in the UK but the couple were overjoyed at sharing their happy news.

It is not exactly clear when McTominay and Reading first crossed paths but they have at least been together since the summer of 2023, when they were pictured on a boat trip in Greece.

Cam Reading and Scott McTominay shared the news that they're expecting a baby

Reading posted this picture of her bump on her Instagram page and wrote of a 'precious gift'

Reading, a director at asset management firm Fortress Capital partners, has seen her personal celebrity skyrocket in that time, zooming up from 10,000 Instagram followers to over 90,000.

According to La Repubblica, they have moved into a house by Lago Patria, a coastal lake near the suburb of Giugliano.

There, McTominay can be by the seaside quickly after popping out of his door and is only around a 20-minute drive from Napoli's training centre.

The couple regularly share photos from their new life together in Italy and McTominay is adored by fans having repeatedly delivered in big moments, none more so than on the final day of the 2024-25 season when an acrobatic strike put Napoli ahead as they clinched the title over Inter Milan.

This season has been less straightforward for McTominay. The Scotland international underwent heart surgery after being diagnosed with 'a mild benign arrhythmia', which is an abnormal or irregular heart rhythm deemed non-serious and posing no significant risk to overall health.

Before the surgery, the British Heart Foundation explained that the procedure McTominay was having would see heat or cold energy used to create tiny scars in the heart to block faulty signals and restore a typical heartbeat.

The procedure took place at the start of September in Manchester, and he was initially supposed to be on the sidelines for two weeks before returning to training.

But he was ruled out of Scotland action during the international break and is now back on the grass with Napoli, scoring the winner against Torino on Saturday.

McTominay and Reading also posted this snap of the ultrasound and positive test

The midfielder scored the winner on Saturday for Napoli against Torino

He has now scored 33 goals in 92 matches across all competitions with the Partenopei and remains one of Serie A's leading lights.

The Italian press gushed over his contribution on Saturday, with Corriere dello Sport writing: 'He played with fire in his belly.

'Three shots in the opening 16 minutes; seven in total—three on target— and a decisive goal (his fourth against Torino, his favourite Serie A opponent, along with Inter), plus the charisma of a leader.'

Sports.title: Ange Postecoglou snaps at reporter as he defends Sadio Mane for missing match to be at birth of child - after defeat which saw Cristiano Ronaldo fail to score a penalty
Sports.content:
Footage has emerged of Ange Postecoglou locked in a fiery exchange with a reporter after Al-Nassr's defeat to Al-Ahli - after he questioned Sadio Mane's commitment to the Saudi Pro League club. The side sits third in the league standings, but were humbled in the 3-1 loss to their fourth-placed rivals on the road. Mane was not named in the matchday squad despite registering two assists in the club's last outing, a 6-2 victory against Asian Champions League opponents Pakhtakor FC. One Saudi journalist is believed to have used Mane's absence to suggest that he was not sufficiently engaged with Al-Nassr's campaign this season. But even the suggestion was enough to incense the former Tottenham head coach, who immediately asked if the journalist was 'a father?' 'Do you have children?' he queried, with the journalist responding that he did not. Ange Postecoglou snapped at the journalist who questioned the strength of Sadio Mane's commitment to Al-Nassr The Senegal forward missed the match as he and his wife await the birth of their second child 'That's probably why you ask the question,' Postecoglou hit back. 'Because when you do, you'll realise it's the most important thing, the biggest blessing you can have. '(Mane) is with his wife while she is having a baby, OK? Nothing is more important in life. 'Yes, he had my permission, my blessing, and Sadio Mane is one of the best people in this world, mate. 'Never question him or his commitment to this football club.' Mane welcomed his first child with wife Aisha Timba last year, after marrying the then-18-year-old in January 2024. In his first match following the happy news, Mane scored and celebrated by rocking an imaginary baby in his arms. Postecoglou and Mane have only worked with one another since the beginning of the season, but appear to have formed a strong bond with Mane a frequent starter in the Riyadh-based starting XI. The Antipodean manager joined the club following a spell without work after his ignominious departure from Nottingham Forest last season. Since arriving in the Gulf state, Postecoglou has overseen a strong domestic campaign, with Al-Nassr registering just one previous defeat this season, against Al-Ettifaq. But Friday's loss may have stung all the more after Al-Nassr initially led against their bitter rivals. Cristiano Ronaldo had opened the scoring for the visitors on Friday evening in Jeddah, but missed a penalty striking the far post and failed to double his side's lead. Instead, it was Ivan Toney who was nerveless from the spot as he netted to put Al-Ahli 2-1 up in the 71st minute, with Roger Ibanez providing the winner four minutes later.
