Under the dry-season farming programme, the bank is working with the All-Farmers Association of Nigeria to develop a pipeline targeting 400,000 farmers for the 2026 farming cycle.

The initiative covers 120,000 hectares of wheat cultivation and an additional 300,000 hectares for rice, maize, sorghum, millet, cassava and soybeans.

Similarly, the Nigeria Ginger Recovery Programme has supported 3,200 farmers in Kachia, Kaduna State, with blight-free seeds and recovered more than 9,000 bags for multiplication. The programme is also planning an expansion across 20,000 hectares in 16 states.

The bank is further targeting at least 50,000 women nationwide through insured cooperative production financing at nine per cent, in partnership with the Federal Ministries of Women Affairs and Agriculture.

On agricultural mechanisation, the council said 1,571 tractors had been deployed to 23 states under the Renewed Hope National Agricultural Mechanisation Programme.

The tractors are expected to facilitate the mechanisation of 1.2 million hectares of farmland, with farming communities accessing the equipment through qualified Mechanisation Service Providers.

It also disclosed that a ₦385 billion productive-use-of-electricity programme would provide 44,000 electric cargo tricycles and 100,000 solar-powered irrigation pumps, targeting 500,000 farming families.

The council said the various interventions reflected the Tinubu administration’s commitment to making agriculture a major driver of economic growth, food security and job creation.

World.title: Miss Grand International winner Jihan Dimack visits Lagos
World.content:
Queen Jihan Dimack, the first African woman to win the Miss Grand International Crown, visited Lagos from Wednesday to Sunday for Experience Lagos 2026, a campaign promoting tourism, cultural exchange, and humanitarian work.

The Tanzanian queen was accompanied by Sir Nawat Itsaragrisil, president of Miss Grand International, an international beauty pageant founded in Thailand in 2013.

Miss Grand International has grown into a global competition with country-level franchises and contestants from around the world, and is among the prominent pageants on the international circuit.

The visit was part of a programme conceived by Tomi Salami, president of the Aurora International Charity Foundation (AICF), which first hosted Ms Dimack in Nigeria in 2018.

Ms Salami described the visit as a full-circle moment, saying the foundation had welcomed Ms Dimack to participate in its humanitarian activities eight years before her historic win.

“Eight years ago, in 2018, the Aurora International Charity Foundation welcomed Jihan to Nigeria to participate in our humanitarian activities,” she said at the World Press Conference on 19 November. “At the time, none of us could have imagined that eight years later, she would return to us having made history on the global stage.”

Ms Dimack won the Miss Grand International crown on 10 October 2026. Her campaign for the title drew more than 116 million comments on a single Instagram post, according to Tanzanian newspaper The Citizen.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Highlights

The visit featured a grand welcome, the press presentation, cultural heritage experiences and engagements with prominent personalities.

Organisers also planned visits to the John Randle Centre for Yoruba Culture and History and Lagos waterfront attractions, as well as collaborations with Nigerian fashion and beauty creatives for editorial features.

Ms Salami said the campaign was designed to present Lagos as more than the setting for an international visit, highlighting its heritage, hospitality, creative talent and commercial opportunities.

She said: “Lagos is not merely the location of this campaign. Lagos is a central part of the story we are telling the world,” she said. “A city of extraordinary energy, creativity, enterprise, cultural richness and ambition.”

She added that the campaign also aligned with areas identified in the Lagos State Government’s THEMES+ agenda, including tourism, cultural heritage, entertainment and youth opportunity. Organisers said Experience Lagos 2026 would provide an independent platform to promote the state’s tourism and creative economy to international audiences.

ALSO READ: US visa rule threatens African contestants at Miss Universe 2026

A major component of the visit was AICF’s Inspire Africa Education and Empowerment Initiative, which aims to reach 5,000 young Lagosians through mentorship, education support, empowerment opportunities and essential resources, including personal-care dignity kits.

Ms Salami said the initiative was intended to help young people see their potential in Ms Dimack’s achievement.

“If a young African girl can rise to become a history-making global queen, then somewhere in our classrooms today could be the next world leader, innovator, humanitarian or global icon,” she said.

AICF said its education, welfare, empowerment and health programmes have reached more than 50,000 people across Nigeria.

World.title: New book details how Tinubu’s ‘it is my turn’ outburst jolted Buhari
World.content:
Simon Kolawole, a veteran Nigerian journalist and founder of TheCable, has documented how President Bola Tinubu emerged as the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC)’s presidential candidate in 2023 and went on to win the election.

The book draws on Mr Kolawole’s interactions with political insiders and personal observations to explain the political manoeuvres, rivalries and strategic decisions that shaped the APC’s presidential primary, including Mr Tinubu’s declaration that it was his turn to succeed the then President Muhammadu Buhari.

The book, titled ‘Winning Formula: The Inside Story of Nigeria’s 2023 Presidential Election,’ will go on sale on 23 November, according to a statement on Friday by its publishers, Cable Books.

The book offers an account of how Mr Tinubu outmanoeuvred his political rivals and navigated his relationship with the late Mr Buhari, who was completing his second term at the time.

It also examines how Atiku Abubakar and Nyesom Wike, both seeking the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP)’s presidential ticket, undermined each other’s ambitions, and how Peter Obi and the Obidient Movement emerged as major forces in Nigeria’s political landscape.

The 2023 presidential election was one of the most fiercely contested polls in Nigeria’s democratic history.

Traditionally, outgoing Nigerian presidents have wielded considerable influence over the emergence of their successors, often backing preferred candidates within their political parties.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, as the Buhari administration neared its end, the former president did not openly endorse any presidential aspirant. Instead, he urged them to reach a consensus on a candidate.

At the time, there were speculations that Mr Buhari favoured a northern candidate to succeed him.

Among the prominent APC presidential aspirants were Mr Tinubu; Yemi Osinbajo, who was Mr Buhari’s deputy; the then Minister of Transportation, Rotimi Amaechi; the then Senate President, Ahmed Lawan, and the then Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Godwin Emefiele.

Others were former governors of Ogun and Akwa Ibom states, Ibikunle Amosun and Godswill Akpabio, respectively. Mr Akpabio is now the Senate President.

During the contest, Mr Tinubu, who was among the oldest aspirants, publicly declared that it was his turn to become president, arguing that he had played a significant role in Mr Buhari’s emergence as president, Mr Osinbajo’s selection as vice president, and the emergence of some APC governors, including Dapo Abiodun of Ogun State.

At a gathering with APC delegates in Abeokuta, the Ogun State capital, Mr Tinubu presented himself as the most qualified candidate to represent the party in the presidential election, referencing his political experience and contributions to the party.

His declaration became widely known as the ‘Emilokan’ (It is my turn) statement.

“It is my time, I’m educated, I’m experienced. I have been serving you for a long time; bring me the presidency, bring it, it is my turn.

“When Atiku was being flogged out of PDP by Obasanjo, he ran to me for help; I left the ticket for him. Nuhu Ribadu came to me, and I backed him,” he said at the time.

He also recounted how he helped Mr Buhari secure the presidency after three unsuccessful attempts.

“If not for me that stood behind Buhari, he wouldn’t have become the president. He (Buhari) tried the first time; he failed. The second time, he failed. The third time, he failed. He even wept on national television and vowed never to contest again, but I went to meet him in Kaduna and told him he would run again. ‘I will stand by you, and you will win, but you must not joke with Yorubas and he agreed.’

“Since he became the president, I have never got ministerial slots; I didn’t collect any contract, I have never begged for anything from him, it is the turn of Yoruba, it is my turn.”

The declaration was widely interpreted as a direct challenge to a sitting president, with some political observers predicting that Mr Buhari would be angered by the remarks and that Mr Tinubu could face consequences within the party.

The book, however, presents a different account of what followed. It suggests that although Mr Tinubu’s declaration was a risky political move, it ultimately worked in his favour rather than undermining his presidential ambition.

According to the book, rather than simply dismissing the statement, Mr Buhari was uncomfortable with the suggestion that he had betrayed a gentleman’s agreement with Mr Tinubu.

The book also provides insider accounts of the role Buhari’s wife, Aisha, played during the period. It says she supported Mr Tinubu’s presidential ambition and encouraged him to sustain his campaign.

According to the account, the encouragement Mr Tinubu received from the former first lady helped allay his concerns and strengthen his resolve to continue pursuing the APC ticket.

World.title: ALBUM REVIEW: Rema tries everything on ‘E-Mortal Boy’, but not everything works
World.content:
Established artistes such as Rema often face pressure to surpass the success of their previous releases with every new project. For the singer, whose career spans nearly eight years, that expectation is heightened by his growing international profile, particularly after the Grammy nomination of his 2024 album, HEIS, at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025, which further reinforced his status as one of Nigeria’s leading music exports. But does his new work ‘E-Mortal Boy’ match up to the challenge?

Rema’s E-Mortal Boy is a seven-track, roughly 22-minute extended play (EP). An Extended Play, or EP, is a musical release with more tracks than a single but fewer tracks and a shorter runtime than a full-length studio album, also called an LP, or Long Play. Released on 20 November 2026, the EP arrives as Rema’s first extended project since Ravage (2023) and his first major project following HEIS (2024).

Featuring a mix of dancehall, rumba, R&B, electronic music, grunge, and house influences, the project opens with the much-anticipated collaboration with Wizkid, ‘Feel Alright’, and incorporates the previously released ‘TEA’ and ‘Oh No’.

Track-by-track

Feel Alright (feat. Wizkid)

Opening E-Mortal Boy with ‘Feel Alright’, featuring Wizkid, is a musically strategic move that endears listeners to the EP. The song is the first official collaboration between the two Afrobeats stars, and they have a natural, appealing chemistry, as though they come from different generations of artists; they both deliver a beautifully complementary single. Feel Alright settles into a comfortable R&B-inflected groove. It is pleasant, polished and entertaining, but it lacks the dramatic lift that could have made it an unforgettable opening statement.

2. Oh No

Previously released ahead of the EP, ‘Oh No’ is one of the project’s more restrained compositions. Produced with Jamaican hitmaker Rvssian’s involvement, the song relies on delicate percussion and a hypnotic rhythm that gives Rema room to explore the emotional uncertainties of a relationship. It is a relatively modest composition, but its restraint works in its favour. ‘Oh No’ is a reminder that Rema’s versatility is not necessarily dependent on sound extravagance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

3. Velvet

‘Velvet’ is among the EP’s enjoyable releases, blending rumba-inspired drums, slick guitar riffs, and a subtle trap-inflected bounce into a composition that feels both familiar and refreshing. What makes Velvet particularly interesting is how effortlessly Rema absorbs influences beyond conventional Afrobeats arrangements. The rumba-inspired elements are not merely decorative; they contribute meaningfully to the song’s character and progression.

4. TANZANIA (feat. BNYX)

On TANZANIA, Rema ventures into more unconventional territory, with producer BNYX giving the song an energetic vibe. It is an adventurous track and one of the clearest examples of Rema’s willingness to explore sounds that don’t necessarily conform to his audience’s expectations.

TANZANIA is intriguing for what it attempts, even if it is not entirely persuasive in what it achieves.

5. TEA

If E-Mortal Boy has a track that most convincingly bridges Rema’s experimental instincts and his commercial appeal, it is ‘TEA ‘. The song blends dancehall-inspired rhythms with glossy pop arrangements and electronic flourishes, creating an infectious composition that feels immediately accessible without being entirely predictable. Its rhythmic foundation is lively, while Rema’s delivery is assured and playful, riding the beat with the confidence of an artist comfortable in his sonic environment. It is the EP’s standout track and perhaps the clearest demonstration of the balance Rema could have achieved across the project: adventurous enough to be interesting, but focused enough to leave a lasting impression.

6. SUGA (feat. Theodora)

‘SUGA’ takes the EP into rougher territory, drawing on grunge-inspired textures and a more abrasive vocal approach. Featuring French-Congolese singer Theodora, the track introduces a tonal shift that feels noticeably different from the project’s predominantly melodic, rhythm-driven compositions. It has merit, but it is one of the less convincing entries on the project.

7. Bang Bang

The closing track, Bang Bang, featuring producer London, also known as Thisizlondon, and Nigerian-American singer Kah-Lo, reinforces Rema’s interest in exploring electronic music beyond conventional Afrobeats.

Review

Released just ahead of Detty December, a period when dance music and party anthems dominate the Nigerian music scene, ‘E-Mortal Boy’ appears strategically positioned to capture the festive mood. However, the seven-track EP offers only five previously unheard songs, as ‘Oh No’ and ‘TEA’ had already been released as singles. For an artist of Rema’s stature, the decision to serve fans an EP when many had anticipated a full-length album feels somewhat underwhelming, particularly with the latter now scheduled for 2027.

The EP’s greatest strength is undoubtedly its sound. Rema remains unwilling to be confined to a single musical identity, moving between dancehall, rumba, R&B, electronic music and grunge. This willingness to explore unfamiliar territories demonstrates an artist who is still curious about his craft and conscious of the need to evolve beyond the formula that established him.

Yet a larger question remains about the direction of this experimentation. As Afrobeats continues to command international attention, some argue that Nigerian artistes must do more than absorb and reinterpret foreign influences. Developing distinctive indigenous sounds and incorporating them into contemporary production should remain an important part of the country’s musical export. Rema’s experimentation is welcome, but the challenge is to ensure his search for musical identity doesn’t come at the expense of the cultural distinctiveness that makes Nigerian music compelling in the first place.

More immediately, the EP struggles with cohesion. Its genre-hopping, while ambitious, occasionally feels less like a deliberate musical journey and more like a series of disconnected experiments competing for attention. The transitions do not always establish a convincing relationship between the tracks, leaving the project without a sufficiently distinctive sonic identity. Experimentation, after all, is not necessarily innovation; the ability to bring disparate influences together into a compelling body of work is what separates adventurous music from an inconsistent collection of ideas. ‘SUGA’, in particular, struggles to justify its place and adds little to the project’s overall appeal.

The songwriting presents another weakness. Much of the EP revisits familiar territory: romance, sexual desire and emotional uncertainty. These are enduring subjects in popular music, but Rema’s treatment of them rarely offers the lyrical depth, compelling storytelling or fresh perspective that could make the songs particularly memorable. For an artiste with his creative range, the writing sometimes feels less adventurous than the production.

Consequently, the instrumentation, rhythm and sonic textures often do more work than the lyrics. ‘TEA’ emerges as the EP’s strongest composition, successfully reconciling its competing impulses of experimentation and accessibility. While ‘Feel Alright’ benefits from the cultural weight of the Rema-Wizkid collaboration, and ‘Velvet’ offers a more elegant fusion of musical influences, ‘TEA’ is where Rema’s curiosity translates most convincingly into a memorable listening experience.

Ultimately, ‘E-Mortal Boy’ is an ambitious but uneven offering. It confirms Rema’s musical ingenuity and willingness to take creative risks, but also exposes the limitations of experimentation without sufficient cohesion or lyrical substance. Its strongest moments suggest an artiste still capable of surprising his audience, while its weaker tracks raise questions about whether every new direction is worth pursuing.

The EP is therefore more convincing as a preview of Rema’s evolving musical instincts than as a fully realised body of work. There are enough highlights, particularly ‘TEA’ and ‘Velvet’, to make it worth revisiting. But beyond its party-ready moments and experimental ambitions, ‘E-Mortal Boy’ leaves an important question unanswered: is Rema building towards a more distinctive musical identity, or does this EP signal the kind of musical evolution that could strengthen his chances of earning further global recognition and possibly clinching a Grammy win in the near future? For an EP expected to set the tone for his 2027 album, that distinction matters.

Verdict: 7/10

E-Mortal Boy is streaming on Spotify and across all platforms

World.title: Residents lament another increase in cooking gas prices
World.content:
Cooking gas prices have risen again in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), selling for between N1,600 and N2,000 per kg, further straining household budgets.

Many residents, who spoke with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Abuja on Sunday, said the latest increase had made it increasingly difficult to afford regular refills.

They said the development had forced some households to ration gas or combine its use with traditional cooking fuels, such as charcoal stoves, as they struggle to cope with the rising cost.

NAN reports that cooking gas, also known as Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG), currently sells for between N1,600 and N2,000 per kg across the FCT, depending on the location and retail outlet.

At the prevailing prices, refilling a 5kg cylinder costs between N8,000 and N10,000, while a 12.5kg cylinder costs between N20,000 and N25,000.

The latest increase represents another setback for households already struggling with the rising cost of living, particularly as cooking gas remains an essential domestic commodity.

Obi Nwosu, a resident of Gudu, said the rising cost of cooking gas had forced her to abandon the practice of filling her cylinder, opting instead to buy smaller quantities depending on the money available to her.

“Refilling my cylinder at N24,000 is no longer possible, especially with the rising costs of transportation and food.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I have to prioritise my expenses, so I only buy the quantity I can afford whenever my gas runs out,” she said.

Maimuna Idris, a resident of Lugbe, said she had resorted to using a charcoal stove alongside cooking gas to reduce her expenditure on fuel.

“For some time now, the price of cooking gas has continued to increase, making it difficult for me to fill my cylinder.

“I had to buy a charcoal stove and use it to prepare meals that require longer cooking time, such as beans, as well as boil water, because relying solely on cooking gas is no longer sustainable,” she said.

Asuquo Morgan, a resident of Karu, said he had reduced the quantity of cooking gas he purchased to cope with the rising cost.

“My income has not increased, but the prices of cooking gas and other essential commodities keep rising.

“One has to find a way to survive, and that means buying gas in smaller quantities; otherwise, some households may run into financial difficulties.

“The government needs to find a lasting solution to the rising cost of cooking gas.

“Many households depend on it for cooking, and if the price continues to increase, people may be forced to return to using firewood,” he said.

Bidemi Ajayi, a resident of Lokogoma, said the latest price increase had further worsened her financial situation, putting additional pressure on her household budget.

“Everything now requires careful calculation, so I buy gas in small quantities, like 5kg, and manage it to enable me to meet other household needs, which has also not been easy.

“We appeal to the government to ensure that cooking gas remains affordable. The prices of everything cannot continue to increase while many people are struggling to afford even one meal a day,” she said.

NAN recalls that in October, cooking gas prices ranged between N1,360 and N1,700 per kg in the FCT.

The development followed an earlier increase reported in September when cooking gas sold for between N1,450 and N2,000 per kg in parts of the FCT after months of declining and relatively stable prices.

NAN reports that industry experts have previously attributed the rising cost of cooking gas to supply disruptions, higher logistics and transportation costs, foreign exchange volatility and developments in the international energy market.

The Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) had also identified inadequate domestic supply, low import volumes, poor distribution infrastructure and logistics challenges as some of the factors contributing to the increase in LPG prices.

NAN further recalls that on 22 June, the federal government directed the NMDPRA and other relevant agencies to intensify surveillance and clamp down on marketers involved in hoarding and diversion of LPG.

The directive was issued by the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekperikpe Ekpo, during an emergency stakeholders’ engagement on rising cooking gas prices.

Mr Ekpo said the government remained committed to increasing domestic supply, reducing dependence on imports and ensuring that locally produced LPG was prioritised for domestic consumption.

(NAN)

World.title: MOVIE REVIEW: Sam Dede returns, but nostalgia cannot carry ‘Issakaba’ alone
World.content:
Nollywood’s growing appetite for reviving its classics has produced some notable returns to the big screen, with varying degrees of commercial success and artistic ambition. In 2026, The Return of Omotara Johnson and Agbara Nla: The Return joined the growing list of films revisiting familiar stories, characters and memories. While Agbara Nla has distinguished itself with an impressive box-office performance, the return of Issakaba, one of Nollywood’s most recognisable crime-action franchises, arrives with a different but equally demanding burden: proving that nostalgia can still translate into compelling narrative.

Released in 2001, Issakaba became a cult favourite during Nollywood’s home-video era, combining crime, supernatural mythology, communal resistance and action in a story inspired by the activities of the Bakassi Boys. This vigilante group emerged in southeastern Nigeria in the late 1990s. Its return, therefore, attempts to reintroduce an old mythology to an audience whose viewing habits, expectations, and perception of Nollywood have changed considerably.

Directed by Lancelot Oduwa Imasuen, who helmed the original, Issakaba: The Return brings back Sam Dede as Ebube, the formidable leader of the vigilante group, more than two decades after his character became a major fixture in his Nollywood career and earned him the moniker Ebube.

The question, however, is whether the film’s contemporary relevance, star power and familiarity with the original material are sufficient to justify another chapter, or whether the filmmakers have mistaken the audience’s affection for the original for an appetite for its continuation.

Issakaba: What audiences remember

Inspired by true-life events, it depicted the Bakassi Boys, a community vigilante group combating crimes like armed robbery and murder that struck fear into the hearts of the people.

It also depicted the battle against the late Eddy Nawgu, a sorcerer who terrorised the people of the Nawgu community in Anambra State.

The plot revolved around the Issakaba Boys, led by Ebube (Sam Dede), who had to fight armed robbers terrorising their society. The armed robbers possessed mystical powers in their robberies. As a result, Ebube and his team of Issakaba boys also gained abilities that enabled them to fight crime. The movie was full of action, horror, and drama.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The five-part film featured Nollywood actors like Sam Dede, Chiwetalu Agu, Pete Eneh, Amaechi Muonagor, Susan Obi, Mike Ogundu, and John Okafor.

The movie also featured Andy Chukwu, Zulu Adigwe, Diewait Ikpechukwu, Remmy Ohajianya, Emeka Nwafor, Tom Njemanze, Uche Odoputa, and Emeka Ani.

Several original cast members, including Pete Eneh, Amaechi Muonagor, John Okafor, and Zulu Adigwe, have since died.

Isakaba: The Return

Issakaba: The Return is set in Amangwa, where criminal activity has overwhelmed the community and exposed the inadequacies of conventional security agencies.

The film opens with a bank robbery that ends in tragedy for Obi, who visits the bank to withdraw money his brother, Ebube, sent him. The robbery, led by Somtom and his gang, turns fatal, and Obi is killed. His wife, watching the incident unfold on television from the hospital after giving birth, dies in the aftermath of the tragedy.

The deaths leave their newborn child orphaned, prompting Ebube to confront the consequences of the tragedy. However, the hospital’s demand for payment amid the family’s grief becomes another source of frustration, and Ebube abandons the child at the facility.

Alex, Obi’s surviving son, later moves in with Ebube but struggles to come to terms with his father’s death. His determination to avenge the tragedy introduces a familiar cycle of grief, anger, and retribution into the film’s narrative.

Meanwhile, Somtom and his elder brother Abuchi lead the criminal network that terrorises the community through robbery, kidnapping and other violent crimes. Their activities, particularly around the governor’s village, expose the state’s helplessness and the growing frustration with the police.

The film also introduces Musa, a police divisional officer whose determination to apprehend the criminals puts his family in danger. As the investigation intensifies, his wife is forced to flee for her safety, while Musa is eventually killed.

As the situation spirals out of control, the governor turns to the traditional ruler for help bringing back the Issakaba, whose reputation as a formidable crime-fighting force precedes them.

But Ebube has moved on. Now living a relatively quiet life as a shoemaker in the market, he is reluctant to return to the violence, danger, and spiritual burden associated with his former identity.

Review

The most compelling question Issakaba: The Return raises is whether the story is genuinely necessary, beyond the commercial appeal of resurrecting a familiar Nollywood franchise.

The film’s premise is undeniably contemporary. Nigeria’s persistent insecurity, kidnapping, armed violence, and public frustration with the effectiveness of security institutions provide a familiar backdrop for the story. The filmmakers understand that the conditions that made the original Issakaba appealing have not entirely disappeared.

But relevance alone does not make a compelling film. The sequel’s attempt to connect contemporary insecurity with the original’s supernatural crime-fighting mythology occasionally feels like an extension of the old formula rather than a meaningful evolution.

The criminal threat is expanded, the stakes are raised, and the circumstances surrounding Ebube’s return are made more tragic. Yet the central dramatic proposition remains largely unchanged: a society overwhelmed by crime turns to a powerful alternative force to restore order.

One thing that clearly stands out is the connection between the old and original story and the sequel. Most of the original cast made their way to the sequel, and that continuation is intriguing.

At 2 hours and 26 minutes, the film demands considerable patience. While its extended runtime lets the story establish the criminal network, the community’s desperation, and Ebube’s reluctance, it also exposes weaknesses in pacing and narrative economy. Some sequences feel unnecessarily long, and the film occasionally struggles to maintain momentum in its central conflict. The action and supernatural elements are recognisable, but their repetition sometimes diminishes their impact.

The production’s ambition to deliver a more contemporary action spectacle is evident, but the technical execution doesn’t consistently match the scale of that ambition. The film occasionally relies on familiar action conventions without refining them enough, and some dramatic moments could have benefited from tighter editing and a better fight stunt. Reviving a home-video classic for the cinema isn’t simply about making it bigger. It is about making it more compelling, more coherent, and more cinematic.

Unlike a revival that successfully transforms nostalgia into a fresh cinematic experience, Issakaba: The Return sometimes appears content to remind audiences of the original rather than convincingly demonstrate what a new chapter can accomplish.

A comparison worth making

The comparison with Agbara Nla: The Return is almost unavoidable, particularly because both films draw from Nollywood’s classic history and seek to reintroduce familiar stories to a contemporary audience.

However, the two films approach nostalgia differently. Agbara Nla returns to a spiritual-warfare narrative deeply rooted in the Christian filmmaking tradition of Mount Zion. Its commercial appeal is tied not only to nostalgia for the 1993 original but also to the familiarity of its spiritual themes, the recognition of its characters, and the chance to revisit a story that has remained central to the Christian audience.

The film’s impressive box-office performance suggests that nostalgia, when supported by a strong audience connection, an identifiable appeal and an effective campaign, can translate into considerable commercial success.

Issakaba: The Return has a similarly recognisable property, an established protagonist, and an action genre that could appeal to a broader audience. It also benefits from Sam Dede’s continued recognition, whose portrayal of Ebube remains one of the defining elements of the original franchise.

But a franchise’s memory does not automatically guarantee a successful revival. Where Agbara Nla benefited from the familiarity of its Christian audience and the enduring appeal of its spiritual warfare narrative, Issakaba must navigate a more complicated relationship between nostalgia, crime, violence, supernatural mythology, and contemporary action filmmaking. Its audience may remember the original fondly, but that memory also creates expectations about the intensity, storytelling and authenticity of the experience.

The question is not whether Issakaba can replicate Agbara Nla’s box-office success, but whether it has built a compelling enough cinematic experience to sustain excitement beyond the nostalgia-driven opening.

The sequel’s commercial prospects may be helped by its title recognition, the return of Sam Dede, and the publicity surrounding its revival. However, Agbara Nla’s success should not be treated as a predictable template. The films have different audiences, themes, genres and marketing opportunities.

For Issakaba, a successful cinematic run would require more than reminding audiences of what they watched two decades agoades ago. It would require convincing them that this new story is worth the cost of a cinema ticket.

It may attract audiences who grew up with Ebube and the Issakaba Boys. Still, whether it can achieve the kind of box-office feat associated with Agbara Nla: The Return remains a different question. Agbara Nla has demonstrated that a Nollywood classic can return to the cinema and command significant commercial attention. Issakaba must now prove that its own legacy can generate more than sentimental curiosity.

Sam Dede and the weight of the legend

Sam Dede remains the film’s most important casting decision. His return as Ebube gives the sequel an emotional anchor that would have been hard to replicate with a new protagonist.

The character’s transition from a feared vigilante to a man who has embraced a quieter existence allows Dede to portray a different dimension of Ebube. Rather than relying entirely on the physicality and authority of the original, the sequel tries to present a man burdened by the memories and consequences of his former life.

The supporting cast adds familiarity and contemporary appeal, with the return of some familiar faces and the inclusion of newer actors like Nosa Rex, Regina Daniels, Phyna, and Ibrahim Yekini. However, the ensemble does not always feel as cohesive as the film’s premise demands. The film’s ambition to bridge Nollywood’s older generation and its contemporary audience is understandable, but star recognition cannot substitute for character development.

Could the story have been told better? Of course, the movie itself gives enough opportunity for growth and expansion. Was this return a bad attempt? Certainly not, but it is a good example that remaking Nollywood classics is more than bringing back the old cast and adding a few new faces.

Verdict: 6/10

World.title: Has the Nigerian Bar Association misplaced its umbrage?, By Chidi Anselm Odinkalu
World.content:
In announcing the referral to the LPDC, the NBA president dwells on the obligations of lawyers in Nigeria “to maintain high standards of professional conduct.” Kalu Kalu was not in court when he spoke the words complained of. He was neither lawyer nor litigant in the case. The referral by the NBA, therefore, invites scrutiny of the association’s record in censuring its members for what they do outside the court. It’s a squalid record.

“Courts exist to dispense justice, not to demand respect from litigants as the price of admission.” – David Pannick, Judges, 135 (1987)

The announcement by the president of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) referring senior lawyer, Kalu Kalu, to the Legal Practitioners’ Disciplinary Committee (LPDC) for using the expression “coconut judge” in relation to a judge, has been predictably controversial. Kalu Kalu invented that expression in response, ostensibly, to the latest controversial judgment handed down by le juge du moment in Nigeria, Peter Lifu.

The reactions to the intervention by the NBA president fall broadly into three categories. Her supporters underscore a duty of the lawyer to “always treat the court with respect, dignity and honour.” There are some, however, who fear that the NBA president chose the wrong case to make her point. Stephen Kola Balogun, for instance, points out that the “charge cannot be reasonably sustained, for three reasons: ambiguity, context, and perception.” Others accuse the NBA president of hurtling under the cover of law into a cauldron of party politics.

In announcing the referral to the LPDC, the NBA president dwells on the obligations of lawyers in Nigeria “to maintain high standards of professional conduct.” Kalu Kalu was not in court when he spoke the words complained of. He was neither lawyer nor litigant in the case. The referral by the NBA, therefore, invites scrutiny of the association’s record in censuring its members for what they do outside the court. It’s a squalid record.

Consider the case of Alhaji Rauph Omobolaji Gaji. Alhaji Rauph was a senior lawyer when, on 3 December 1972, at his home in Kaduna, he fatally assaulted his secretary, Miss Cordelia Ego Ejiofor. As life seeped out of her, Alhaji Rauph drove more than 16 kilometres to the outskirts of the city where, along Kachia Road, he disposed of Cordelia’s body.

The police recovered only parts of the remains after Alhaji Rauph led them to the point where he dumped her. On 23 May 1975, the Supreme Court unanimously affirmed his conviction for culpable homicide not punishable with death (manslaughter), with a sentence of 12 years in prison.

Nigeria law treats Alhaji Rauph’s case as a classic on circumstantial evidence, but the case is significant for much more. Lawyers obviously do not attend law school to acquire qualifications in perpetrating homicide or grievous bodily harm, or in the disposal of human remains. It is difficult to see how a person convicted of such heinous crime can remain a lawyer. If anything was done, however, to disbar or strike Alhaji Rauph from the roll of lawyers in Nigeria, there appears to be no public record of it.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Tafa Balogun was a senior lawyer and former Inspector-General of the Nigeria Police Force, when he pleaded guilty in 2005 to eight counts of laundering and plundering over ₦13 billion in public funds. The Federal High Court convicted and sentenced him to six months in prison. He also forfeited over $150 million-worth of stolen cash and property, but Mr Balogun happily remained on the roll of lawyers until his death in 2022.

There was the case of Kunle Kalejaiye, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria who was found to have been involved in corrupt relations with a judge, Thomas Naron, in an election petition. In 2013, Thomas Naron lost his job. Six years later, the Supreme Court interposed a confounding technicality to ensure Mr Kalejaiye kept his.

In 2021, the same court similarly decided that there should be no consequences in the case of Dr Joseph Nwobike (SAN), whose specialty was “inducing court registrars to ensure that his cases were assigned to his preferred judges so he could obtain favourable judgments.” The NBA did nothing.

On 10 December 2021, the Supreme Court of Nigeria determined that former Attorney-General of the Federation (HAGF), Michael Aondoakaa, “had, by his conduct, undermined and subverted the administration of justice and the independence, authority and integrity of the judiciary” and “ought not to be entrusted with any other public office at all.” The antecedents of this decision were staggering.

In the Uyo Federal Constituency of Akwa Ibom State, Bassey Obot prevailed in primaries conducted in December 2006 by the then ruling party, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), for the right to fly its flag in the election to the House of Representatives in 2007. Some unknown persons contrived to remove Mr Obot’s name from the records of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), substituting him with one Mr Bassey Etim as the PDP candidate.

In December 2007, the Court of Appeal ordered the President of the Court of Appeal to constitute a new tribunal in Uyo to hear Mr Obot’s case. Mr Aondoakaa, then newly installed as the HAGF, wrote to the President of the Court of Appeal (PCA) presuming to instruct him to disobey the order of the Court of Appeal because, he claimed, he was considering a petition from Mr Etim. Unable to contrive a sensible excuse for casualising the court over which he presided, the PCA disregarded Mr Aondoakaa’s importuning.

In April 2008, the Tribunal decided in favour of Mr Obot, ordering INEC to certify him as the winner. The Court of Appeal, the final arbiter then in disputes over elections to parliament, affirmed the tribunal. In separate letters thereafter to the INEC Chairman and to the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Mr Aondoakaa again required them to disregard the Court of Appeal. They complied. Allegations that Mr Aondoakaa issued those letters in exchange for value were not implausible.

On 15 May 2009, Mr Obot, whose victory the HAGF had frustrated, returned to the Federal High Court asking it to declare that Mr Aondoakaa had abused his office and desecrated the third arm. On 1 June 2010, the Federal High Court obliged, lamenting that “the hallowed office of the HAGF has been gradually desecrated and put into disrepute with the likes [of Mr Aondoakaa] being appointed and occupying it. It is meant for learned, eminent members of the Bar and not for political charlatans, jobbers or latter-day praise singers/converts….”

On 3 September 2015, the Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court with the hope that “that office [of HAGF] should never again be occupied by individuals of such poor quality as [Mr Aondoakaa].” The Court went further and invited the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) “to subject [Mr Aondoakaa] to its appropriate disciplinary processes.” Nothing of the sort followed.

When it dismissed Mr Aondoakaa’s appeal, the Supreme Court called him “reprehensible”, “reckless” and “unbecoming of the occupant of such an exalted office.” It accused him of violating Rule 30 of the Rules of Professional Conduct (RPC) in the Legal Profession which requires every lawyer to refrain from doing “any act or conduct….in any manner that may obstruct, delay or adversely affect the administration of justice.” Mr Aondoakaa remains a lawyer.

In July 2026, the Federal High Court ordered the final forfeiture of 48 different items of property valued at over ₦212.8 billion, belonging to or connected with former Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Abubakar Malami. In Malami, the office of the HAGF finally met an appointee arguably of poorer quality than Mike Aondoakaa. The NBA has not yet noticed.

No one should suffer adjectives for honest work, with emphasis on honest; and no person should abide that. When, however, a professional association suddenly discovers umbrage at what its members say and how they say it, but not when its senior-most practitioners kill, steal, plunder the patrimony, and pervert the course of justice, questions are bound to be asked about both its motives and its votives.

Any suggestion in such a system that official institutions alone enjoy a monopoly on scrutiny of judicial conduct misapprehends both the source of judicial authority and the vocation of democracy.

On 20 November, in the spirit of balance, I shared an adulatory piece authored by a faceless group called “Friends of Justice Peter Odo Lifu”. None of those previously concerned about “high professional standards” have complained. The reason is obvious: Viewpoint discrimination can hide under cover of concern for professional standards. That said, the NBA President deserves our thanks for triggering a long overdue debate on the professional priorities of the organisation that she now leads.

Chidi Anselm Odinkalu, a lawyer, teaches at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy and can be reached through [email protected].

World.title: Amnesty International demands probe of Emir of Daura over sexual assault allegations
World.content:
Amnesty International Nigeria has called on the authorities to immediately investigate allegations of sexual assault against the 92-year-old Emir of Daura, Faruk Umar Faruk, following an incident involving a female foreign tourist at his palace in Katsina State.

The human rights organisation made the call in a statement published on its X platform on Sunday.

Amnesty International said viral videos shared by the alleged survivor showed what it described as attempts by the emir to sexually violate the visitor despite her resistance.

The organisation said the tourist alleged that the emir touched her inappropriately during her visit to the Daura Emir’s Palace.

Condemning the alleged conduct, Amnesty International urged the Katsina State Government and the Nigeria Police Force to immediately commence a transparent and independent investigation into the incident.

It specifically called on Governor Dikko Radda and the police to ensure that the emir is held accountable for the alleged attempted rape through a fair trial, while ruling out the death penalty.

“The Nigerian authorities must immediately and effectively investigate strong allegations of sexual assault on a female foreign tourist by the 92-year-old Emir of Daura, Faruk Umar Faruk,” the organisation said.

Amnesty International said the incident presented an opportunity for the authorities to demonstrate that nobody was above the law in Nigeria.

It also expressed concern over what it described as the normalisation of rape and sexual violence in the country, alleging that such offences were frequently committed with impunity.

The organisation urged relevant authorities to ensure that the allegations were thoroughly investigated and that appropriate legal action followed.

World.title: FG orders probe into deadly Bayelsa boat accident
World.content:
HE Adegboyega Oyetola, Minister of Marine &Blue Economy.

By Folarin Kehinde

The Federal Government has ordered an immediate investigation into the boat accident that claimed several lives in Bayelsa State, warning that it would no longer tolerate avoidable safety violations on the nation’s waterways.

The Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, gave the directive to the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA), asking it to investigate the immediate and remote causes of the accident and submit its findings to him.

The mishap occurred on Friday, November 20, in Ukubie, near Oweikorogha Community, Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of Bayelsa State.

In a statement issued on Sunday by his Special Adviser, Dr Bolaji Akinola, Oyetola also directed NIWA to work with relevant government agencies and the Bayelsa State Government to ensure a transparent and comprehensive investigation.

The minister described the loss of lives as worrisome and unacceptable, expressing concern over reports that passengers involved in the accident were not wearing life jackets.

He also raised concerns over the alleged absence of a passenger manifest, stressing that proper documentation of passengers was a critical safety requirement that must be strictly enforced.

“Safety lapses on our waterways are no longer acceptable. The Federal Government will not fold its arms and watch its citizens perish on the waterways. We must get to the root of this tragedy and ensure that those responsible for enforcing safety regulations do their jobs,” he said.

Oyetola recalled that he visited Bayelsa State on May 2, 2025, where he distributed 3,500 life jackets to water transport users as part of efforts to improve safety on the waterways.

He also renewed his call on state governments to gradually phase out wooden boats and replace them with safer and more durable fibreglass or fibre-reinforced plastic vessels, particularly for passenger transportation.

The minister disclosed that he had contacted Bayelsa State Governor, Douye Diri, to commiserate with him, the state government and families of the victims.

He sympathised with the bereaved families and prayed for the repose of the souls of those who died in the accident, while urging stakeholders to work together to prevent a recurrence.

World.title: Otti begins construction of new Umuahia traffic corridor
World.content:
By Steve Oko

Abia State Governor, Dr Alex Otti, has commenced construction of a new road linking Bende Road through the Umuahia Post Office Tower and railway crossing to First Bank/Akanu Ibiam Road, with completion targeted before Christmas.

The project, being executed by the Umuahia Capital Development Authority (UCDA), is designed to provide an alternative traffic corridor, ease congestion around Government House and Isigate, and improve connectivity within the state capital.

The General Manager of UCDA, Engr. Kingsley Agomoh, who conducted journalists round the project site, said the road would allow motorists coming from Bende and Ikot Ekpene roads to connect to Abia Line, Aguiyi Ironsi Boulevard, Abia Express Tower and Onuimo Road without passing through the Government House axis.

He said the project would significantly reduce traffic pressure on major roads, stimulate economic activities and improve the aesthetics of Umuahia.

” If you are coming from Bende Road, you pass through the Post Office Tower, cross the railway station and connect to First Bank, Ridge Club and Abia Line without going through the Government House axis,” Agomoh said.

He explained that the project was part of Otti’s broader urban renewal programme, adding that the governor had also directed the relocation of Umuahia Railway Station to the Nnennaya Oti Bus Terminal.

According to him, the state government has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Nigerian Railway Corporation to facilitate the construction of the access road across the railway corridor.

Agomoh also disclosed that another road linking First Bank to the Keystone, Sterling and FCMB bank areas would be reopened and reconstructed to provide motorists, particularly those coming from the Federal Medical Centre, Umuahia, with a shorter alternative route.

He said the road, which had been encroached upon by adjoining property owners, was being reclaimed to restore access and ease movement within the commercial district.

Describing the railway-crossing road as a signature project of the Otti administration, Agomoh said the governor’s urban renewal drive was repositioning Umuahia for increased economic activities and orderly development.

He urged Abians to support Otti and other Labour Party candidates in the 2027 elections, arguing that continuity would ensure the completion of ongoing infrastructure projects across the state.

World.title: APC challenges NDC over candidates’ eligibility
World.content:
By Hadiza Yusuf

The All Progressives Congress (APC) in Kano State has challenged the New Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) to address questions surrounding the eligibility of its governorship candidate, Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo, and running mate, Mustapha Rabiu Kwankwaso, before accusing the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) of electoral irregularities.

The APC said political parties should ensure that their candidates meet the legal requirements for contesting elections before raising concerns about the electoral process.

The NDC, led by the Kwankwasiyya Movement, had on Saturday accused INEC and the ruling APC of plotting to manipulate the electoral process ahead of next year’s election.

At a press conference, Director-General of the NDC Governorship Campaign Council, Shehu Wada Sagagi, alleged that the APC was mounting pressure to interfere with the process through the Coalition Supports and Results Verification System (CSRVS).

But the APC Chairman in Kano, Umar Haruna Doguwa, dismissed the allegations and challenged Sagagi to provide evidence to substantiate his claims.

Doguwa described the accusations as false, alleging that the opposition was attempting to divert attention from its own challenges.

He said the APC was prepared for the election and would not allow any party or individual to interfere with the electoral process under the guise of protecting its credibility.

“Instead of dissipating energy on matters of little concern, the NDC should concentrate on issues surrounding the eligibility and qualifications of its candidates,” Doguwa said.

He added that a party yet to meet the electoral requirements for its candidates to appear on the ballot should not be preoccupied with accusing INEC and the APC of wrongdoing.

“Such conduct is not only reckless but also a clear attempt to play the victim card,” he said.

The APC chairman also faulted what he described as premature allegations against the electoral commission and the ruling party over an election yet to be conducted.

He urged the NDC to address the questions surrounding its candidates and allow INEC and other relevant institutions to discharge their constitutional responsibilities.

The APC said it remained confident ahead of the forthcoming election and urged political parties to respect electoral laws.

World.title: Alia, Akume, Suswam, others meet over Benue APC crisis
World.content:
By Peter Duru, Makurdi

Governor Hyacinth Alia of Benue State has reiterated his commitment to reconciliation and unity within the All Progressives Congress (APC) following a meeting with prominent party stakeholders in Abuja.

The meeting, held on Saturday, November 21, 2026, was convened by the North Central Presidential Reconciliation Committee, chaired by former Katsina State Governor, Senator Ibrahim Shema, as part of efforts to resolve disagreements among party leaders in Benue.

Those in attendance included the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume; former Benue State Governor, Senator Gabriel Suswam; Senator Barnabas Gemade; Senator Jack Gyado; and Elder Simon Shango.

Alia disclosed the meeting in a post on his verified social media handle, saying the engagement lasted about two hours and provided an opportunity for the stakeholders to discuss the future of the party in the state.

He said: “Today, (Saturday, November 21, 2026) I joined fellow Benue APC stakeholders in Abuja for a reconciliation meeting convened by the North Central Presidential Reconciliation Committee, chaired by Sen. Ibrahim Shehu Shema, former Governor of Katsina State.

“The meeting, which lasted about two hours, brought together the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Sen. George Akume, former Benue State Governor, Sen. Gabriel Suswam, Sen. Barnabas Gemade, Sen. Jack Gyado and Elder Simon Shango.

“I thank Sen. Shema and his committee for bringing us together. Reconciliation takes a willingness to listen, to speak frankly and to keep working together even where differences remain.

“My commitment is clear. I will continue to engage with our leaders and stakeholders in the interest of a united APC, while keeping the peace, security and development of Benue State at the centre of my work.

“The people of Benue entrusted us with the responsibility to serve, and that responsibility must continue to guide us.”

World.title: Tinubu approves ₦1.5tr recapitalisation of BoA, says APC-PCC
World.content:
….Commits ₦450b to farm financing

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: The All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council APC-PCC on Sunday said President Bola Tinubu has approved a ₦1.5 trillion recapitalisation of the Bank of Agriculture BoA and committed ₦450 billion to agricultural financing programmes.

The council said the commitment is meant “to strengthen food security, expand domestic production, and improve the productivity of smallholder farmers across the country, especially in Northern Nigeria.”

In a statement issued by its Spokesperson, Dele Alake, the council said the bank had reached “over 500,000 smallholder farmers.”

It added that the President “also approved a ₦1.5 trillion recapitalisation to expand agricultural financing and support the cultivation of 500,000 hectares under the Renewed Hope Agenda.”

According to the statement, the Federal Government “went beyond providing farmers with loans; it also addressed access to quality seeds, fertiliser, mechanisation, irrigation, storage facilities, commodity markets, and other essential components of the agricultural value chain.”

On the recapitalisation, the council said it was “a major campaign promise of the President in 2023.” It said the move was designed “to enhance the bank’s financial capacity and ability to provide more affordable and accessible funding to farmers, agricultural cooperatives, processors, aggregators, and other businesses operating across the agricultural value chain.”

The statement added: “Under President Tinubu, a stronger Bank of Agriculture would be better positioned to support large-scale agricultural investments, expand its reach to underserved farming communities, and mobilise additional resources for domestic food production.”

The council disclosed that the Renewed Hope Smallholder Support and Value Chain Fund, which has a programme value of ₦250 billion, finances farmers through Farmer Aggregation Companies.

These companies, it said, “coordinate farmer registration, input distribution, extension services, and market linkages.” The programme, according to the statement, has reached more than 500,000 smallholder farmers across 16 states, including over 70,000 women.

It has also supported the distribution of approximately 2.5 million bags of fertiliser and 300,000 bags of certified seeds. The council said the programme targets two million farmers and the distribution of more than 10 million bags of fertiliser. It named Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Niger, Borno, Gombe, Taraba, Adamawa, Yobe and Bauchi among the states receiving attention under the scheme.

To shield farmers from price shocks, the statement said, the bank is implementing a ₦200 billion Guaranteed Minimum Price Programme. Under it, the bank “has procured approximately 170,000 metric tonnes of maize, rice, sorghum, and cassava to strengthen commodity markets and protect farmers against distress sales.”

The council also said the bank created an Onion Financing Programme in partnership with the National Onion Producers, Processors and Marketers Association of Nigeria (NOPPMAN), which “represents over 11,800 onion farmers.”

The scheme provides onion farmers with improved seeds and fertiliser, supports processors with commodity purchase funds, and helps develop storage and solar-powered cooling facilities to cut post-harvest losses.

“Under the arrangement, cooperatives will contribute 30 per cent of their input costs, while BOA will finance the remaining 70 per cent,” the statement said.

On dry-season farming, it said the bank is working with the All-Farmers Association of Nigeria “to develop a pipeline targeting 400,000 farmers for the 2026 farming cycle.” The initiative covers financing for 120,000 hectares of wheat and another 300,000 hectares for crops including rice, maize, sorghum, millet, cassava and soybeans.

The council added that the Nigeria Ginger Recovery Programme has supported 3,200 farmers in Kachia, Kaduna State, with blight-free seeds. It said more than 9,000 bags have been recovered for multiplication, with an expansion planned across 20,000 hectares in 16 states.

For women, the bank is “targeting at least 50,000 women nationwide through insured cooperative production financing at nine per cent, in partnership with the Federal Ministries of Women Affairs and Agriculture.”

On mechanisation, the statement said 1,571 tractors have been deployed to 23 states under the Renewed Hope National Agricultural Mechanisation Programme. They are expected to mechanise 1.2 million hectares of farmland.

It also cited a ₦385 billion productive-use-of-electricity programme, which “provides 44,000 electric cargo tricycles and 100,000 solar irrigation pumps, targeting 500,000 farming families.”

“The interventions demonstrated President Tinubu’s commitment to transforming agriculture into a major driver of economic growth, food security, and job creation”, the council added.

World.title: NDC dismisses allegations of hoarding ₦6bn campaign funds
World.content:
Party says money is reserved for operations, accuses critics of seeking access to development fund

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA – The national leadership of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has dismissed allegations that it is withholding more than ₦6 billion meant for its presidential campaign, describing the claims as false and misleading.

The party said the allegations reflected a lack of understanding of party administration and the funding requirements of political campaigns.

Some members of the NDC National Campaign Council (NCC) had reportedly accused the party’s national leadership of failing to release adequate funds for campaign activities, including grassroots mobilisation, billboard s and the printing of posters.

The aggrieved members alleged that more than ₦6 billion realised from the sale of nomination forms and contributions by aspirants had been kept in a fixed deposit account while the campaign council struggled to finance basic activities.

They also claimed that 75 per cent of the money came from the South-East, following the entry of aspirants who joined the party alongside its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and expressed concern that the alleged funding constraints could affect his electoral prospects.

However, speaking with Vanguard, the party’s National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, dismissed the allegations as rumours allegedly being promoted by individuals seeking to create divisions within the party.

He said the claims were intended to create friction between Obi and the party’s national leadership.

“These are rumours and machinations of mischief makers who don’t wish the party well, and want to create problems where there is none between our presidential candidate and the national leader of our party.

“Also, it shows acute ignorance on the part of those peddling the rumours about party administration and how presidential campaigns are funded,” he said.

Director advised those making the allegations to familiarise themselves with party administration and the provisions of the Electoral Act on campaign financing.

However, a senior party source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed that the campaign council had yet to receive substantial funding from the national leadership, despite the revenue reportedly generated from the sale of nomination forms.

The source expressed concern that the funding situation could hamper publicity, grassroots mobilisation and other campaign activities.

According to the source, the party disclosed at its third National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting that it had generated about ₦8 billion, spent approximately ₦2 billion and retained about ₦6 billion in a fixed deposit account.

The source said the funds were generated through the sale of nomination forms and development levies.

“Let me also inform you that more than 80 per cent of the candidates could not pay for the nomination and expression of interest forms. They were given forms free. Many states still do not have offices, and the party is assisting them. The national leadership recently got its office.

“The Obidient Movement is coming out crying about money. Where are the funds for senatorial, governorship and other positions?” the source queried.

The source further disclosed that the party had proposed the establishment of a National Campaign Fund involving its presidential candidate, his running mate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso, and the national leadership.

According to the source, the arrangement proposed the allocation of ₦1 billion to the South-South, another ₦1 billion to the South-East, while the remaining ₦3 billion would be managed by the Campaign Council.

The source claimed that Obi was asked to contribute ₦5 billion towards establishing the fund but provided only ₦220 million, out of which ₦200 million was subsequently transferred to the National Campaign Council.

“The party is not holding any campaign money,” the source insisted.

The source further alleged that those demanding access to the money were seeking the release of funds contributed for the party’s development.

“They want the development fund money people paid to be given to them. The ₦6 billion is to run the party. Only Aisha Yusuf has helped to open an account to assist the party. The party has not raised funds, Obi has not raised funds.

“The party will be going to Edo State on Wednesday. The party has no money; the people of Edo State will finance the visit.

“If we give them the money we saved to run the election, we will not have money to run the party,” the source said.

The source also lamented the absence of adequate funding for campaign publicity, including posters, billboards and youth mobilisation, as well as activities involving various support groups.

Vanguard’s efforts to obtain the reaction of the National Campaign Council spokesperson, Dr Constance Ikokwu, were unsuccessful, as she did not respond to a WhatsApp message sent to her over a period of more than five hours.

Recall that the NDC, at its third NEC meeting held on October 24 at JD Event Centre, Abuja, announced that it had generated ₦8,529,632,438.77 in revenue since its establishment seven months earlier.

The party attributed the revenue to the sale of nomination forms, contributions from supporters, membership dues and levies.

Presenting the financial statement, the National Treasurer, Dr Peter Onigah, said the party had spent approximately ₦2.40 billion and retained a balance of about ₦6.13 billion.

He said the expenditure covered party activities, including primaries, publicity, salaries and other administrative expenses.

Onigah said the party had maintained financial discipline and ensured that resources entrusted to its leadership were managed prudently.

He explained that its financial management was guided by the experience of party officials, advice from national leaders and the National Working Committee (NWC).

According to him, the party would provide a detailed breakdown of its financial transactions as it approached the end of its first accounting year.

“We have been very prudent. Our chief is made up of technocrats, people who are experienced and people who have different capacities,” he said.

Onigah also appealed to Nigerians and party members to support the party financially, noting that it was still developing its structures and had yet to control government at any level.

“As a new party, we don’t have people in government yet. All of us are outside the government. So we need to contribute together and ensure that our party will prevail and achieve the desired objectives,” he said.

World.title: I didn’t politicise it — Gov Yusuf narrates how wife left Kano Govt House
World.content:
Kano State Governor, Abba Yusuf, has broken his silence on his marital crisis with wife, Zainab, recounting how she allegedly left the Government House and later initiated divorce proceedings against him in Abuja.

The governor, in an interview with BBC Hausa aired on Sunday, said he had remained quiet despite developments in the marriage, which he said had lasted about two decades and produced children.

Yusuf said Zainab, a niece of his former political ally, Rabiu Kwankwaso, was previously married before they got together.

He recalled that their relationship eventually deteriorated, leading to her departure from the Government House, an experience he said he endured without publicly discussing the matter.

“Many things happened, to the point where her belongings were packed and she was taken away from my house, and through it all, I remained patient and did not speak out,” Yusuf said.

He said he had tried to reassure their children that their mother would return, but was subsequently taken aback when the matter ended up in court.

The governor said he was particularly surprised that the divorce suit was filed in Abuja rather than Kano.

“Suddenly, she dragged me to court, a court in Abuja, not even in Kano,” he said.

Yusuf described the development as distressing, adding that he had information about the circumstances surrounding his wife’s departure but would not publicly disclose the details.

Asked whether he was using the family dispute for political purposes, the governor denied bringing politics into the matter, questioning how anyone in a similar situation would react.

“I am not the one who politicised it. If this was done to you, how would you feel?” he asked.

He further lamented that his wife’s belongings were removed and she was taken to another residence without his knowledge, before he learnt that she had instituted legal proceedings against him.

The marital dispute is before the Upper Area Court in the Gudu District of Abuja, where the divorce case, marked CV/97/26, was adjourned until December 15.

The adjournment followed a request by Kano Commissioner for Information, Sanusi Bature, who represented Yusuf, for more time to brief the governor on the court proceedings.

The crisis has drawn political attention because of Yusuf’s relationship with Kwankwaso, who played a significant role in his political rise. Their relationship reportedly deteriorated after Yusuf defected from the New Nigeria Peoples Party to the All Progressives Congress in January 2026, while Kwankwaso later joined the New Nigeria Democratic Congress.

World.title: Nigerian Breweries Unveils Legendary Christmas as it Marks 80th Anniversary
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Vanessa Obioha

Nigerian Breweries Plc has unveiled its Legendary Christmas 2026 programme, featuring concerts, street light-ups and other entertainment experiences across several Nigerian cities as the company marks its 80th anniversary.

The programme will include the company’s participation in major concerts such as Wizkid Live in Abuja and Davido Live at the National Theatre, alongside music events and brand activations in Lagos, Ibadan, Enugu, Aba, Onitsha, Benin, Awka and Port Harcourt.

Announcing the programme at a media soirée in Lagos, Sampson Oloche, Portfolio Manager, Beyond Beer and Flavoured, said the activities would cater to different audiences across the country.

He also disclosed that the company was developing a digital platform to enable consumers to discover events and access tickets to participating experiences.

“What we have tried to do is create something for different consumers in different places. There is something for everybody. In the coming weeks, we will announce a platform, which we are building into an app, where people can explore these activations and access tickets,” Oloche said.

The festive calendar will feature street light-ups in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan, Enugu, Aba and Port Harcourt. It will also include Goldberg’s Gold Standard concerts in Benin and Ibadan, as well as Life Continental Lager’s concert experiences in Onitsha and Aba.

Other activities include Heineken’s festive experiences in Port Harcourt and Amstel Malta Festiville in Enugu, Aba and Awka. Beer Villages and other brand activations will also feature in the programme.

The unveiling formed part of Nigerian Breweries’ 80th anniversary celebration, held under the theme ‘Together Every Moment’. The company also announced an N80 million consumer reward initiative, through which 80 selected participants in its NB@80 storytelling campaign will each receive N1 million for sharing photographs, videos and memories associated with its brands.

Speaking at the event, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Thibaut Boidin, said the company’s activities supported an estimated N1.6 trillion contribution to Nigeria’s Gross Domestic Product in 2025, according to its Socio-Economic Impact Study.

The study also estimated that the company’s operations and wider value chain supported approximately 310,700 jobs, while its sorghum procurement sustained about 55,400 farming households.

“For me, these figures speak to something larger than our financial performance. They show the extent to which Nigerian Breweries is connected to the economic lives of people and businesses across Nigeria,” he said.

Boidin said the company’s contribution extended beyond its breweries to farmers, suppliers, distributors, retailers and hospitality businesses connected to its operations.

Established in 1946, Nigerian Breweries began production with Star Lager Beer in 1949. As it enters its ninth decade, the company said it would continue investing in innovation, local sourcing and partnerships across Nigeria.

World.title: Eko Open Taps Into Creative Pulse of Detty December
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Vanessa Obioha

A new Wimbledon-inspired tennis competition, Eko Open, is set to debut in Lagos during the Detty December festive season, as its organisers seek to bring sports into the city’s bustling end-of-year entertainment calendar.

The three-day event, featuring veteran and professional tennis players, will run from December 4 to 6, 2026, at the Lagos Lawn Tennis Club in Onikan, Lagos.

December in Lagos is largely associated with music, arts and culture. However, the organisers of Eko Open hope to tap into the season’s creative energy and establish tennis as part of the activities that draw people to the city during the festive period.

Speaking at a press parley, founder Tosin Giwa said the tournament would leverage social media influencers to attract a wider audience. One of its opening-day highlights will be a celebrity match between social media content creator Brain Jotter and forex trader Jeffery Benson.

Taking a cue from Wimbledon, where fashion has become an integral part of the tournament’s appeal, Eko Open will also incorporate lifestyle and fashion into its programme.

“We are inviting over 100 influencers who will be able to create an experience around fashion and lifestyle,” Giwa said.

The event is also designed to offer a luxury experience while encouraging wider participation in tennis, according to its Head of Communications, Itty Okim.

“Our aim is to see tennis gain wider acceptance in Nigeria, and the Eko Open is our contribution to that. It will be an annual event, so every December Lagos will have a tennis weekend to look forward to, and more people will have a reason to take a seat on the lawn or pick up a racket.”

The organisers also hope to secure sanctioning from the International Tennis Federation (ITF), the world governing body for tennis. They said the process would be pursued one edition at a time.

The tournament will feature an eight-player championship involving professional players, including Barakat Oyinlomo Quadre, one of Nigeria’s top female tennis players, with cash prizes available to players and coaches after each win.

World.title: Transatlantic University Gets NUC Approval to Admit 700 Students, Commences Academic Activities Dec. 1
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

David-Chyddy Eleke in Awka

Transatlantic University of Medicine and Health Sciences, Umuchukwu, in Orumba South Local Government Area of Anambra State, has secured the approval of the National Universities Commission (NUC) for an initial intake of 700 students.

The Vice-Chancellor of the university, Prof. Charles Esimone, disclosed this while briefing journalists at the institution’s administrative block in Umuchukwu.

He stated that the newly approved university will commence academic activities on December 1, 2026.

Esimone told journalists that all arrangements had been concluded for the take-off of the university, describing the institution as unique, given its focus on medicine and health sciences.

The university which is newly licensed is owned by Umuchukwu-born, US-based medical practitioner, Dr. Godwin Maduka, proprietor of Las Vegas pain institute, and former governorship candidate in Anambra State.

Esimone stated that considering the calibre of the proprietor of of the university as a renowned pain doctor in the US, nothing short of the very best is expected, adding that it was established to provide quality education and professional training in the health sector.

He explained that, “This university had commenced in principle in October following the issuance of our operational licence by the NUC and the completion of the commission’s resource verification exercise.

“We will commence full academic activities on December 1.”

Speaking of the university’s tuition fee, he disclosed that students in other programmes would pay N3 million, while those studying Medicine and Pharmacy would pay between N5 million and N7 million per session.

Earlier, the Registrar of the university, Rev. Sam Ufoh, led journalists on a guided tour of the institution’s facilities, showcasing the infrastructure put in place ahead of the commencement of academic activities.

World.title: UBEC Pledges More Support, As Abia Pupils Emerge Overall Champions At Debate Championship In Qatar
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 



Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

Pupils of Abia State public schools have emerged overall champions at the 2026 International Schools Debate Championship in Doha, Qatar.

Beating teams from six other countries, team Nigeria, which won four major trophies and 12 laurels at the event, include Best International School Debate Team, Overall Best Team (Junior Category), Best Leadership Award and Best Debater Award.

The Executive Secretary of the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), Dr. Aisha Garba, described the victory as a proud moment for Nigeria, saying the achievement showed what Nigerian public school pupils can do when given the right platform, adding that UBEC interventions in teaching, learning, instructional materials and digitalisation of basic education have brought development to basic education in Nigeria.

She said under the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, UBEC is proud to support states and initiate opportunities that take children to international competitions.

Garba commended Governor Alex Otti, the Executive Chairman of ASUBEB, Ambassador Lydia Ezihe Onuoha, the Presidential School Debate Nigeria, and the five pupils, Christian Chinweotitom Esther, Chikodi Maureen, Akamnonu Franklin, Ifeanyichukwu Prisca and Simon Divine, as well as their teachers and parents.

She said UBEC will continue to support and initiate participation in international competitions in debate, science, technology, arts and sports, and urged other State Universal Basic Education Boards to identify and nurture talent in their schools.

“UBEC remains committed to ensuring that every Nigerian child receives quality basic education and the chance to shine locally and globally. We are proud of these students and look forward to many more victories,” she said.

World.title: 2027: Trust, Accountability, Responsible Communication Will Determine Credibility of Nigeria’s Democratic Process, Say Jega, Kukah
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

A former Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Attahiru Jega, and Bishop of Sokoto, Rev.
