World.title: ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ star Catherine Bach says co-star stripped naked except for cowboy hat to cheer her up
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"Dukes of Hazzard" star Catherine Bach recalled a wild behind-the-scenes prank that her co-star, James Best, pulled on her while they were filming the iconic 1980s sitcom.

The 72-year-old actress recently spoke with Fox News Digital at Cure Addiction Now's third annual Fundraising Evening at the Beverly Hills Hotel, which raised money for research into treatments for substance-use disorder.

During her interview alongside her daughter, Laura Lopez, Bach revealed that Best, who played Sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane on the show, stripped down naked to cheer her up when she was struggling with homesickness on the "Dukes of Hazzard" set.

‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR CATHERINE BACH STUNS FANS IN NEW PHOTO AFTER REPORTED HOSPITALIZATION

"I was a little depressed," Bach remembered. "I was so far away from home. I'm in Georgia and it's all guys."

However, Bach said that her spirits were lifted after Best enlisted the help of a makeup artist for an outrageous stunt, which unfolded during what appeared to be a routine touch-up.

"He has the makeup man. He goes, ‘Catherine, we need to get the makeup underneath your eyes. We need to straighten it out,'" Bach recalled. "And I said, ‘OK.' Close my eyes. He goes, ‘No, open your eyes so I can get underneath,' and I was like, ’What are you talking about?' So he goes, ‘Just look at my hat.' And I say, OK.’"

‘LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE’ STAR SAYS BRUTAL FILMING CONDITIONS LEFT CAST MEMBERS UNCONSCIOUS

"And there's Jimmy, naked, except for his cowboy hat and his holster and guns," Bach remembered with a laugh.

WATCH: ‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR CATHERINE BACH SAYS CO-STAR PULLED NAKED PRANK TO CHEER HER UP

According to the actress, her co-star received an enthusiastic reception from the men on set afterward.

"So then, when he came to set, 30 people were waiting for him, and they all bowed down, all the guys," she said. "But he got a laugh out of me because I hadn't been laughing very much."

"The Dukes of Hazzard" aired for seven seasons on CBS from 1979 to 1985 and initially filmed in Georgia before production moved to California. The action comedy series followed cousins Bo and Luke Duke, played by John Schneider and Tom Wopat, and their adventures in fictional Hazzard County. Bach played their cousin Daisy Duke, while Best's Sheriff Coltrane frequently found himself outmaneuvered by the Duke boys.

The series was a major hit, drawing in as many as 20 million viewers per episode. By its third season, "The Dukes of Hazzard" had become the second-biggest show on TV, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

"The Dukes of Hazzard" catapulted the cast to stardom, especially Bach, whose short shorts made her a sex symbol. The cast members also became genuinely close both on and off set, forming lifelong friendships that have lasted decades after the show ended.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Best died in April 2015 at age 88 due to complications from pneumonia. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Bach shared how Best's sense of humor remains part of her memories of making the series.

Asked to name the biggest troublemaker on set, Bach declined to limit the distinction to one cast member.

"Everybody, everybody. Jimmy Best, he was hilarious," she said.

The actress has previously said that practical jokes were a regular part of life on the "Dukes of Hazzard set."

"We all became such a family; there were so many pranks," Bach told the audience at a 2025 Hollywood Museum event with Schneider and Wopat, according to Remind magazine.

During her interview with Fox News Digital, Bach also recalled how Daisy's wardrobe became a defining part of the series. The character's denim cutoffs became so closely associated with her that the style became widely known as "Daisy Dukes." During her time on the show, Bach posed as Daisy Dukes for a poster that sold five million copies, and her legs were insured for $1 million.

The actress said she had a hands-on role in creating the clothes audiences saw onscreen, saying that she "made them all," including the Daisy Dukes.

"And the bathing suit and the shirt," she added.

‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR JOHN SCHNEIDER BREAKS SILENCE ON EX-WIFE'S COURT BATTLE: 'EVERYTHING'S A NEGOTIATION'

Bach explained that her sewing skills came from her mother's insistence that she learn a practical skill alongside pursuing acting.

"My mother said I needed to have a craft in case I didn't make it as an actress," she said.

Bach previously discussed her influence over her character's costume choices in a 2019 interview with Fox News Digital. She said producers initially wanted her to wear a poodle skirt, but she suggested the denim shorts that became a fashion sensation.

However, Bach shared that the Daisy Dukes presented a familiar problem when it came time to put them on, saying that "gaining weight" in between seasons was "impossible."

"Every year I would say, 'Wait a minute, you guys wash these in the washing machine, and you dried them, I know it. You're supposed to dry-clean them,'" she recalled. "They said, ‘No, we did, we do.’ I said, 'No, you didn't. See, I can't zip them up.'"

"It might be me," she admitted with a laugh.

The famed Daisy Dukes are not the only pieces of "Dukes of Hazzard" that remain part of Bach's life.

"I'm building a General Lee," she told Fox News Digital. "A Charger."

The orange 1969 Dodge Charger nicknamed General Lee that was driven by Bo and Luke was a signature part of the series, appearing in the high-speed police car chases and long stunt jumps that helped define the show.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Bach said her own car began as a surprise gift from her husband, although she suspected he had another reason for choosing it.

"I think he wanted it for himself," she said.

She told Fox News Digital that the vehicle has since become connected to her charity activities, with students currently getting an opportunity to work on it.

"Anyhow, I got it, and it's been a continuation of charity events," Bach said. "It's at a college right now, and all the kids are working on it."

Once the work is completed, Bach said she plans to bring the car to a hospital and offer children rides around the parking lot.

"You know, just stuff like that. It's fun," she said.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Weighing in on what she missed about classic television, Bach said "wholesome" entertainment.

"But funny, and a little edgy, but that you can watch with the whole family, because that's what you can do with ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ and with many other shows," she said. "The whole family can sit around without getting, you know, getting ruffled. Grandma, grandpa, the kids, the mom and dad, everybody. That's what I miss."

While attending the Cure Addiction Now's third annual Fundraising Evening, Bach also shared a health update during an interview with People alongside her daughter, Laura. Bach was hospitalized for an embolism in October 2025, according to multiple reports.

"I’m good ... Everything’s on the up and up," she said. "It was very serious. Yeah. It was a very serious situation."

The actress told the outlet that Laura, 28, "took care of me during that time." Bach shared Laura and daughter Sophia, 30, with her late husband Peter Lopez, who died in 2010.

"She’s back and better than ever," Laura said of her mother.

World.title: FAA lifts ground stop on Atlanta-bound Delta flights after system outage
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Sunday morning outage in Delta Air Lines' automated weight-and-balance system forced the Federal Aviation Administration to briefly halt Atlanta-bound flights and has reportedly delayed at least 3,500 Delta flights across major hubs, including Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport and New York's LaGuardia Airport.

The technical failure rippled through Sunday's travel schedule, but the ground stop led to roughly an hour delay before being lifted.

UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’

"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," Delta told Fox News in a statement. "We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism."

Before any commercial aircraft can take off, crews must verify that its total weight and center of gravity fall within strict safety limits – a process that relies heavily on baggage and cargo data. With the automated system offline, Delta staff were calculating weight and balance figures manually for departing flights while technicians work to bring the software back online.

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

The airline coordinated with air traffic controllers to manage the flow of planes and prevent congestion at airport gates and on the tarmac at its Atlanta hub. A ground delay for Atlanta had remained in effect for some time after the ground stop had been lifted, but as of shortly before noon ET, it was no longer listed on the FAA's National Airspace System website.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The issue comes more than a week after a historic nationwide FAA ground stop and an ensuing week of ongoing cybersecurity issues from reported system upgrades and patches throughout the U.S. The issues caused panic online that percolated into the stock market, causing massive dips in tech and artificial intelligence stocks.

Fox News' C.B. Cotton contributed to this report.

World.title: WWE star LA Knight requests fans respect ex-girlfriend's privacy after flirty exchange with Nikki Bella
World.content:
WWE star LA Knight batted away vivacious pro wrestling fans in a video on Saturday, asking them to refrain from dragging his former girlfriend into things involving him.

Knight, whose real name is Shaun Ricker, made clear he is a single man after a flirty interaction between him and Nikki Bella caught the attention of fans during a special collaboration the WWE is doing with WhatsApp for NFL games called The Chat.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

Pro wrestling fans immediately wondered whether Knight was married or at least had a girlfriend while those messages went viral earlier this month across social media. Knight was forced to put out a PSA on social media addressing his relationship status and making clear that he was single.

"I’m a single man. I’m not married. I’ve never been married. I was in a long-term relationship. That relationship ended in July of 2025," he said. "Why am I telling you this? World.title: Progressives unveil $25 minimum wage push to solve affordability crisis despite economist inflation warning
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

House Democrats are pushing to raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, calling the current hourly pay a "remnant of slavery" to "oppress women," despite warnings from conservative economists that the proposal could drive up costs and threaten jobs.

The proposal from the Congressional Progressive Caucus would more than triple the current $7.25 federal minimum wage, raising questions about its potential impact on businesses and workers in states with significantly lower living costs than major cities.

"We should be rallying around (a minimum wage of) $25 at minimum, and it should be cost adjusted for inflation, so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., told Fox News Digital.

AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?

Asked whether a nationwide $25 minimum wage could hurt workers and businesses in lower-cost states, Blair argued that the proposed rate should serve as a national baseline.

The congressman said $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living."

Blair acknowledged concerns that raising the minimum wage could contribute to inflation but said lawmakers must find a way to increase workers' earnings while "keeping people afloat."

Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., echoed Blair's support for the proposal, pointing to the high cost of living in cities such as Seattle and Washington, D.C., as justification for raising wages.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD

"The truth is that the boogeyman, the corporations, don't want to pay their workers liveable wages," Ramirez told Fox News Digital.

Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni warned that a $25 federal minimum wage could increase costs and unemployment, arguing that the economic consequences would extend beyond major metropolitan areas.

"Whenever a price floor on labor is set above the market equilibrium, a surplus of labor is created. In this case, we call that surplus unemployment," Antoni told Fox News Digital.

DEMOCRATS PLOT MASSIVE SPENDING SPREE AFTER MIDTERM ROUT — AND TRUMP COULD HELP THEM PULL IT OFF

Despite those warnings, progressive lawmakers expressed confidence that the proposal could gain support from Democratic leadership in both chambers and potentially reach President Donald Trump's desk.

"There's a widespread coalition of folks in the Democratic caucus who have long been saying that one job should be enough to pay the bill," Blair told Fox News Digital.

Ramirez also expressed cautious optimism about the possibility of Trump signing the legislation, pointing to his previous willingness to discuss bipartisan immigration reform.

She said she "never knows what the president might or might not be willing to do."

SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS

The Living Wage for All coalition, which joined lawmakers in unveiling the proposal, says support for a $25 minimum wage extends beyond Democratic voters.

"Not a blue wave," the coalition said, citing polling it claimed showed 63% of Republicans support a $25 federal minimum wage. "There is a blue collar demand that says that this is how we address the affordability crisis."

Coalition members also drew comparisons between the history of minimum-wage policies and slavery-era labor practices, arguing that the current wage system has historically disadvantaged women and marginalized workers.

The proposal comes as Democrats prepare to advance their affordability agenda in the 120th Congress, with progressives seeking to make higher wages a central component of the party's economic platform.

World.title: COP31 climate talks break down after angry dispute over fossil fuels
World.content:
International climate talks in Turkey broke down Sunday after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement that had cut all references to fossil fuels.

Negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya fell apart two days after the United Nations’ COP31 conference was meant to end, after delegates from 196 countries and the European Union struggled to agree on new pledges for climate action and how to deliver on previous promises.

COP31 President Murat Kurum said Sunday that there would be no new climate agreement draft after a fourth draft was rejected.

“There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” said Kurum, who is host nation Turkey’s environment minister. “​We will not ​be carrying out ​work on a new ⁠text in an environment ⁠where there ​is no consensus.”

He later added that he had wanted a a “much stronger outcome” from the summit.

Chris Bowen, COP31’s president of negotiations, told reporters that there were “unbridgeable red lines” in the discussions.

“The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory,” the Australian minister said. “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time,” Bowen added.

The latest draft agreement, released on Sunday, had set out proposed measures for countries to accelerate climate action, but the 12-page document drew immediate criticism over its failure to mention a move away from fossil fuels, a key demand of the E.U. and other nations.

Irish minister Darragh O’Brien, representing the E.U. in Antalya, said the bloc “strongly objects” to the deal, which he called “greenwashing.”

“These decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change,” O’Brien said. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels.”

Panama also rejected the deal, saying it didn’t go far enough, as did the Marshall Islands, a low-lying Pacific nation that faces an existential threat from sea-level rise.

Kate Hughes, the spokesperson for the United Kingdom delegation, called the draft text the “lowest common denominator.”

All countries had to agree on the text for it to pass. The talks were the longest in COP history, surpassing the delay in negotiations at COP25 in Madrid.

The summit began on Nov 9. A first draft was circulated a week later and mentioned “fossil fuel” or “fossil fuels” six times. But a second draft, published Thursday, had removed all references, to the anger of many countries.

The conference officially ended on Friday without an agreement. Members have continued talks in a bid to find a resolution, but a fourth draft released Sunday still contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia and India have pushed back on including any reference to the words in the text, amid concerns that phasing out fossil fuels, central to their economies, could pose a financial risk.

The United States, one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases, is officially absent from the conference, having withdrawn from a series of international climate commitments under President Donald Trump.

The latest draft started by “recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety,” a reference to COP28 in the UAE, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away” from fossil fuels in energy systems.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said the world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

“We love the petroleum guys,” he told a press conference on Wednesday. “We can’t live without them, and they are so smart, they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa called COP31 the “worst ever.”

“The collapse of climate talks at COP31 in Antalya needs to be a wake-up call for the world,” he wrote in a statement. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.”

“But this setback does not change the facts,” he posted on X. “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

The latest draft also acknowledged that the goal set by the 2015 Paris Agreement of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius is going to be missed.

As warming goes beyond 1.5 C, the impacts of climate change, including extreme heat and other weather events, are expected to ramp up significantly.

As the talks break down, Kurum could choose to convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year’s conference, hosted by Ethiopia.

Talks last failed at COP6 at The Hague in the Netherlands in 2000.

World.title: Princeton neuroscientist detained by ICE at D.C. airport after leaving conference
World.content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested a Princeton University Ph.D. student at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she was preparing to fly back to New Jersey after presenting her research at a conference, her adviser said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student from China, has had an asylum application pending for 10 years after her family came to the U.S. when she was 14, according to her attorney, Kerry Doyle. The Department of Homeland Security said Xie was in the country illegally, which Doyle disputed, saying she had permission to live, work and study in the country while her case was pending.

“Her arrest and detention is without legal basis as ICE and DHS are fully aware,” Doyle told NBC News.

DHS said in a statement about her arrest that Xie was admitted to the United States temporarily in March 2016 and was required to leave by Sept. 15 of that year. The agency said she stayed past that date.

“Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States,” the statement said. “To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.”

Xie, 24, was being held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, according to a detainee search on ICE’s website.

Doyle filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court in Virginia challenging the legality of Xie’s arrest. She argued that ICE had no grounds to arrest Xie without a warrant because Xie was not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Doyle said people with pending asylum cases “have permission to be here” while their cases are decided.

“It’s their over-the-top enforcement used as a way to scare people,” Doyle said. She called Xie’s arrest “an incredible waste of time and resources — to what end?”

Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., on July 30. Kevin Carter / Getty Images file

The Trump administration has detained asylum-seekers and others with pending immigration applications as part of its broader immigration crackdown.

In its statement on Xie’s arrest, DHS repeated a warning it issued in recent press releases, saying it was working to prevent people it considered to be in the country illegally from flying domestically.

Xie’s adviser, Carlos Brody, described the research she presented at the conference in an emailed statement.

“There, Eva described her work discovering and researching an unexpected link between how brains make decisions and how they navigate through space,” Brody said.

Brody said Xie mentors undergraduates and sent messages to colleagues from the detention center “to make sure that her experiments could move forward and the grant applications she is part of could be submitted.”

“Eva is a gentle, kind, caring person who is contributing enormously to the United States,” Brody added. “She belongs back home in Princeton, doing the science that she loves, and helping our country excel and grow.”

Princeton’s graduate school dean, Rodney D. Priestley, said that Eva’s arrest “is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community.”

“The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support,” Priestley said in a statement. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s attorney did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday.

According to Xie’s professional biography page, she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics. She was helping to plan a cognitive computational neuroscience conference in the U.K. in 2027, according to the page.

World.title: Delta tech issue delays Atlanta-bound flights head of Thanksgiving
World.content:
A problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance delayed flights into its Atlanta hub Sunday, as travelers headed out ahead of Thanksgiving.

The Federal Aviation Administration briefly halted Atlanta-bound flights Sunday morning, then replaced the ground stop with a program that allowed flights to depart at staggered times. The delay program, requested by Delta, applied to the airline and its regional carriers flying into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport from the contiguous United States.

The FAA projected delays of 57 minutes on average and up to 1 hour and 51 minutes. The program was scheduled through 12:50 p.m. ET.

Delta said it was working to restore the automated system that calculates how much a plane weighs and how that weight is distributed before takeoff. The airline said it was coordinating with air traffic controllers to prevent congestion at gates and on the tarmac in Atlanta.

The delays at Hartsfield-Jackson came after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 because of a technical issue with its air traffic control network. Flights resumed later that evening, but travel disruptions continued through the weekend.

A separate system outage delayed United Airlines departures on Nov. 16, disrupting crew communications and the airline’s ability to send pilots final aircraft weight data, according to the union representing United pilots. United said it resolved the issue that day.

World.title: California prepares for flooding as king tides and storms threaten Thanksgiving week
World.content:
California officials this weekend are preparing for storms that could coincide with the year’s highest tides, Thanksgiving and some of its busiest holiday travel days.

“A series of winter storms is impacting California, bringing heavy rain, mountain snow, and potentially hazardous travel conditions,” the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services said Friday.

A Pacific storm is expected to strike the Northern California coast Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing with it an atmospheric river of rain drawn from nearly tropical climes in the ocean, forecasters said.

National Weather Service forecasters in the San Francisco Bay Area said the storm would bring “widespread” and persistent rainfall — up to 3 inches in northern portions of the region. A coastal flood warning covering the Bay Area coastline from 6 a.m. Monday to 4 p.m. Thursday said nearly 3 feet of inundation was possible in low-lying areas.

World.title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen says ‘momentum is in our direction’ in battle for majority leader
World.content:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that “momentum is in our direction” in his bid for Senate majority leader.

Asked directly how much support he had within the Democratic caucus, Van Hollen said the number is “north of 15” although it’s short of the 28 votes needed to win the leadership race against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.

Democratic senators and senators-elect will hold a vote in December to determine the next majority leader, a dominant role in shaping the party’s agenda and its response to the Trump administration.

Van Hollen’s allies have sought to frame him as a leader who can push for change, while Schumer’s allies have argued that his leadership helped usher in historic Democratic wins across the country.

Asked whether he believes he can secure enough votes, Van Hollen said yes.

“Yes, because if you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change,” he said in the Sunday interview. “They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate.”

Van Hollen also said he believes the Democratic Party is “on probation” and needs to earn Americans’ trust.

“You don’t earn people’s trust by going back to business as usual,” he said.

Van Hollen said he personally believes that the filibuster, which requires that most bills in the Senate need at least 60 votes to pass, “is an anti-democratic provision.”

“But I also understand that the job of the majority leader is to work with the caucus,” he continued.

“So we should set sort of standards and criteria for at what level of obstruction by Republicans — to root out political corruption, to move forward on voting rights — at what level will we consider alternatives?” he said, listing two major policy fights for which Democrats could potentially change the rules.

One possibility, he said, is requiring a talking filibuster so that Republicans would have to show their opposition to popular proposals on the Senate floor.

Van Hollen, who has been floated as a potential presidential candidate, also confirmed on “Meet the Press” that he will not run for president, even if he loses the leadership race. Van Hollen initially said he was “kicking the tires” on a presidential run, but after jumping in the Senate leadership race, he said he was not pursuing a presidential run anymore.

“After I saw the scope of this victory, this call from the American people, my view is now we have to deliver, we have to earn people’s trust, and that would be my focus entirely,” he said. “So no, I’m not running for president in 2028.”

World.title: Transcript: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
World.content:
The following is the transcript of the interview with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to the incoming Speaker of the House, Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who joins us from New York. Good morning, Mr. Speaker-designate.

REP. HAKEEM JEFFRIES: Good morning. Great to be with you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you have — really a huge role to take over in January, and I want to lay out for you what we saw in our exit polls as the message sent by voters. 89% said cost of living was crucial or a major factor in their vote. 90% said the same about corruption. Given those dual messages, what is the first bill you try to pass, and will it be bipartisan?

REP. JEFFRIES: We're going to work incredibly hard to deliver on our promises to the American people around affordability and accountability. We have to drive down the high cost of living. Life is way too expensive. There are far too many people who are working hard, they're playing by the rules, they can't thrive, and they can barely survive. There are several things that we plan to do very early on in the new Congress. We need to end this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran that has skyrocketed gas prices, food prices, and diesel prices. We need to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We need to restore SNAP benefits. We need to deal with the Trump tariffs, which have also increased costs on everyday Americans by thousands of dollars per year —

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. JEFFRIES: — and of course we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when I asked about whether or not it would be bipartisan, some of the things you just laid out, it really doesn't seem likely that the president, a Republican president, would sign off on. Some of the things you listed- they were part of his signature tax and spending bill that Republicans passed. Are you going to send these as messaging vehicles?

REP. JEFFRIES: No, we're committed to delivering the type of bold, dramatic, and meaningful change that the American people are demanding. When we moved earlier this year to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, that was bipartisan in the House of Representatives because the reality is tens of millions of people in this country, hardworking, working-class, middle-class folks, those who aspire to be part of the middle class, have experienced dramatically increased health insurance premiums. In some cases, more than $1,000 per month. That's unacceptable. Reversing the Medicaid cuts will help out people all across this country —

MARGARET BRENNAN: You don't think Trump will veto that?

REP. JEFFRIES: — rural America, urban America, small town America, the heartland of America, and Black and Brown communities all throughout America. Listen, that remains to be seen. We have three areas that we need to work on. We need to drive down the high cost of living and deal with the affordability crisis. We have a broken healthcare system. We need to fix it, and then make sure that we actually don't simply return to the status quo, but we do much better than what currently exists. And we need to fix our broken immigration system as well. And those are three possible areas to explore whether we can work together with the president and our colleagues on the other side of the aisle.

MARGARET BRENNAN: There are a lot of different ways to define accountability. Rahm Emanuel, the former congressman, mayor, and ambassador- I know you know him well, told my CBS colleague that Democrats seeking accountability should move on ethics reform. He suggested a ban on stock trading in prediction markets, mandatory blind trust for everyone with over $1 million in wealth and no foreign money when you're in government or two years afterwards. Do you have an appetite for that kind of proposal?

REP. JEFFRIES: Yes, we have promised the American people that, in addition to our affordability agenda, we know, in the face of the unprecedented corruption that has been unleashed on the American people and the country over the last two years, that we need to deal with accountability, and we've made that clear. And no one is going to get a pass because--

MARGARET BRENNAN: But how do you define that?

REP. JEFFRIES: --there's a cost to corruption that adversely impacts everyday Americans. So, well listen, we've got to clean up the mess in Washington. That means the Congress, that means the Supreme Court, and that also means with respect to the administration. And we should begin by dealing with our own House, which is why very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we will see if that gets the bipartisan support needed. I want to ask you as well about what President Trump said he thinks he can work with you on. He said we can get a lot of great things done. Take a listen.

[START SOUND ON TAPE]

DONALD TRUMP: I'm open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.

[END SOUND ON TAPE]

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, what would working with him on healthcare do apart from, like you said, repealing the things that have already been passed?

REP. JEFFRIES: In addition to what I've talked about in terms of fixing our broken healthcare system, of course, we can't simply return to the status quo. In my view, we should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental, and we should make sure that we cover the kids so that every single child and young American in this country can afford to go see a doctor when they need one. That's a place where we can explore coming together. I know it has strong support amongst Democrats in the House and the Senate, and let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare. Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if over the next two years, we fail to do anything--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. JEFFRIES: --about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration? We're committed to bringing about the type of dramatic change the American people are demanding.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you also have constraints on you given the already over $40 trillion in debt America is carrying. You have constraints with the rising cost of Social Security and Medicaid. How do you pay for expanding this?

REP. JEFFRIES: Well, those are conversations that we look forward to having as members of Congress, both sides of the aisle, and certainly with the administration. But we have to do better. The economy is broken. Life is not working for far too many Americans, and it's clear we can't simply return to the status quo. This is a great country. When you work hard and play by the rules, you should be able to live an affordable life, and a comfortable life, and a good life. And that's what we're committed to bringing about for every single American in this great country of ours.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, when you were elected as Speaker-designate, there were seven of the 11 lawmakers who voted against you who released a statement. Some of them are democratic socialists, and they said that they had secured commitments from you already. It was in a positive direction, still wasn't enough to win their vote. But can you tell us what commitments you have made to the left of your party?

REP. JEFFRIES: The only commitments that I've made is to continue to deliver upon the aggressive agenda that we've talked about with respect to making life more affordable for the American people, and that's in every area. We believe we have to drive down the high cost of healthcare, and housing, and gas, and groceries, and goods, and utilities, and caregiving, and we have plans to make sure that we aggressively engage in every single one of those areas. With respect to the House Democratic Caucus, I'm going to continue to have an open-door policy and talk to everyone. But what I believe unites us is our shared commitment to the affordability agenda and our shared commitment to making sure that if you have folks out there who've been stealing from the American people, screwing over the American people, or shortchanging the American people, we will also hold the crooks accountable.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But that doesn't mean impeachments come January? It's not an immediate plan?

REP. JEFFRIES: We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out. We're focused on actually delivering and keeping our commitment. And it's my expectation that with respect to the accountability agenda that everyone involved and whatever investigations are unveiled, they're going to follow the facts, they're going to apply the law, they're going to be guided by the Constitution, and they're going to let the chips fall where they may, so we can deliver a government of the people, by the people, and for the people that's focused on actually making life better for everyday Americans.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Speaker-designate, we will watch your work. More questions for you, but we have to leave it there for today.

REP. JEFFRIES: Thank you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be right back with a lot more Face the Nation. Stay with us.

World.title: Jeffries talks about where Democrats may be able to work with Trump
World.content:
Washington — Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's set to become House Speaker when his party takes control of Congress next year, outlined areas on Sunday where he said Democrats "can explore coming together" with President Trump.

"Let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare," Jeffries said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

As Democrats are poised to take control of both the House and Senate in the new year, following a slew of victories in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump expressed openness to working with Democrats in recent days — citing healthcare as a possible area for compromise.

"I'm open to great healthcare," Mr. Trump said at a press briefing on Friday. "Now, can it be what they want? No. But it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans."

Jeffries identified a couple of areas where Democrats and Republicans might come together, pointing to lowering the age of Medicare eligibility, expanding healthcare coverage to include vision, hearing and dental, and making sure that children get coverage, "so that every single child and young American in this country can afford to go see a doctor when they need one."

"That's a place where we can explore coming together," Jeffries said. "I know it has strong support amongst Democrats in the House and the Senate, and let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare."

The New York Democrat repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"

"The economy is broken — life is not working for far too many Americans, and it's clear we can't simply return to the status quo," he said.

Jeffries said Democrats are "committed to bringing about the type of dramatic change the American people are demanding."

Beyond healthcare, where Democrats more broadly would like to see a reversal to the Medicaid cuts in the GOP's One Big Beautiful Bill last year, Jeffries said the two other key areas of focus in the next Congress will be the high cost of living and the immigration system.

"Those are three possible areas to explore whether we can work together with the president and our colleagues on the other side of the aisle," Jeffries said.

Jeffries also highlighted combating corruption as an early focus, saying that Democrats have promised the American people that "we need to deal with accountability" among lawmakers, the Supreme Court and members of the administration.

"No one is going to get a pass," he said.

Jeffries said stock trading by lawmakers will be high on the Democrats' agenda.

"Very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock," adding, "we will see if that gets the bipartisan support needed."

The president's relationship with Jeffries still remains to be defined. But Mr. Trump has already cast doubt on his ability to work with Jeffries' expected counterpart on the other side of the Capitol, Sen. Chuck Schumer.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Mr. Trump said in a post on Truth Social earlier Sunday. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again. All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one. Here we go again!"

When asked whether impeachment efforts would be a focal point for the House Democrats in the new Congress, Jeffries said, "We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out."

"We're focused on actually delivering and keeping our commitment. And it's my expectation that with respect to the accountability agenda, that everyone involved in whatever investigations are unveiled, they're going to follow the facts," Jeffries said. "They're going to apply the law. They're going to be guided by the Constitution, and they're going to let the chips fall where they may."

World.title: U.N. climate summit ends without deal after contentious fossil fuel debate
World.content:
COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.

The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement that Sunday he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome of the summit.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," he said. "But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."

The United States sent no representatives to the climate conference for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. That accord set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a target that has anchored every U.N. climate summit since and that the world is now poised to overshoot.

Talks reached an impasse Sunday, as the European Union opposed a draft agreement that failed to mention fossil fuels and which, its delegates argued, placated countries that export them.

"We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuel, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU in Antalya. "And we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

The EU joined a group of smaller nations facing heightened threats of climate extremes and challenged oil producers, like Saudi Arabia, that staunchly rejected their views. The finale came after days of tense discussions over some of the core topics at issue during the summit, including whether to establish new rules and goals around transitioning away from coal, oil and natural gas in favor of renewable energy.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkey's environmental minister, said in televised comments from Antalya on Sunday that a draft had not been adopted due to a lack of consensus. The conference rules require unanimous agreement to reach a deal, so even a single nation's dissent can derail the process.

"We have always emphasized that this process is one that respects the will of the parties. We did everything we could," Kurum said. "In the end, we did not impose this text on anyone. We did not pressure anyone with a take-it-or-leave-it approach. There are parties in the hall that oppose this text, and we see that there is no agreement on it. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted."

Australia's climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, who shared the COP31 presidency with Kurum as Turkey and Australia jointly hosted this year's summit, said Sunday that talks broke down because of "unbridgeable red lines" and added that "the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory," reported CBS partner BBC News.

On Friday, the scheduled final day of the conference, a coalition led by France and Panama and including countries from Europe, Africa, Latin America and the Pacific rejected the latest draft agreement as too weak, according to the U.N. The group demanded explicit language on fossil fuels and stronger commitments on climate finance.

"We cannot continue to be held hostage by petroleum producers," said Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, at a news conference last week. He also vowed that Panama would formally object to any deal omitting issues related to fossil fuels.

People protest on the scheduled final day of the COP31 climate conference on November 20, 2026 in Antalya, Turkey. Chris McGrath / Getty Images

An initial draft of negotiators' agreement had called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels," a recurring goal at these summits, and urged an end to inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. It also resolved to bring warming back below 1.5 degrees as early as possible this century. But that language was gone days later, reflecting deep divisions over timelines and financing.

Later drafts still did not contain language about fossil fuels, although they did include proposed targets to capture billions of tons of carbon dioxide annually from the atmosphere by 2035, using technology that critics have said distracts from the need to cut fossil fuel use. They also called for electricity to supply more than a third of the world's energy by the same deadline, alongside goals around renewable energy and energy efficiency.

Negotiators had expressed "deep concern" in drafted text over global warming, which at its peak is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees. They also reaffirmed the need "for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions," warning that every increment of additional warming will increase the frequency and intensity of climate-related loss and damage. If current international climate plans were fully implemented, they noted, the world would be on track for just over 2.5 degrees of warming, down from projections of more than 4 degrees before the Paris accord.

The COP31 summit unfolded in a year marked by deadly disasters, record heat, destructive wildfires, tumultuous surf and other anomalies, which meteorologists have largely tied to a powerful El Niño. Scientists say its effects are amplified by climate change.

Speaking in Antalya last week, Guterres urged governments to move away from fossil fuels, triple adaptation funding by 2035 and tax fossil fuel companies' windfall profits to help vulnerable nations recover from disasters. "Polluters must pay," he said. At a press conference two days later, he linked the climate crisis to deeper social and political instability.

"You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it," Guterres said. "You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause the crisis suffer first and worst."

Some environmental advocates felt the conference proposals didn't go far enough to meet the needs of communities that are already facing real consequences of the climate crisis.

Ellen Dorsey, named this month to the TIME100 climate list, told CBS News after leaving Antalya over the weekend that she hadn't expected substantial action from COP31, despite clear signs of urgency.

"The time for simply talking about phasing out fossil fuels is over. Governments need to act," Dorsey told CBS News. "That means no fossil fuel expansion, an end to fossil fuel subsidies, and an equitable phaseout that protects workers and communities."

Dorsey said fossil fuel lobbying has grown over the past decade, as has the presence of industry interests in national delegations at U.N. climate talks, including this one. Still, she sees promise in efforts pushing back, from grassroots movements to the Santa Marta process, a coalition using diplomacy to drive a transition away from coal, oil and gas.

"Momentum is building beyond the negotiations," said Dorsey, who called this "a historic inflection point" for climate policy. "The opportunity for real systemic change is here."

World.title: Tony Shalhoub on food, family, and his book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave"
World.content:
He was a detective with a quirk in "Monk," and played an alien opposite the "Men in Black." But if you really want to feel the soul of Tony Shalhoub, this character might be it: the stubborn chef Primo in "Big Night," his 1996 film with Stanley Tucci about food, family and … even more food.

Tony Shalhoub and Stanley Tucci as brothers running a struggling Italian restaurant in New Jersey in "Big Night" (1998). Samuel Goldwyn Pictures/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images

Shalhoub is himself an investor in a New York City restaurant, Massara, where he invited us last week to break bread with his daughter, Josie Adams. The act of breaking bread, he said, is very important: "It's part of the family tradition, really. Having bread at the center of the table, it's how we were formed."

He's even made a TV series, "Tony Shalhoub Breaking Bread," about different types of bread from different places.

For him and his family, the passion for food can be traced back to a time when there wasn't any. Shalhoub's father, Joseph, was born in war-torn Lebanon. Orphaned at a young age, he faced hunger and food shortages as a child. "A lot of his early memories were about that hunger," he said, "so that ties into our current family situation and our appreciation for and devotion to preparing food and feeding each other."

Actor Tony Shalhoub with his daughter, Josie Adams, discuss their book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family." CBS News

The Shalhoubs settled in Green Bay, Wisconsin, and by the time Tony came along in 1953, there were a lot of mouths to feed; he was one of ten children.

The family was close, and stayed that way. Every summer, the entire extended Shalhoub clan – more than 50 in all – gathers in Wisconsin for a reunion. It's a week of big, homecooked meals and intense family bonding. And when the party's over, everyone gets a traditional Shalhoub family send-off: "At the end of the week," Tony said, "as people are loading up their cars, everyone else who's remaining gathers in a line in the drive and raises their hands," and a chorus cries out: "We thought they'd never leave!"

Gallery Books

"We Thought They'd Never Leave" became the title of a book Shalhoub co-wrote with Josie, the story of their family and its recipes.

She actually started it during the pandemic, when both of her parents (Tony and actor Brooke Adams) were sick with COVID, and she feared that their memories and recipes would be lost forever. So, she gave them both journals to write it all down. "My dad was like, 'Do you think we're going to die? Why are you giving us this right now?'" Josie said. "He's like, 'I'm better now!' So I said, 'OK, well, will you maybe work on this cookbook with me? I'd like to do the family cookbook for real.' And he said yes."

Shalhoub and his wife raised two daughters in Los Angeles as he navigated the feast-or-famine life of a Hollywood actor. But for every Emmy-winning success like "Monk," there were lesser roles. "Sometimes there were jobs that I did that were just for the money," he said. "Do I regret doing those jobs? Not really. I mean, maybe one or two, but sometimes you just got to eat."

In 2016 he said he wanted to take a break from screen acting, move to New York, and just do live theater. He won a Tony Award for best lead actor in a musical for "The Band's Visit."

But then he got a job offer that was irresistible. As family patriarch Abe Weissman in "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel," Shalhoub won his fifth Emmy.

In real life, Shalhoub has been married to Brooke Adams for 34 years, and he actually does a lot of the cooking at home. Josie said, "Yeah, you cook for Mom a lot. Every morning my dad wakes up before my mom and makes her a cappuccino and brings it to her in bed. Every single morning."

"Except when I'm not there!" he laughed.

And that's the Shalhoub family's love language: cooking and serving each other, whether it's one loved one, or a crowd of 50.

Waving goodbye at the end of a Shalhoub family reunion. Tony Shalhoub

Josie said, "It's really easy to send a text and say, 'I love you, thinking about you.' But it's a lot harder to do something for someone else. And that's what this whole reunion is about: getting together and showing the people that you love, that you love them."
