World.title: Why cybersecurity matters from your phone to your fridge
World.content:
Jevon Davis, Chief Operating Officer from Guardsman Cyber Intelligence Limited

Cyberattacks targeting supermarkets and cooling systems across Europe earlier this month reaffirmed the expanding threat to digital security, where hackers aren’t just going after personal information.

Guardsman Cyber Intelligence Limited Chief Operating Officer Jevon Davis told Observer Online that as homes and items become more interconnected and people depend more on operational technology, the Internet of Things (IoT) grows, including everything from smart cameras to televisions and appliances.

He also noted that what hackers want isn’t always clear-cut or financially motivated.

“It’s a matter of risk versus reward… what happened in Europe demonstrates that cyberattacks can also be a case where it affects physical equipment and basic operations,” Davis explained.

“Let’s use the supermarket as an example: if an attacker gains access to a food system and manipulates, let’s say, the temperatures, the business could potentially lose significant amounts of inventory and experience operational disruption…something that sounds unusual, like hacking a refrigerator, can reward hackers,” he shared.

Davis stressed that the “reward” can extend past stealing financial information.

“Even in the case of the everyday user, you may say that hackers don’t want to necessarily hack me, You might think so, but at the same time, some of them are just in it for just causing disruption, so sometimes the motivation isn’t financial gain or extortion. It’s sometimes just deliberate disruption,” he said.

The Europe attack, now being described as unprecedented, affected France in October and around seven other European companies in November, hitting over 700 stores. Hackers gained control of refrigerators remotely and increased the temperatures, resulting in millions of euros in losses.

Jamaica is not exempt from attacks because it is a small country, Davis explained.

“We do see where it happens every day, every minute, every second. So at Guardsman Cyber Intelligence, one of our duties is to protect the existing client environment. So we see live attacks happening every day,” he explained.

Davis added that hackers are also always looking for the next way to compromise an organisation or even a country.

As the government and populace prioritise efficiency and Jamaica continues to move toward increased digital infrastructure, there is more at risk, according to Davis.

“Any time technology tends to grow more and more, whether it would be in an organisation or even at an individual level, there’s always more risk. But one of the things that we can do is to essentially have an idea of what we’re implementing or growing from a technological perspective,” he said.

He urged businesses to maintain an inventory of connected equipment, understand their purpose, identify who is responsible for managing them, and review where they can be accessed.

“It shouldn’t just be limited to traditional computers and servers. It should include the relevant IoT devices and operational equipment, just like we discussed earlier with the fridge,” he explained.

Davis also said it was important to reduce unnecessary exposure.

“Not every device needs to be directly accessible from the internet; in fact, for critical operational equipment, direct internet exposure should generally be avoided,” he said.

For individuals at home, the recommendation is to have a good internet router that is properly secured.

“That is often the main connection between your devices on the internet… If you have bought a recent appliance and you have to set up the internet on it, change the default password…that is something that attackers like to take advantage of,” he added.

World.title: Special Olympics officials request privacy for loved ones after Beach Games tragedy
World.content:
Onlookers at the Harmony Beach Park in Montego Bay, St James, after an athlete went missing in a swimming competition during the Special Olympics Caribbean Beach Games on Friday. (Photo: Collin Reid)

MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica — Special Olympics officials are requesting privacy for the friends and family of the Rwandan athlete who died during the Caribbean Beach Games at Harmony Beach Park on Friday.

The athlete went missing during swimming competition on Friday morning, and his body was later discovered in the water.

READ: Rwandan athlete at Special Olympics Beach Games believed to have drowned

“We are saddened to confirm that an individual involved in a water-related incident during the Beach Games event has died. The cause of death has not yet been determined.

“Our deepest condolences are with their family and friends, and we ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time,” said a statement from Special Olympics North America, which has oversight of the Caribbean programmes.

The 2026 Caribbean Beach Games — the first of its kind to be held in Jamaica — officially began with the opening ceremony on Thursday. The closing ceremony is set for this evening.

The Beach Games comprise delegations from 18 Special Olympics regional programmes, as well as the invited contingent from Rwanda. Athletes have been competing in swimming, football, volleyball, basketball, and bocce.

World.title: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
World.content:
The gathering drew lawmakers from the U.S. Congress and opposition leaders from Italy, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands, united in the belief that taxing the super-rich could help the left regain the political initiative.

Their pitch was that Zucman’s proposed annual minimum tax of 2% on billionaires’ wealth is a modest measure that most voters already support — and a potent answer to the far right.

“It’s the status quo which is radical,” said Zucman, who cites polls that put support for his tax in France at 86%.

“Remigration will not make your life better, but redistribution will,” said Elly Schlein, leader of Italy’s Democratic Party.

The summit ran for almost 12 hours in a hall the size of a small community theater that was packed for much of the day. Proceedings spilled into corridors and side rooms, where politicians and union leaders from the U.S., Europe and Latin America met between panels.

The event also marked the launch of the Paris Manifesto, a declaration against “international oligarchy” that pairs a minimum tax on the ultra-rich with protections for journalists and a new ownership model for AI companies. More than 100 researchers have signed it, including Nobel Prize-winning economists Joseph Stiglitz, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Daron Acemoglu.

World.title: Cyprus expels Russian diplomats on suspicion of espionage
World.content:
They added that the two diplomats were forced to leave Cyprus last week and were suspected of working for Russian intelligence under diplomatic cover. The men were in contact with Cypriot citizens who had access to confidential information, the officials said.

POLITICO contacted the Russian Embassy in Cyprus for comment on the matter but did not receive a response at the time of publication.

Moscow was once considered a primary source of foreign direct investment for Nicosia and the Mediterranean island previously served as a banking hub for Russian investors, from arms dealers to gambling firms.

But in recent years, EU sanctions, regulatory pressure and shifting geopolitical alignment have forced Nicosia to move away from these kinds of investments. Cyprus, an EU member, has backed the bloc’s escalating sanctions against Russia in the wake of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

European countries have expelled more than 700 Russian officials from diplomatic establishments since Russia began its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

World.title: COP31 : l’accord capote sur fond de désaccord sur les énergies fossiles
World.content:
Près de 200 pays ont débattu sur différents aspects de la transition énergétique, et notamment l’impossibilité de limiter le réchauffement climatique à long terme à 1,5 ° au-dessus des niveaux préindustriels.

Alors que les négociations touchaient à leur fin, les parties n'ont pas réussi à surmonter leurs divergences. C'est la première fois en 17 ans, à Copenhague, que les négociations de la COP n'aboutissent pas à un accord.

“Il est inacceptable que nous ayons une décision-cadre qui ne fasse aucune référence aux combustibles fossiles […] C’est pour cette raison que l’Union européenne s’oppose fermement à ce texte”, a déclaré le ministre irlandais du Climat, Darragh O’Brien, s’exprimant au nom de l’UE.

Le Panama a qualifié cet accord de “revers”. Les Iles Marshall ont déclaré qu'accepter cet accord reviendrait à une trahison. “Nous n'accepterons pas un résultat qui compromettrait notre sécurité et menacerait notre avenir”, a déclaré la négociatrice Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

La ministre britannique de l'Energie, Miatta Fahnbulleh, qui dirigeait la délégation de son pays à la COP, a déclaré : “La situation exigeait une ambition audacieuse, et nous avons travaillé sans relâche pour tenter de parvenir à un consensus. Il est extrêmement décevant que nous n'ayons pas réussi à y parvenir.”

“Ce texte nous ramène en arrière. Il efface toute mention de la sortie des énergies fossiles, relègue la science au second plan et laisse croire que des technologies dont le déploiement à grande échelle reste incertain suffiront à régler le problème”, regrettait Monique Barbut, ministre de la Transition écologique un peu plus tôt dans la journée.

World.title: Climate deal crumbles amid fossil fuel rows
World.content:
Nearly 200 nations were locked in intense debate over issues involving energy transitions and how to respond to the reality that the world will miss its most urgent climate target — to limit long-term global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

As talks sped toward a conclusion, they were unable to bridge the divides. It is the first time in 17 years that COP talks have failed to reach agreement.

“It is unconscionable that we will have a cover decision that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transition away from fossil fuel, and it is for that reason that the European Union strongly objects to this text,” said Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU.

Panama called the deal a “setback.” The Marshall Islands said accepting the deal would be a betrayal. “We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future,” said negotiator Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

The U.K.'s Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who led her country's COP delegation, said: “The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”

Fossil fuel silence

The inability to land a deal on a deeply divisive text illustrates how fraught the talks have become, at a time when the world’s climate targets are drifting further out of reach and energy price shocks, war and inflation are testing governments’ willingness to embrace new pledges.

World.title: ‘Brexit is done’: Theresa May tells Burnham to move on
World.content:
Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership. On Friday, he proposed an “informal brainstorming process” to explore the future relationship, without explicitly putting rejoining on the agenda.

His European relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told POLITICO on Friday that the government would take its time setting out those options, given the divisive nature of the debate.

May said she was “slightly aghast” at the prospect of further negotiations over EU membership, warning that such talks would consume time across government, from the prime minister to officials.

She also accused Burnham of patronizing voters who backed leaving in the 2016 referendum.

“He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer,” she added.

May campaigned to remain in the EU but became prime minister after the referendum, promising to carry out the result. She resigned in 2019 after repeatedly failing to get her Brexit deal through Parliament.

World.title: All flights to and from Brussels, Charleroi airports canceled Monday amid strike
World.content:
Charleroi's management criticized Skeyes for the short notice of the action, saying the company had informed it of the disruption less than 36 hours in advance, despite the airport having prepared to operate normally.

In a statement Saturday, Charleroi accused air traffic controllers of showing a "completely cavalier attitude" toward airlines, passengers and airport staff.

It said thousands of travelers and some 3,400 people working at Charleroi would be affected, and called on Belgian authorities to develop a coordinated plan to prevent recurring disruptions.

“Skeyes has been informed that a group of air traffic controllers will participate in the national strike on Monday, November 23," the agency said in a press release, adding, "Staffing levels will be insufficient to ensure the management of normal air traffic under optimal safety conditions during this period. Consequently, Skeyes is compelled to temporarily suspend the affected services."

Monday's protest is organized by Belgium's main trade unions against spending cuts and economic reforms pursued by Prime Minister Bart De Wever's government.

Public transport across Brussels is also expected to be disrupted.

Passengers have been advised to check with their airlines before heading to either airport.

Tommaso Lecca contributed to this report. This story has been updated.

World.title: 14 missing after Russian strike as Zelenskyy presses US over Patriot missiles
World.content:
He urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s partners through NATO’s PURL program, which allows allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said earlier this month that deliveries under the program, including Patriots, were continuing.

Russia launched 186 drones overnight, including 72 jet-powered models, Ukraine’s air force said. Ukrainian defenses shot down or disabled 161, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations.

Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked 20 Ukrainian regions over the past week, launching around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles.

Many were ballistic missiles, including North Korean-made weapons, he said, accusing Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy.

World.title: Europeans dare to believe Trump could deliver security for Ukraine
World.content:
Neither is yet certain, and one Russian official dismissed the idea.

But Russian President Vladimir Putin himself has not yet publicly rejected Kushner’s plan, and European negotiators are taking it seriously, even if they want more information about how it would work.

A security guarantee for Ukraine based on NATO’s Article 5 collective defense clause, which states that an attack on one member shall be treated as an attack on all, would change the game when it comes to deterring Russia from invading Ukraine again after this war ends. That is particularly true if, as implied, America, with its mighty military, is bound into such a guarantee.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, back, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave a Coalition of the Willing media call in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool photo by Hannah McKay/Getty Images

While few details are known about the proposal, it would, if backed up by robust legal, military and political commitments, mean that a new attack on Ukraine would risk a direct conflict with the U.S.

An aide in French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the U.S. is heading in “the right direction” but called on the White House to go a step further and give Ukraine full NATO membership.

An Article 5 guarantee “is obviously the best guarantee of solidarity among allies,” said the aide, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “So, if we say we’re giving Ukraine Article 5-type guarantees, we shouldn’t overcomplicate things: It means that Ukraine is joining NATO. The alliance’s credibility rests above all on Article 5. Article 5 is an article of faith.”

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 22nd, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: West Bank: Four Palestinian villages targeted in suspected settler attacks
World.content:
In Deir Abu Mashaal, northwest of Ramallah, footage showed residents inspecting the charred remains of their vehicles outside homes marked with graffiti. Similar scenes unfolded in Kafr Malik, east of the city, where Palestinians gathered around burnt cars and examined Hebrew slogans sprayed on walls.

 

Local activist Jihad al-Qaq told AFP that settlers had entered the outskirts of Kafr Malik at around 2 am, setting fire to approximately eight vehicles and leaving racist messages on houses. Israeli police confirmed that an investigation had been launched, while the military said soldiers and officers had been deployed to four affected villages and condemned the attacks.

The incidents also affected Deir as-Sudan and Al-Tuwani, amid continuing tensions in the occupied West Bank. Violence in the territory has intensified since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the subsequent war in Gaza. According to an AFP tally based on Palestinian health ministry figures, at least 1,119 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since then.

Official Israeli figures indicate that at least 51 Israelis, including soldiers, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or clashes over the same period. More than 500,000 Israeli settlers live alongside approximately three million Palestinians in the territory, where settlements are considered illegal under international law. The latest incidents follow new British and Australian sanctions targeting eight Israeli companies linked to settlement activity.

World.title: Autopsy report reveals: Baltic Sea whale 'Timmy' starved to death
World.content:
A Danish report has revealed that Timmy, the humpback whale that stranded several times off Germany's Baltic Sea coast last spring, died of starvation.

 

For months, Timmy struggled to swim with a heavy fishing net trapped in its mouth. By the time he died, the whale was severely emaciated and ultimately drowned.

Timmy was given its nickname in reference to the beach where the whale first stranded, on Timmendrofer beach.

The whale soon became a global sensation after multiple sightings attracted widespread attention. However, the case also sparked strong criticism from animal rights activists, who questioned how local authorities handed the situation.

An investigation by the German weekly newspaper Die Zeit has shed new light on the whale's fate and the controversial rescue attempts.

According to the report, Timmy had previously become entangled before being stranded in a gillnet of the type legally used for cod fishing at depths of around 50 metres between Denmark and Sweden. Two experts who analysed fragments of the net for the newspaper ruled out the possibility that it had been used by fishermen in the Baltic Sea.

This suggests that the net was not a so-called ghost net drfiting freely in the water. Fisheries biologist Daniel Stepputtis told Die Zeit that Timmy had probably torn the net from its anchors, dragging a section measuring about 150 metres long and three metres wide behind her.

"And that costs an awful lot of energy," he said.

Fishing-net dealer Eike Peters added that the obstruction in the whale's mouth had likely made it impossible for the animal to feed.

The report found that Timmy's stomach was completely empty during the post-mortem, with lead pathologist Tim Kåre Jensen claiming the animal had not eaten in months.

It is unclear when exactly Timmy became entangled in the net, and the report found no underlying illness that could have been the cause of death.

Rescue team "chaotic and divided"

Die Zeit also revealed serious mistakes in the rescue operation, and indications that Timmy endured considerable suffering during its rescue operation.

Local authorities approved a private rescue operation under growing public pressure, despite experts warning that the mission could cause more harm than good to the humpback whale.

Voice messages, documents and video material reportedly reveal that members from the private rescue operation team had acted in a "divided, unqualified and chaotic" manner.

World.title: BepiColombo space probe enters Mercury's orbit after eight-year journey
World.content:
The BepiColombo probe has entered Mercury's orbit following an eight-year journey through outer space, the European Space Agency (ESA) said early on Sunday.

 

The BepiColombo mission is a joint venture between the ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

It launched in 2018 from French Guiana and aims to study all aspects of Mercury - the closest planet to the sun - in the hopes of providing scientists with a better understanding of the planet and of the evolution of our solar system.

"We've heard back from Bepi - the spacecraft is now in contact with Ground and the teams at ESOC are busy assessing the telemetry, but Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury," the ESA announced in a post on X.

The agency added that it would share a fresh update early next week.

According to the mission plan, the European and Japanese orbiters are set to separate from each other on 9 to 10 December, while the mission’s science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027.

"BepiColombo will be the second and most complex mission ever to orbit Mercury. Close to the Sun and more difficult for an orbiter to reach than Saturn, this small desert world is the least explored planet of the inner Solar System," the ESA says on its website.

The smallest planet in our solar system, Mercury also experiences extreme temperature fluctuations, reaching highs of 430°C and lows of -180°C.

NASA's Mariner 10 probe became the first spacecraft to visit Mercury after launching in 1973.

World.title: COP31 climate talks fail after EU and others reject final deal proposal
World.content:
The COP31 talks have failed to agree a climate deal after the European Union and a number of countries rejected a final proposal over the omission of fossil fuels.

 

COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum acknowledged that the deal had failed to reach consensus.

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," he told the closing session of the conference in Antalya, Turkey.

Darragh O'Brien, the climate and energy minister for Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, had earlier said the EU would "not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change."

He added that the EU and its member states "object" to the draft because it "does not meet the moment."

A new COP31 draft agreement had been published early on Sunday amid a row over fossil fuels, which have been a flashpoint at the late-running talks.

It came after a previous draft had called for an accelerated phasing out of the energy sources before a second version released on Thursday removed all mentions of them.

A group of countries including France and Panama then released a letter on Friday insisting that a deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."

COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

United Nations Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed" that the talks had ended without consensus.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," Guterres said in a statement. "Those who profit from the destruction of our planet must never dictate the terms of the fight to save it. Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis."

Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who led negotiations, has also expressed his disappointment at the outcome.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision... And that's disappointing. Very disappointing," he said.

The summit became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday, with negotiations stretching two days past their scheduled finish time.

World.title: Emergency workers recover at least six body bags after Indonesian factory fire
World.content:
Emergency workers in Indonesia have recovered at least six body bags after a major factory fire in western Java.

 

Indonesian police said the blaze broke out at a candy factory in the Serang Regency of Banten province on Saturday.

A joint emergency team removed the six body bags from the site, police said.

A further 42 out of 54 recorded employees remain unaccounted for, "while 11 returned home and one is receiving medical treatment," the force added.

"We are also continuing to coordinate with families and the company to verify the whereabouts of employees suspected to have been inside the factory area when the fire broke out," senior superintendent Maruli Ahiles Hutapea said in a statement.

"Meanwhile, search and evacuation operations inside the production and office buildings will be carried out once the cooling process is complete and the site is declared safe by personnel."

The fire began at around 4:30 pm on Saturday and was extinguished by 6:30 am on Sunday, according to police.

Video footage posted on social media by Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas), showed emergency crews looking through the charred remains of the building.

The candy company, Fonusa Agung Mulia, describes itself online as a subsidiary of Indonesia's UNIFAM food company.

World.title: 15 people missing after Russian drone strike on Kyiv region
World.content:
Fifteen people are missing after a Russian drone strike destroyed part of a five-story apartment building in the Kyiv region, Ukrainian police said on Sunday.

 

Search and rescue operations are underway at the scene of the attack in Dymer, north of the Ukrainian capital.

"Fifteen people are currently listed as missing, including two children: an 11-year-old girl and a seven-year-old boy," Ukraine's National Police wrote in a post on Telegram.

Images from the scene show emergency crews picking through the debris as they work to find survivors.

Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said the bodies of two people had been recovered from the rubble and that at least four people had been injured.

He added that a command centre had been set up to help coordinate a response to the attack, with social services and psychologists working out of the site.

Emergency services personnel work at a damaged apartment building following a Russian attack in Dymer, Kyiv region, Ukraine, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

It comes after Russian forces fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles at Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it "one of the largest attacks" of the war so far.

At least seven people were killed in Kyiv in those strikes, while key bridges across the Dnipro River were also damaged.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian forces had launched around 2,700 drones, close to 1,460 aerial bombs, and 165 missiles at 20 Ukrainian regions this week.

"A significant number were ballistic missiles, including North Korean ones, which the Russians are constantly helping Pyongyang modernize to improve their accuracy," Zelenskyy said, as he renewed calls for allies to speed up deliveries of interceptor missiles.

"It is particularly difficult to understand the delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors to Ukraine," the Ukrainian leader added, urging Washington to authorise transfers of interceptors already paid for through NATO's PURL initiative.

Ukrainian forces reportedly also carried out their own strikes overnight, targeting a Russian National Guard facility in an attack on Krasnodar.

Five people are reported to have been injured in the strikes on the region, including four in Afipsky, a settlement home to an oil refinery that has previously been targeted by Ukraine.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.

“This is part of a process of basically closing down all independent media that might risk reaching followers of the ruling party,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb of Human Rights Watch.

“The whole tactic of the Erdogan government has been to use court orders. The court orders are so problematic in themselves, so overreaching, so disproportionate, that this has nothing really to do with the legal process. This is all about a political crackdown.”

Turkey talks green at Cop31 while cracking down on activists

Sinclair-Webb noted that television remains the primary news source for most Turks, making both networks and individual journalists who question government policies prime targets.

Four journalist have been detained or placed under house arrest for reporting on the investment scandal.

Authorities accuse Sozcu TV of ties to followers of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for masterminding a failed 2016 coup. Four of its executives and officials have been detained. Halk TV faces separate corruption allegations.

Both broadcasters strongly deny the charges.

Investment scandal

The closing of the channels comes amid fallout from the collapse of more than 100 investment funds, which wiped out $20 billion, stranded more than 500,000 investors and triggered a stock market crash.

The scandal has implicated numerous figures linked to Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party).

According to recent polls, 80 percent of Turks are closely following the scandal, with a similar majority blaming the government.

On Thursday, protesters demonstrated outside the Capital Markets Board, the country's financial regulator, in Ankara.

Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next

Around 500 people are under investigation and more than 100 suspects have been jailed. Erdogan vowed this week that no one would escape justice and promised to expedite repayments to affected investors.

Political analyst Sezin Oney said the government is scrambling to control the public narrative as its reputation among its own voter base unravels.

“Up to now, AK Party and government circles were able to project to their base the idea that the opposition [is involved in] all sorts of corruption. So all of a sudden, that facade, that rhetoric has collapsed. Now it’s the government circles who are massively corrupt."

Debate moves online

Atilla Yesilada, a Turkey analyst at New York-based consultancy firm Global Source Partners, warned that the scandal has exposed deep flaws in financial oversight, threatening severe economic and political fallout for Erdogan.

“Turkey is heading for a recession because the institutional structure has completely collapsed,” Yesilada said. “In a free market economy, you really need regulatory boards to do their work which clearly, as we see in this instance, they don't. In fact, they enable or incentivise thieves [and make] their jobs easier."

Yesilada added that Erdogan lacks a clear path to resolve the crisis, as opposition figures release new allegations implicating AK Party associates daily.

Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy

Following the state takeover of another broadcaster last year, the loss of Sozcu TV and Halk TV marks a grim turning point for Turkish media, Oney said. However, she questioned whether the government can successfully suppress public discourse.

“It’s the end of the road for TV journalism, you don’t have any oppositional voice or oppositional debate. But people talk, people think, one way or another. Because Turkey was a thinking and talking nation before, it's very difficult to stop [that]. It is just [being done now] on social media.”

The government has accelerated efforts to police online dissent, shutting down hundreds of critical social media accounts, although new ones are emerging just as rapidly.

Meanwhile Koza TV, a previously fringe station, has seen its ratings surge after becoming a new outlet for independent reporting on the scandal – although mounting regulatory fines make its future uncertain.
