World.title: Horne-Francis planning to recruit Nasiah during AFL Origin camp
World.content:
Jason Horne-Francis is open to throwing his weight around in South Australia's AFL Origin camp to recruit St Kilda superstar and friend Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera.

South Australia and Western Australia today named their first five representatives for next year's Origin match, to be played at Perth Stadium on February 27.

Wanganeen-Milera and Port Adelaide's Horne-Francis were picked by SA coach Craig McRae, along with Saints co-captain Callum Wilkie, Adelaide skipper Jordan Dawson and Collingwood boom recruit Lachie Neale.

Players committed to 2027 AFL Origin SOUTH AUSTRALIA: Jason Horne-Francis, Callum Wilkie, Lachie Neale, Jordan Dawson, Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera WESTERN AUSTRALIA: Patrick Cripps, Charlie Cameron, Kysaiah Pickett, Luke Jackson, Tom Barrass

Wanganeen-Milera rejected massive interest from his native South Australia in 2025 to re-sign on a two-season, $4 million deal with the Saints.

Locking away the silky 23-year-old playmaker on an extension is top of St Kilda's agenda.

This year's Origin revival match between WA and Victoria allowed Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli to build a connection with Zak Butters, who crossed from Port Adelaide in the off-season.

While already mates with Wanganeen-Milera, Horne-Francis is mindful of the recruitment opportunity Origin camp presents.

"That worked, didn't it," he told reporters, referring to the Butters-Bontempelli connection developed through Victoria's Origin team.

Marcus Bontempelli (background) successfully recruited Victorian teammate Zak Butters (foreground) to the Western Bulldogs. (Daniel Carson/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

"So maybe I've got to try to do the same thing. Not that we need any more bonding time — we see each other bloody all the time anyway.

"We ran out together in the [Indigenous] All-Stars as well, so it will be good to run out with him again and see what he's got for us."

The 23-year-old admitted he might have to battle with Crows rivals to wrap an arm around Wanganeen-Milera, who finished fourth in St Kilda's best-and-fairest this season.

"There might be a bit of push and shove there," the Port ball-winner said.

St KIlda star Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera is once again in high demand as he comes out of contract. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Horne-Francis and other Adelaide-based SA representatives may have to go through Wilkie to get some alone time with Wanganeen-Milera.

"I won't let him talk to Dawson or anyone from Port," Wilkie joked.

"He'll stay right under my wing.

"Nas is amazing at putting that [contract speculation] to bed and focusing on us and what he brings to the club on field and off field."

Wilkie said he and Wanganeen-Milera had been speaking about the possibility of donning the SA jumper all year.

Collingwood coach Craig McRae will lead Wanganeen-Milera and South Australia in the Origin clash. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"That's what's so special about it," he said.

"You think when you're getting drafted you're never going to be able to pull the colours on again."

WA coach Dean Cox's first selections are Hawthorn defender Tom Barrass, Brisbane forward Charlie Cameron, Carlton skipper Patrick Cripps, Fremantle ruck Luke Jackson and Melbourne livewire Kysaiah Pickett.

Cripps, who captained WA against Victoria this year, is also due to come off contract at the end of next season.

Carlton captain Patrick Cripps has no plans to finish his AFL career in WA. (Getty images/AFL Photos: Matt King)

But the dual Brownlow Medal winner hosed down the possibility of finishing his illustrious career in his home state after the Blues made the finals under now-permanent coach Josh Fraser, despite starting last season 1-8.

"I've been here that long, you sort of become ingrained in the club," Cripps said.

"I sort of feel like a Carlton supporter these days … this is my 14th season.

"I've always loved playing footy at Carlton and been driven to try and build the club from the ground up, and I'm really excited about where we are right now."

AAP

World.title: India breaks New Zealand Test record with monster innings in Wellington
World.content:
India has broken the record for the highest Test score in a match played in New Zealand as it put itself in a commanding position to win the first Test in Wellington.

New Zealand reached 2-119 at the close of play on day four as it fought to save the first Test after India declared on a mammoth 9-720 with an imposing first-innings lead of 352.

India's assault was led by Rishabh Pant (128), whose six sixes took his career tally to 108 in just 53 Tests, now second behind all-time best Ben Stokes (138). Pant surpassed former NZ captain Brendon McCullum (107) during the innings.

New Zealand's hopes of a result rest on batting for much of the remainder of the match and forcing a draw, despite losing Tom Latham for a duck and first-innings centurion Henry Nicholls for 31.

Opener Devon Conway, who scored his 22nd Test half-century on his way to an unbeaten 59, and Rachin Ravindra (27 not out) will resume on day five with the Black Caps still 233 runs from forcing India to bat again.

India's pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah (1-33) again made an early breakthrough, sending Latham back on the second ball of the innings, the New Zealand skipper edging behind to take a pair.

Nicholls, whose 175 was the backbone of New Zealand's first-innings 368, got an edge and a bit of thigh pad on a Prasidh Krishna delivery, and Dhruv Jurel showed stunning reflexes to take the catch at short leg.

Jurel had earlier become the sixth batter to score a half-century in India's innings before being caught in the deep for 78, triggering the declaration an hour before tea.

India had resumed on 4-486 on another sunny morning at the Basin Reserve with the clear intent of pushing their 118-run lead out to the sort of tally that would take the possibility of a New Zealand victory out of the equation.

There are few better batters for such a task than Pant, and the swashbuckling wicketkeeper showed the full range of his shots as he approached his ninth Test hundred.

Pant was finally caught on the boundary for 128 off the bowling of Ravindra to bring up lunch, but the punishment for New Zealand continued into the second session.

Jacob Duffy finished with 1-201 off 33 overs. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

India's final score was well clear of its previous best innings tally in New Zealand of 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009 — a match they won by 10 wickets.

All-rounder Glenn Phillips (3-154) picked a couple of wickets as the Indian batters went for their shots ahead of the declaration to make his figures a bit more respectable.

Seamer Jacob Duffy, though, finished with unenviable figures of 1-201 from his 33 overs, only 28 runs shy of New Zealand's most expensive ever bowling display, which spinner Stephen Boock tallied against Pakistan in 1989.

Reuters

World.title: Watch how a quiet Huntingdale street became a ‘drug house’ battleground authorities couldn’t stop
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAPublic housing Watch how a quiet Huntingdale street became a ‘drug house’ battleground authorities couldn’t stop Hannah Murphy November 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tina and her husband Tom thought they had seen it all after living next door to public housing in Huntingdale. Brazen drug-dealing, screaming, shouting, fighting in the street, home invasions and even a firebombing had become a part of their day-to-day. Loading But one Wednesday afternoon in September, they realised just how serious things had gotten. Tina was home alone while Tom was at work about 1pm on September 23, when she began to hear commotion outside. She saw two men were fighting on the street, hurling abuse at one another.



“I actually called Tom and said, ‘I don’t feel comfortable with this, they’re yelling, and they’re abusing each other. It looks like it’s going to get vicious’,” she said. And over the next half an hour, it did. The incident is another example of the plight neighbours of problematic public housing tenants face when attempting to report unruly and dangerous behaviour to the responsible authorities. Tina and Tom, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, have made dozens of reports over the last five years, with little to show in the way of resolutions. Footage from the couple’s CCTV, which was described by WA’s housing minister as “confronting” when this masthead sent it to his office, showed a man parked across from Tina and Tom’s property in a purple ute, screaming at another man to come out and fight.



They have a brief altercation where they attempt to fist fight, before the man from the house grabs a baseball bat and sets upon the visitor, who runs back to his ute, picks out tools from under the canopy, and begins hurling them. Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Debra complained about her Rivervale neighbours 60 times in three years. It’s worse than ever After another fight, the visitor takes cover behind his car, before firing up his ute and driving it straight at the front of the property, where the other man is standing. After one near miss, the ute reverses and drives straight at him again – this time, he hits the man, and the car can be seen bouncing as he runs him over. A woman’s scream is heard in the background, and the visitor does a quick donut on the front lawn before peeling off down the road.



All the while, Tina was stuck inside, “terrified”, and glued to her CCTV livestream on her phone. The driver was later charged with grievous bodily harm. The other man was not charged. Tina said for her and Tom, incidents such as these have become their norm. The problems started in 2020, when a new tenant moved in to the property they had lived next to for the last 10 years. Previously, the home had been occupied by an older man with dementia and he was allowing his family to move in.



Tina and Tom went over to introduce themselves but instead found a teenager in their front garden, stripping their plants. When Tina asked him to stop, he hurled slurs at her. Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Megan is a Perth public housing tenant. Her neighbours are making her life hell From there, things began to spiral. Tom, who is a shift worker, began counting the cars that would visit the property at all hours, landing on a figure of about 130 just in one week, and captured CCTV of drug deals happening out in the open. The house was raided twice, and on one occasion, police allegedly told the couple they were aware it was a known “drug house”.



The property has been graffitied, had its windows caved in, and petrol bombed. Tina was threatened by the same teenager at the property, who said he would “put a bullet in her head”, though police deemed it an empty threat as he did not have a firearm licence. CCTV has caught screaming at all hours, and even a woman at the property physically fighting with a police officer. Tina and Tom believe their property value dropped by as much as $200,000, and they have spent thousands fortifying their home with roller shutters and locks, and rarely get more than four hours’ sleep in a night. Ultimately, they said, they are tired. They have made 60 to 70 complaints over the last five years, they estimated, and even proceeded to eviction on one occasion. The magistrate shot it down, and the family were allowed to stay.



“There needs to be like a discussion about how we protect the community rather than just the tenants,” Tom said. “We can protect both. I mean, if the tenant occasionally has a loud party or occasionally, there’s a bit of swearing – that’s suburbia. But the things that have gone on there – that’s not normal.” “It’s a bad normal, if that makes sense,” Tina said. “You see these things happening and think, OK. I’ve got to call the police, and I’ve got to make another report. “But am I going to bother when they’re not going to do anything? The Department of Housing says under the tenancy laws, they can’t just evict them. They’ve got to take it to court, and the judge has to decide.”



WA’s public housing waitlist currently has more than 24,000 applications. Housing Minister John Carey said he had viewed the footage of September’s incident, and understood the couples’ frustrations. Minister for Planning & Lands; Housing & Works and Health Infrastructure John Carey. Oscar Colman “The footage is incredibly confronting – no one wants to see violence and anti-social behaviour in our community, regardless of where it takes place,” he said. “As the housing provider of last resort, the Department of Housing and Works accommodates some of the most vulnerable members of our community.



“The vast majority of our public housing tenants are good neighbours and their tenancies are observed without issue.” Carey said when issues arose, the department aimed to work with the tenants. But if problems continue, it worked with police and built a case in line with the Residential Tenancies Act. “The decision to terminate a tenancy agreement ultimately sits with a magistrate, who will only evict a tenant if they are satisfied that there has been a breach of the tenancy agreement, and that the tenant has been given every opportunity to rectify the breach and has failed to do so,” Carey said. Tina said this is where the system has let her and Tom down.



The couple believed more needed to be done to free up homes for other struggling families.

World.title: UN global climate talks led by Chris Bowen end in discord and recrimination
World.content:
Breaking EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement UN global climate talks led by Chris Bowen end in discord and recrimination Nick O'Malley Updated November 23, 2026 — 12:55am ,first published 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global climate talks led by Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen have failed to secure an agreement in Turkey after a standoff between oil producing nations led by Saudi Arabia and nations seeking more ambitious action on climate change, including Europe. Bowen described the outcome as “very disappointing” and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers. He commended delegations for pulling all-nighters to try to reach a deal, but said “the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory”. Chris Bowen, Climate Change and Energy Minister and president of COP31 negotiations watched on as nation after nation rejected a climate agreement at the talks. AP Photo/Khalil Hamra After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime - making it the longest COP on record - Turkey’s conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.



“There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” he said. “There will be no new text from now on.” The Saudi-led bloc backed by Russia rejected on Sunday a final agreement – known as a cover decision – that reiterated calls for a transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union said it could not support an agreement that would take backwards steps by refusing to address the need to do so. Further objections were raised by other nations over the inclusion of a call to increase the use of controversial climate capture and storage technology, also championed by the Saudi-led bloc, and by the failure of developed nations to pledge more financial support for poorer nations hardest hit by climate impacts. Cover decisions at UN climate talks can only be adopted by consensus of all parties. Speaking on behalf of the EU, Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, rejected the draft agreement on the floor of the final plenary session.



“We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change, and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel. Related Article Analysis

Paris Agreement ‘Heat records keep shattering’: Time is running out for COP to save us “I do want to, however, Mr President, commend both you and the President of Negotiations [Chris Bowen] for your unstinting efforts. However, the draft put before us does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either. And it is for that reason and those reasons that the European Union strongly objects to this text.” The failure of negotiators to arrive at an agreement comes as a huge blow to the COP process, at which almost 200 parties to the Paris Agreement sought to advance climate action, and to Bowen, who secured the role of president of negotiations when the bid he led for Australia to host the talks failed last year at talks in Brazil.



Bowen had sought to sidestep the standoff over references to fossil fuel in the cover decision by including language recognising the agreement made at previous talks in Dubai, where the world pledged to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Speaking after the EU, a member of the Panamanian delegation also rejected the deal, saying: “We need to be clear: our message is not a criticism of the presidencies. “Our disagreement is with a much deeper problem... One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it wages too much upon technologies such as CCS capture storage of carbon instead of calling for deep changes and three because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback.” A representative of the Marshall Islands said her nation had been failed by all sides at the COP. “We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. “Over the past two weeks, we have been offered next to nothing. Even as we have said again and again, our needs are so great, the costs are so high, the finance gap keeps growing. We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises. People are dying, seas are rising, ecosystems are collapsing.”



Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen (right) with Turkey’s Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum in Fiji at pre-COP. Getty As it became clear that the negotiations had failed Bowen remained silent while Turkish officials oversaw the meeting, with many speakers noting that the talks were being held just weeks after the UN Environment Program had acknowledged that the world was set to miss the Paris target of 1.5 degrees warming and head into what is now being described as climate “overshoot”. A Russian delegate told the session that Russia stands by the goals of the Paris Agreement, but that the conference made rapid phase-out of fossil fuels that he said should not have been included central to the talks. He said that the UN’s own scenarios charting a course to limiting warming to 1.5 degrees acknowledged the world will continue to use approximately 40 per cent of the oil and 50 per cent of the gas of the levels of 2019. A Saudi representative said the 22 member states of the Arab League represent less than 2 per cent of historical greenhouse gas emissions, “whereas other groups are responsible for 55 per cent of those emissions.”



In line with this he said the Arab League had called for a tripling of climate finance from wealthy to poorer nations. “This was removed from the text due to lack of flexibility from some parties on mentioning any quantitative aspects related to climate finance.” Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, took aim at the EU, which he said had failed to offer new financial support to developing nations. “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow. The EU cannot help sabotage the negotiations, then pose as the climate conscience of the world.” China noted its reservation about some of the content of the agreement, but said to demonstrate unity of collective efforts it had decided to accept the cover decision and called on “all parties to show necessary compromise spirit to push forward our process.” As president of negotiations Bowen had declared at the pre-COP meeting in Fiji that the presidency would pursue the cover decision that the COP has just rejected, in order to drive more momentum for action than might have been achieved with a series of agreements over individual agenda items.



Australia had hoped that in doing so it would champion the cause of Pacific island nations which view climate change as an existential threat, thereby deepening ties across the region as China’s influence grew. Fiji’s Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya said that though the cover decision text was not perfect she regretted it was not adopted. “Honorable Chris Bowen, you have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it,” she said. “Your commitment, patience, and determination throughout these negotiations have not gone unnoticed. “This work is hard. Sleepless nights, hours and days of constant negotiations, managing over 190 parties. This is not easy, but we do it. We do it for our people. The failure to reach consensus on the cover decision is not yours to carry. It is a collective responsibility that rests with all parties. Consensus requires compromise, courage, and political will from all of us.” Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and a member of The Elders, an independent group of global leaders founded by Nelson Mandela in 2007 to work on peace, human rights, and global challenges like climate change was more scathing.



“Recognition of the dangers of overshoot should have shaken leaders into action, instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership from the co-presidencies Turkey and Australia,” she said in a statement. “This was compounded by disturbing politicised attacks on the science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Strapped for memories
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Geoff Carey of Pagewood makes the cut: “The Christian Brothers didn’t use the cane (C8) at school. ‘Six of the best’ was delivered via a thick, handmade leather strap. Apparently, the local boot maker had a roaring trade supplying the school. The skilled and experienced brothers learnt to anticipate the involuntary withdrawal of the hand of wimps like me, following it to deliver the perfect strike on the ends of the fingers. The bravest of souls bore the boot maker’s stitching marks across the wrist, unflinching as the strap descended.”

“Thank you, Christine Perrott for the shopping bag (C8) reminder,” writes Janice Creenaune of Austinmer. “While on teacher exchange in Kidlington, near Oxford in 2007, one of the first pieces of advice from my new teacher friends was the type of plastic shopping bag to carry my lunch. I’d been using Tesco and Asda, and they assured me that Waitrose and M&S were far more acceptable. Pride was not the position, class distinction and image reigned, and while we remained on our NSW teacher’s salary for the year, we couldn’t afford the top tier of supermarkets, too.”

Anne McCarthy of Marrickville says that “the expression ‘Heavens to Betsy’ used by Serge Nemaz (C8) reminded me of other old sayings such as ‘Lawdy, lawdy Miss Maudie’ [according to the great Lloyd Price, it’s Miss Clawdy – Granny] and ‘God willing and the creek don’t rise.’ I have used the latter sometimes when discussing future commitments, often to the listener’s puzzlement.”

“Highly disagree, George Zivkovic (C8),” says a shaken Seppo Ranki of Glenhaven. “As a Whovian from William Hartnell days, I couldn’t countenance Doctor Who jumping the shark to a female Doctor, and stopped watching altogether. Jamie Bond would meet the same fate.”

Regarding the “there’s no other store like David Bowie” theory presented by Anthony Fretwell (C8), Nelson Bay denizen Judy Archer thinks name changes have worked before: “A fish named slimehead was renamed orange roughy.”

World.title: Australia’s power prices would be 50 per cent worse without renewables, says top economist
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRenewables Australia’s power prices would be 50 per cent worse without renewables, says top economist Shane Wright November 22, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s wholesale power prices would be up to 50 per cent higher if the country had embraced coal, gas or nuclear power rather than renewables and batteries, a leading economist has declared while arguing the nation had been “de-risked” from the full cost of the surge in fossil fuel prices. Guy Debelle, a former deputy governor of the Reserve Bank who is now non-executive director of independent think tank e61, has used a major address to argue Australia was lucky to embrace renewable energy sources to replace the nation’s network of coal- and gas-fired power stations. Former RBA deputy Guy Debelle said said power prices would be much higher if not for the rollout of renewable energy across the country. Bloomberg Critics of the rollout of solar and wind power plus batteries have claimed renewables have driven up Australians’ power prices. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has claimed government energy policy had prevented the construction of gas- and coal-fired power plants, leading to a 40 per cent surge in prices. But Debelle, who also sits on the board of the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, said critics ignored the pressing need to replace the Australian power system, given its suite of fossil fuel power sources had come to the end of their lifespan.



He said the huge fall in the price of renewables and batteries, and the surge in the cost of coal- and gas-fired power stations, meant Australian households were substantially better off. Related Article Electricity The biggest energy crisis in history brings on the age of electricity “The counterfactual of not doing this energy transition is that we would have a lot higher energy prices than we have today. The energy transition isn’t costless, but the alternatives are considerably more costly,” Debelle said. “Wholesale energy prices would be 30 to 50 per cent higher today than if we had not installed this renewable energy capacity. When coal and gas prices rise higher as they have done recently, than the cost savings are even larger.” Last week, former prime minister Tony Abbott linked the growth in renewable energy across Australia to the surge in household power bills while arguing for “climate warriors” to back nuclear power.



“If renewables really are cheap, they don’t need to be subsidised or mandated; and if it really is necessary to limit emissions, the climate warriors should be the strongest advocates for nuclear power because it’s the only proven emissions-free form of the base-load electricity a modern economy needs,” Abbott said. But Debelle said by every measure, renewable energy sources were cheaper to build and operate than their fossil fuel alternatives, which meant households had avoided even larger power bills. A nuclear energy plant in the American state of Illinois. Debelle says calls for nuclear power ignore the problems of building and running them. Getty Images He said that since 2010, the number of coal-fired power stations had fallen from 26 to 15 with their output dropping from 28 gigawatts of power to 21 gigawatts. Over that period, renewable energy output had grown to 36 gigawatts. In the 2025-26 financial year, Australian households installed more than 13 gigawatt hours of battery storage, or more than the United States has ever put in place.



According to Debelle, coal-fired power stations would not be competitive against renewables while calls for nuclear power ignored the long-term problems of building and running them. “Nuclear at the moment is also not a viable cost-effective solution. Cheap nuclear has been just around the corner for about the past 50 years,” he said. Record levels of renewable energy in the electricity grid are displacing coal and driving down emissions. Bloomberg “We can’t wait until that technological challenge is solved. We need the generation capacity now.” But the renewable rollout is currently running well over headline, as planning logjams and community opposition gum up project in the pipeline.



Last year, the Australian Energy Market Regulator warned projects, including new transmission links, faced cost blowouts of up to 100 per cent. A failure to streamline the national rollout could add 30 per cent to projects’ costs, the regulator estimated in a report last December. Debelle noted whole power prices had fallen across the national electricity market in recent months. But in most of the rest of the world, prices have increased by a large amount due to the US-Israel war on Iran. Australian homes with solar panels. Sitthixay Ditthavong “We’ve been able to insulate ourselves from that,” he said. Apart from the collapse in the cost of solar and wind, which are now cheaper sources of energy than coal, the fall in the use of fossil fuels is aiding Australia’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.



Debelle said that by 2030, electricity would no longer be Australia’s largest source of emissions. It would be overtaken by transport due to ongoing use of diesel- and petrol-powered vehicles. But Debelle said continuing the rollout of renewables, and providing access to the overall energy grid, remained a major challenge. He said finding ways to encourage the installation of solar on businesses and warehouses in urban areas would increase the amount of electricity available to the grid while reducing the cost of transmission lines. World.title: Cut and cut now: Economists urge next Victorian government to swing the axe
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalVictorian election Cut and cut now: Economists urge next Victorian government to swing the axe Shane Wright November 22, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The next Victorian government should immediately wind back the scale of, delay or cancel major building projects to help bring the state budget under control while looking to reduce the number of bureaucrats, the nation’s top economists have urged. A survey of high-profile economists by the Economic Society of Australia has revealed strong support for an overhaul of government spending plus the adoption of new fiscal rules to prevent a future blowout in state debt. The site of the Suburban Rail Loop in Burwood. Economists say the next Victorian government needs to slash infrastructure spending to stabilise the budget. Joe Armao They also believe Spring St needs to adopt a raft of policies to safeguard the budget and improve the economy, including a shift from stamp duty towards a broad-based land tax. The state of the Victorian budget and economy is one of the key issues at the weekend election.



Related Article Employment Unemployment hits five-year high as RBA squeezes jobs market Victoria’s net debt, forecast by Treasury to reach $197 billion by 2029-30, is the highest of all state and territories. Figures from the bureau of statistics released last week showed the Victorian economy was the slowest growing in the federation through 2025-26. The Economic Society put to members at least a dozen proposals that have been floated publicly as ways to bring down state debt and improve the performance of the Victorian election. Respondents included current Reserve Bank board member Melinda Cilento, prominent independent economist Saul Eslake, former director of the Melbourne Institute Deborah Cobb-Clark and Queensland University’s John Quiggin. Only one proposal – a reduction in infrastructure spending – was backed as a priority by most of those surveyed.



Matthew Butlin, a former Productivity Commission member, said the state was in an “appalling mess” and had choices had to be made that would require sharing pain across Victoria. “We are over-borrowed as a state, the public sector capital obligations are too large relative to our debt and income, our productivity is far too low, government spending is inadequately targeted, the tax burden is too high and we need to take a very sharp lens to what is very important over the next five years to build productivity growth,” he said. Bob Breunig, director of ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, was blunt about the choices facing the party taking office from Saturday night. “They have to cut expenditure and decide what is really needed and what isn’t,” he said. Hugh Sibly, a senior lecturer in economics from the University of Tasmania, said the Victorian budget was heavily exposed to rising interest rates because of the amount of debt it had taken on for its infrastructure program.



“Unfortunately, Victoria has engaged in some infrastructure projects, notably the Suburban Rail Loop, for which the benefits are significantly less than the costs,” he said. ANU tax expert Bob Breunig says the next Victorian government has to decide what is important and what is not. Rhett Wyman “Reprioritising towards those projects with a benefit cost ratio greater than one would help Victoria’s economic position.” The survey also showed strong support for either reducing the size of the Victorian public service or restraining public sector wages growth. Figures released last week showed that since 2014, when Labor took office, public sector wages only in Queensland had grown faster than those in Victoria. The NSW government has pledged to keep net debt under 15 per cent of state economic output. Many economists believe such a set target should be adopted by Victoria.



Uwe Dulleck, from the Crawford School of Public Policy in Canberra, cautioned that while spending cuts were necessary, they would hurt the economy in the short term. “Major repair can only be achieved with major cuts in infrastructure investments, which will have negative impact on the local economy, and a restructure of the public service (again, it has an impact on the local economy),” he said. “Thus, the balance between raising revenue and reducing expenditure is needed.” Apart from cuts, the economists largely agree there is scope for major tax reform with the number one item a shift from stamp duty on property sales to a broad-based land tax. Such a proposal was rejected by the Andrews government. Lisa Magnani, the head of Macquarie University’s economics department, said the next government should examine the state’s entire tax system, starting with its stamp duty system.



Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes “With one of the highest state debts in Australia, Victoria’s budget position is vulnerable to the negative effects of rising interest rates,” she said. “Victoria would benefit from a full review of its tax structure to possibly find new sources of revenues (particularly those with progressive features, such as taxes on high-income recipients and wealth owners).” Victoria University senior economist Janine Dixon said making the state more attractive to investors would go a long way to improving the budget. “Making Victoria an attractive place to invest would be a good start, and fits well with making sure Victoria’s considerable workforce, particularly in the outer suburbs, is well connected to employment opportunities. Addressing crime would also give potential investors more confidence,” she said.



While most economists believed budget cuts were a priority, some argued the new government should put its attention into other areas. Julie Toth, from the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia, said while budget repair was important in the long term, it was not the most urgent financial priority. She said it was more important that public services and infrastructure kept pace with Victoria’s growing population and that there was support for the state’s most disadvantaged and vulnerable residents. “Economic and social inclusion matters for everyone. We all feel the impact of ineffective safety nets and support services, directly and indirectly. This will become more urgent if unemployment rises, as is widely forecast over the next two to three years,” she said. Apart from spending cuts and tax reforms, the surveyed economists backed changes including a reduction in free services or universal concessions, introduction of road user charges and broadening of the payroll tax base.



There was also support for an overhaul of the Commonwealth Grants Commission GST allocation system which is the centre of a Productivity Commission report due by the end of the year. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: China on verge of eclipsing US power in Asia after Trump stumbles
World.content:
PoliticsFederalChina relations China on verge of eclipsing US power in Asia after Trump stumbles Matthew Knott November 22, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US President Donald Trump’s costly war against Iran has allowed China to come within a skerrick of overtaking the United States to become the most powerful country in Asia, a respected report card has found. The Lowy Institute’s latest Asia Power Index finds the US advantage over China, measured across 131 metrics, has plunged to its lowest level since the annual survey began in 2018, with the gap between the two nations’ military capabilities narrowing to its lowest level on record. The release of the report comes after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in a historic trilateral summit last week. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a rare trilateral meeting last week. Getty Russia remains ahead of Australia in fifth place in the index and behind only the US, China, India and Japan as middle powers struggle to exert influence in a region dominated by great power rivalry.



The warp-force speed of artificial intelligence developments was under the spotlight at APEC last week in Shenzhen, where Xi and Trump agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence. This Tuesday, five days after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese directly implored Xi, Trump and Putin to “make sure that AI is developed and deployed safely”, Foreign Minister Penny Wong will flag that Australia should have a role in forming AI safeguards as the frontline technology becomes a national security challenge. Citing reporting about the use of AI to attempt to sway elections in the US, Wong is expected to say: “We have long known actors beyond our shores seek to interfere in Australia’s democracy and in the lives of those who call Australia home. These tools make that interference faster, cheaper and harder to recognise.“ Wong emphasises that every advanced AI company operating in Australia - such as Anthropic - will have to build in security and safety protections. “We must do what we can to ensure that the race to develop frontier AI, concentrated in a handful of companies and countries, does not reward speed over prudence,” she will say, according to notes from an extract of her speech.



Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale is set to visit Canberra this week to strike a comprehensive treaty with Australia in the Albanese government’s latest attempt to push back China’s growing influence in the Pacific. “The conflict in the Middle East, following coordinated US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February, has fuelled perceptions of Washington’s waning interest in Asia,” authors Hunter Marston and Jack Sato argue in their report. The Trump administration’s decision to shift military resources from the Indo-Pacific to the Persian Gulf to support its war effort highlighted its lack of focus on Asia, the authors state. US strikes on Iran have depleted American missile stocks and weakened its military capabilities, and the US military has conducted fewer joint exercises and defence dialogues with its primary regional allies over the past year, including Australia, Japan, and South Korea.



Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Trump’s War Barbie is terrible at the one thing he’s supposed to be good at Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist The US received a comprehensive power score, measured across a range of areas from military capability to economic strength and cultural influence, of 78.9, just 5.3 points ahead of China. “This narrowing divide owes more to Washington’s missteps than to any major advances on Beijing’s part,” the authors state, arguing the decline demonstrated “how quickly a superpower can erode its credibility”. However, they credit Xi for continuing to expand China’s maritime warfare capabilities, noting Beijing is increasingly willing to use its naval power to challenge the territorial claims of smaller countries such as the Philippines and test Washington’s willingness to honour its security commitments. US President Donald Trump speaks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney after posing for a “family photo” during the APEC summit. Getty



Despite the attention given to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for middle powers to work closer together to expand their clout, the report found they had only a middling year in Asia, including Australia. The “middle power moment remains largely rhetorical, unmatched by the kind of action that would signal a reorientation of regional power”, the authors write. Expert respondents to the survey praised Albanese’s ability to

advance Australia’s economic interests, including his successful regional visits to secure fuel and fertiliser supplies during the Iran war. But they rated him less effective at advancing Australia’s diplomatic interests in Asia.

World.title: ‘Terrible to witness’: Man killed in second CBD stabbing attack
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘Terrible to witness’: Man killed in second CBD stabbing attack James Costa and Shelby Brooks Updated November 22, 2026 — 10:07pm ,first published 1:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Five teenagers have been arrested over a fatal stabbing in Melbourne’s CBD on Saturday night, which came hours after another stabbing only blocks away. Police said a 21-year-old Narre Warren man was killed on La Trobe Street near Elizabeth Street about 8.40pm on Saturday in a knife attack. Emergency services were called to the scene and took the man to hospital, where he died a short time later. Police pictured on Sunday in La Trobe Street, where a 21-year-old Narre Warren man was fatally stabbed on Saturday night. Luis Enrique Ascui A video posted to social media and seen by this masthead showed blood on the side of a parked white car, and a man collapsed in the bike lane between the road and the footpath. “It would have been terrible for members of the public to witness, and we have a significant number of witnesses for this event,” Superintendent Laura McCarthy said at a press conference on Sunday.



A 19-year-old man from Croydon, an 18-year-old man from Mooroolbark and a 17-year-old boy from the Maroondah area were arrested nearby before 12.30am in relation to the alleged attack. Related Article Crime Man critical after random stabbing attack in Bourke Street Mall On Sunday morning, a stolen Mazda 6 linked to the stabbing was recovered in Croydon, McCarthy said. The two occupants, an 18-year-old Mooroolbark man and a 17-year-old boy from the Yarra Ranges area were arrested and will also be interviewed by homicide squad detectives. The Mazda is understood to have been stolen from a Blackburn address overnight between November 10 and November 11.



Police are yet to lay any charges over the death. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the death of the young man was “a stain on this great state”. Police block entry to the scene of the La Trobe Street stabbing on Saturday night. @benwaterworth62/X “We can have a team committed to ending the crime crisis in this state, to investing in Victoria Police, in strengthening our bail laws and our sentencing laws this side of Christmas,” she said. Premier Ben Carroll condemned the attacks on Sunday, and pointed to government funding for the Salvation Army services and Flinders Street Health aimed at helping prevent crime.



“I want to make sure that every Victorian knows that I’m sickened by these crimes, and I’ll do everything I can in my power to prevent them,” he said. Related Article Tribute ‘I have completely broken down’: Wife’s grief after delivery driver’s death Earlier on Saturday, a 24-year-old man suffered non-life-threatening injuries after he was stabbed once in the chest about 2.30pm outside the H&M store, near the corner of Bourke and Elizabeth streets. Superintendent Laura McCarthy said it was believed the incident occurred after the man had failed to comply with the demands of the alleged attacker to hand over his phone. A 31-year-old man of no fixed address was on Sunday evening charged with attempted armed robbery, intentionally causing serious injury and intentionally causing injury in relation to the incident. He was remanded in custody to appear before Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on November 23.



The 21-year-old man died after he was stabbed on La Trobe St. Luis Enrique Ascui A third man was stabbed on Saturday night in Melbourne’s north, outside a fast-food restaurant. The 33-year-old suffered stab wounds about 8.40pm following an altercation with another man and two women on Pascoe Vale Road in Broadmeadows. Police said the victim drove himself to Upfield railway station, where he sought assistance from protective service officers on duty. The man was taken to hospital with serious injuries. It is believed the parties were known to each other; however, no arrests have been made.



Lord Mayor Nick Reece told 3AW the number of random stabbing attacks within the CBD over the past 12 months was “a big, big concern”. “It’s not just a law and order issue,” Reece said. “In [some of the random attacks], the common thread was somebody with an acute mental health issue, who frankly was not safe to themselves or to the community out on the streets. So we need to look at what we can do around the crisis in the mental health system,” he said. Police outside the GPO building after a man was stabbed on Saturday afternoon. Shelby Brooks “Maybe we need to go back to asylums, maybe not like they were in the old days ... [but] I think this policy of de-institutionalisation that commenced in the 1990s has not worked.” McCarthy said she believed the city was safe, but understood community concern.



“We do our very best as police to ensure that is safe through Operation Harmony, which we’ve had over 2500 patrols,” she said on Sunday. “I do take comfort, though, that our intelligence tells us that knife crime has decreased by 13 per cent, and that we have seized 10,000 or more knives.” Related Article Crime Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court Reece said there had been a rise in rough sleeping throughout the CBD over the past six months, climbing from about 80 people to 173. However, he said this was probably a seasonal change due to the warmer weather. Earlier this month, food delivery rider Feng Jianming, 47, was killed in the CBD after he and another rider were allegedly stabbed by a man they caught tampering with their bikes. Feng’s death has rocked Melbourne’s Chinese and business communities, prompting something of a reckoning. A vigil in his honour quickly turned into a protest voicing general feelings of unsafety in the CBD.



Reece said at the time that people were rightfully angry but that Melbourne was still a safe city “relative to other cities around the world ... but when you have an incident like [Feng’s stabbing] … it’s just a reminder that we need to do more”. Roberto Urbano, 51, was arrested in Footscray over that stabbing and has been charged with murder. In August, a 27-year-old man was charged after he allegedly assaulted a child and stabbed the boy’s mother with a pair of scissors in the CBD outside Victoria Police headquarters. “This really rarely occurs in the CBD in Melbourne. It’s an issue that doesn’t come up every day,” Inspector Dale Huntington said on Saturday afternoon. “We really want to encourage people to come in and enjoy the city,” he said, noting the area was popular with Christmas shoppers.



With Alexander Darling and Eleanor Campbell Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Watch how a quiet Huntingdale street became a ‘drug house’ battleground authorities couldn’t stop
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAPublic housing Watch how a quiet Huntingdale street became a ‘drug house’ battleground authorities couldn’t stop Hannah Murphy November 23, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tina and her husband Tom thought they had seen it all after living next door to public housing in Huntingdale. Brazen drug-dealing, screaming, shouting, fighting in the street, home invasions and even a firebombing had become a part of their day-to-day. Loading But one Wednesday afternoon in September, they realised just how serious things had gotten. Tina was home alone while Tom was at work about 1pm on September 23, when she began to hear commotion outside. She saw two men were fighting on the street, hurling abuse at one another.



“I actually called Tom and said, ‘I don’t feel comfortable with this, they’re yelling, and they’re abusing each other. It looks like it’s going to get vicious’,” she said. And over the next half an hour, it did. The incident is another example of the plight neighbours of problematic public housing tenants face when attempting to report unruly and dangerous behaviour to the responsible authorities. Tina and Tom, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, have made dozens of reports over the last five years, with little to show in the way of resolutions. Footage from the couple’s CCTV, which was described by WA’s housing minister as “confronting” when this masthead sent it to his office, showed a man parked across from Tina and Tom’s property in a purple ute, screaming at another man to come out and fight.



They have a brief altercation where they attempt to fist fight, before the man from the house grabs a baseball bat and sets upon the visitor, who runs back to his ute, picks out tools from under the canopy, and begins hurling them. Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Debra complained about her Rivervale neighbours 60 times in three years. It’s worse than ever After another fight, the visitor takes cover behind his car, before firing up his ute and driving it straight at the front of the property, where the other man is standing. After one near miss, the ute reverses and drives straight at him again – this time, he hits the man, and the car can be seen bouncing as he runs him over. A woman’s scream is heard in the background, and the visitor does a quick donut on the front lawn before peeling off down the road.



All the while, Tina was stuck inside, “terrified”, and glued to her CCTV livestream on her phone. The driver was later charged with grievous bodily harm. The other man was not charged. Tina said for her and Tom, incidents such as these have become their norm. The problems started in 2020, when a new tenant moved in to the property they had lived next to for the last 10 years. Previously, the home had been occupied by an older man with dementia and he was allowing his family to move in.



Tina and Tom went over to introduce themselves but instead found a teenager in their front garden, stripping their plants. When Tina asked him to stop, he hurled slurs at her. Related Article Exclusive

Public housing Megan is a Perth public housing tenant. Her neighbours are making her life hell From there, things began to spiral. Tom, who is a shift worker, began counting the cars that would visit the property at all hours, landing on a figure of about 130 just in one week, and captured CCTV of drug deals happening out in the open. The house was raided twice, and on one occasion, police allegedly told the couple they were aware it was a known “drug house”.



The property has been graffitied, had its windows caved in, and petrol bombed. Tina was threatened by the same teenager at the property, who said he would “put a bullet in her head”, though police deemed it an empty threat as he did not have a firearm licence. CCTV has caught screaming at all hours, and even a woman at the property physically fighting with a police officer. Tina and Tom believe their property value dropped by as much as $200,000, and they have spent thousands fortifying their home with roller shutters and locks, and rarely get more than four hours’ sleep in a night. Ultimately, they said, they are tired. They have made 60 to 70 complaints over the last five years, they estimated, and even proceeded to eviction on one occasion. The magistrate shot it down, and the family were allowed to stay.



“There needs to be like a discussion about how we protect the community rather than just the tenants,” Tom said. “We can protect both. I mean, if the tenant occasionally has a loud party or occasionally, there’s a bit of swearing – that’s suburbia. But the things that have gone on there – that’s not normal.” “It’s a bad normal, if that makes sense,” Tina said. “You see these things happening and think, OK. I’ve got to call the police, and I’ve got to make another report. “But am I going to bother when they’re not going to do anything? The Department of Housing says under the tenancy laws, they can’t just evict them. They’ve got to take it to court, and the judge has to decide.”



WA’s public housing waitlist currently has more than 24,000 applications. Housing Minister John Carey said he had viewed the footage of September’s incident, and understood the couples’ frustrations. Minister for Planning & Lands; Housing & Works and Health Infrastructure John Carey. Oscar Colman “The footage is incredibly confronting – no one wants to see violence and anti-social behaviour in our community, regardless of where it takes place,” he said. “As the housing provider of last resort, the Department of Housing and Works accommodates some of the most vulnerable members of our community.



“The vast majority of our public housing tenants are good neighbours and their tenancies are observed without issue.” Carey said when issues arose, the department aimed to work with the tenants. But if problems continue, it worked with police and built a case in line with the Residential Tenancies Act. “The decision to terminate a tenancy agreement ultimately sits with a magistrate, who will only evict a tenant if they are satisfied that there has been a breach of the tenancy agreement, and that the tenant has been given every opportunity to rectify the breach and has failed to do so,” Carey said. Tina said this is where the system has let her and Tom down.



The couple believed more needed to be done to free up homes for other struggling families.

World.title: UN global climate talks led by Chris Bowen end in discord and recrimination
World.content:
Breaking EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement UN global climate talks led by Chris Bowen end in discord and recrimination Nick O'Malley Updated November 23, 2026 — 12:55am ,first published 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global climate talks led by Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen have failed to secure an agreement in Turkey after a standoff between oil producing nations led by Saudi Arabia and nations seeking more ambitious action on climate change, including Europe. Bowen described the outcome as “very disappointing” and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers. He commended delegations for pulling all-nighters to try to reach a deal, but said “the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory”. Chris Bowen, Climate Change and Energy Minister and president of COP31 negotiations watched on as nation after nation rejected a climate agreement at the talks. AP Photo/Khalil Hamra After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime - making it the longest COP on record - Turkey’s conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.



“There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” he said. “There will be no new text from now on.” The Saudi-led bloc backed by Russia rejected on Sunday a final agreement – known as a cover decision – that reiterated calls for a transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union said it could not support an agreement that would take backwards steps by refusing to address the need to do so. Further objections were raised by other nations over the inclusion of a call to increase the use of controversial climate capture and storage technology, also championed by the Saudi-led bloc, and by the failure of developed nations to pledge more financial support for poorer nations hardest hit by climate impacts. Cover decisions at UN climate talks can only be adopted by consensus of all parties. Speaking on behalf of the EU, Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, rejected the draft agreement on the floor of the final plenary session.



“We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change, and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel. Related Article Analysis

Paris Agreement ‘Heat records keep shattering’: Time is running out for COP to save us “I do want to, however, Mr President, commend both you and the President of Negotiations [Chris Bowen] for your unstinting efforts. However, the draft put before us does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either. And it is for that reason and those reasons that the European Union strongly objects to this text.” The failure of negotiators to arrive at an agreement comes as a huge blow to the COP process, at which almost 200 parties to the Paris Agreement sought to advance climate action, and to Bowen, who secured the role of president of negotiations when the bid he led for Australia to host the talks failed last year at talks in Brazil.



Bowen had sought to sidestep the standoff over references to fossil fuel in the cover decision by including language recognising the agreement made at previous talks in Dubai, where the world pledged to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Speaking after the EU, a member of the Panamanian delegation also rejected the deal, saying: “We need to be clear: our message is not a criticism of the presidencies. “Our disagreement is with a much deeper problem... One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it wages too much upon technologies such as CCS capture storage of carbon instead of calling for deep changes and three because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback.” A representative of the Marshall Islands said her nation had been failed by all sides at the COP. “We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. “Over the past two weeks, we have been offered next to nothing. Even as we have said again and again, our needs are so great, the costs are so high, the finance gap keeps growing. We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises. People are dying, seas are rising, ecosystems are collapsing.”



Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen (right) with Turkey’s Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum in Fiji at pre-COP. Getty As it became clear that the negotiations had failed Bowen remained silent while Turkish officials oversaw the meeting, with many speakers noting that the talks were being held just weeks after the UN Environment Program had acknowledged that the world was set to miss the Paris target of 1.5 degrees warming and head into what is now being described as climate “overshoot”. A Russian delegate told the session that Russia stands by the goals of the Paris Agreement, but that the conference made rapid phase-out of fossil fuels that he said should not have been included central to the talks. He said that the UN’s own scenarios charting a course to limiting warming to 1.5 degrees acknowledged the world will continue to use approximately 40 per cent of the oil and 50 per cent of the gas of the levels of 2019. A Saudi representative said the 22 member states of the Arab League represent less than 2 per cent of historical greenhouse gas emissions, “whereas other groups are responsible for 55 per cent of those emissions.”



In line with this he said the Arab League had called for a tripling of climate finance from wealthy to poorer nations. “This was removed from the text due to lack of flexibility from some parties on mentioning any quantitative aspects related to climate finance.” Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, took aim at the EU, which he said had failed to offer new financial support to developing nations. “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow. The EU cannot help sabotage the negotiations, then pose as the climate conscience of the world.” China noted its reservation about some of the content of the agreement, but said to demonstrate unity of collective efforts it had decided to accept the cover decision and called on “all parties to show necessary compromise spirit to push forward our process.” As president of negotiations Bowen had declared at the pre-COP meeting in Fiji that the presidency would pursue the cover decision that the COP has just rejected, in order to drive more momentum for action than might have been achieved with a series of agreements over individual agenda items.



Australia had hoped that in doing so it would champion the cause of Pacific island nations which view climate change as an existential threat, thereby deepening ties across the region as China’s influence grew. Fiji’s Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya said that though the cover decision text was not perfect she regretted it was not adopted. “Honorable Chris Bowen, you have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it,” she said. “Your commitment, patience, and determination throughout these negotiations have not gone unnoticed. “This work is hard. Sleepless nights, hours and days of constant negotiations, managing over 190 parties. This is not easy, but we do it. We do it for our people. The failure to reach consensus on the cover decision is not yours to carry. It is a collective responsibility that rests with all parties. Consensus requires compromise, courage, and political will from all of us.” Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and a member of The Elders, an independent group of global leaders founded by Nelson Mandela in 2007 to work on peace, human rights, and global challenges like climate change was more scathing.



“Recognition of the dangers of overshoot should have shaken leaders into action, instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership from the co-presidencies Turkey and Australia,” she said in a statement. “This was compounded by disturbing politicised attacks on the science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Strapped for memories
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Geoff Carey of Pagewood makes the cut: “The Christian Brothers didn’t use the cane (C8) at school. ‘Six of the best’ was delivered via a thick, handmade leather strap. Apparently, the local boot maker had a roaring trade supplying the school. The skilled and experienced brothers learnt to anticipate the involuntary withdrawal of the hand of wimps like me, following it to deliver the perfect strike on the ends of the fingers. The bravest of souls bore the boot maker’s stitching marks across the wrist, unflinching as the strap descended.”

“Thank you, Christine Perrott for the shopping bag (C8) reminder,” writes Janice Creenaune of Austinmer. “While on teacher exchange in Kidlington, near Oxford in 2007, one of the first pieces of advice from my new teacher friends was the type of plastic shopping bag to carry my lunch. I’d been using Tesco and Asda, and they assured me that Waitrose and M&S were far more acceptable. Pride was not the position, class distinction and image reigned, and while we remained on our NSW teacher’s salary for the year, we couldn’t afford the top tier of supermarkets, too.”

Anne McCarthy of Marrickville says that “the expression ‘Heavens to Betsy’ used by Serge Nemaz (C8) reminded me of other old sayings such as ‘Lawdy, lawdy Miss Maudie’ [according to the great Lloyd Price, it’s Miss Clawdy – Granny] and ‘God willing and the creek don’t rise.’ I have used the latter sometimes when discussing future commitments, often to the listener’s puzzlement.”

“Highly disagree, George Zivkovic (C8),” says a shaken Seppo Ranki of Glenhaven. “As a Whovian from William Hartnell days, I couldn’t countenance Doctor Who jumping the shark to a female Doctor, and stopped watching altogether. Jamie Bond would meet the same fate.”

Regarding the “there’s no other store like David Bowie” theory presented by Anthony Fretwell (C8), Nelson Bay denizen Judy Archer thinks name changes have worked before: “A fish named slimehead was renamed orange roughy.”

World.title: Australia’s power prices would be 50 per cent worse without renewables, says top economist
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRenewables Australia’s power prices would be 50 per cent worse without renewables, says top economist Shane Wright November 22, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s wholesale power prices would be up to 50 per cent higher if the country had embraced coal, gas or nuclear power rather than renewables and batteries, a leading economist has declared while arguing the nation had been “de-risked” from the full cost of the surge in fossil fuel prices. Guy Debelle, a former deputy governor of the Reserve Bank who is now non-executive director of independent think tank e61, has used a major address to argue Australia was lucky to embrace renewable energy sources to replace the nation’s network of coal- and gas-fired power stations. Former RBA deputy Guy Debelle said said power prices would be much higher if not for the rollout of renewable energy across the country. Bloomberg Critics of the rollout of solar and wind power plus batteries have claimed renewables have driven up Australians’ power prices. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has claimed government energy policy had prevented the construction of gas- and coal-fired power plants, leading to a 40 per cent surge in prices. But Debelle, who also sits on the board of the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, said critics ignored the pressing need to replace the Australian power system, given its suite of fossil fuel power sources had come to the end of their lifespan.



He said the huge fall in the price of renewables and batteries, and the surge in the cost of coal- and gas-fired power stations, meant Australian households were substantially better off. Related Article Electricity The biggest energy crisis in history brings on the age of electricity “The counterfactual of not doing this energy transition is that we would have a lot higher energy prices than we have today. The energy transition isn’t costless, but the alternatives are considerably more costly,” Debelle said. “Wholesale energy prices would be 30 to 50 per cent higher today than if we had not installed this renewable energy capacity. When coal and gas prices rise higher as they have done recently, than the cost savings are even larger.” Last week, former prime minister Tony Abbott linked the growth in renewable energy across Australia to the surge in household power bills while arguing for “climate warriors” to back nuclear power.



“If renewables really are cheap, they don’t need to be subsidised or mandated; and if it really is necessary to limit emissions, the climate warriors should be the strongest advocates for nuclear power because it’s the only proven emissions-free form of the base-load electricity a modern economy needs,” Abbott said. But Debelle said by every measure, renewable energy sources were cheaper to build and operate than their fossil fuel alternatives, which meant households had avoided even larger power bills. A nuclear energy plant in the American state of Illinois. Debelle says calls for nuclear power ignore the problems of building and running them. Getty Images He said that since 2010, the number of coal-fired power stations had fallen from 26 to 15 with their output dropping from 28 gigawatts of power to 21 gigawatts. Over that period, renewable energy output had grown to 36 gigawatts. In the 2025-26 financial year, Australian households installed more than 13 gigawatt hours of battery storage, or more than the United States has ever put in place.



According to Debelle, coal-fired power stations would not be competitive against renewables while calls for nuclear power ignored the long-term problems of building and running them. “Nuclear at the moment is also not a viable cost-effective solution. Cheap nuclear has been just around the corner for about the past 50 years,” he said. Record levels of renewable energy in the electricity grid are displacing coal and driving down emissions. Bloomberg “We can’t wait until that technological challenge is solved. We need the generation capacity now.” But the renewable rollout is currently running well over headline, as planning logjams and community opposition gum up project in the pipeline.



Last year, the Australian Energy Market Regulator warned projects, including new transmission links, faced cost blowouts of up to 100 per cent. A failure to streamline the national rollout could add 30 per cent to projects’ costs, the regulator estimated in a report last December. Debelle noted whole power prices had fallen across the national electricity market in recent months. But in most of the rest of the world, prices have increased by a large amount due to the US-Israel war on Iran. Australian homes with solar panels. Sitthixay Ditthavong “We’ve been able to insulate ourselves from that,” he said. Apart from the collapse in the cost of solar and wind, which are now cheaper sources of energy than coal, the fall in the use of fossil fuels is aiding Australia’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.



Debelle said that by 2030, electricity would no longer be Australia’s largest source of emissions. It would be overtaken by transport due to ongoing use of diesel- and petrol-powered vehicles. But Debelle said continuing the rollout of renewables, and providing access to the overall energy grid, remained a major challenge. He said finding ways to encourage the installation of solar on businesses and warehouses in urban areas would increase the amount of electricity available to the grid while reducing the cost of transmission lines.
