World.title: Cut and cut now: Economists urge next Victorian government to swing the axe
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalVictorian election Cut and cut now: Economists urge next Victorian government to swing the axe Shane Wright November 22, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The next Victorian government should immediately wind back the scale of, delay or cancel major building projects to help bring the state budget under control while looking to reduce the number of bureaucrats, the nation’s top economists have urged. A survey of high-profile economists by the Economic Society of Australia has revealed strong support for an overhaul of government spending plus the adoption of new fiscal rules to prevent a future blowout in state debt. The site of the Suburban Rail Loop in Burwood. Economists say the next Victorian government needs to slash infrastructure spending to stabilise the budget. Joe Armao They also believe Spring St needs to adopt a raft of policies to safeguard the budget and improve the economy, including a shift from stamp duty towards a broad-based land tax. The state of the Victorian budget and economy is one of the key issues at the weekend election.



Related Article Employment Unemployment hits five-year high as RBA squeezes jobs market Victoria’s net debt, forecast by Treasury to reach $197 billion by 2029-30, is the highest of all state and territories. Figures from the bureau of statistics released last week showed the Victorian economy was the slowest growing in the federation through 2025-26. The Economic Society put to members at least a dozen proposals that have been floated publicly as ways to bring down state debt and improve the performance of the Victorian election. Respondents included current Reserve Bank board member Melinda Cilento, prominent independent economist Saul Eslake, former director of the Melbourne Institute Deborah Cobb-Clark and Queensland University’s John Quiggin. Only one proposal – a reduction in infrastructure spending – was backed as a priority by most of those surveyed.



Matthew Butlin, a former Productivity Commission member, said the state was in an “appalling mess” and had choices had to be made that would require sharing pain across Victoria. “We are over-borrowed as a state, the public sector capital obligations are too large relative to our debt and income, our productivity is far too low, government spending is inadequately targeted, the tax burden is too high and we need to take a very sharp lens to what is very important over the next five years to build productivity growth,” he said. Bob Breunig, director of ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, was blunt about the choices facing the party taking office from Saturday night. “They have to cut expenditure and decide what is really needed and what isn’t,” he said. Hugh Sibly, a senior lecturer in economics from the University of Tasmania, said the Victorian budget was heavily exposed to rising interest rates because of the amount of debt it had taken on for its infrastructure program.



“Unfortunately, Victoria has engaged in some infrastructure projects, notably the Suburban Rail Loop, for which the benefits are significantly less than the costs,” he said. ANU tax expert Bob Breunig says the next Victorian government has to decide what is important and what is not. Rhett Wyman “Reprioritising towards those projects with a benefit cost ratio greater than one would help Victoria’s economic position.” The survey also showed strong support for either reducing the size of the Victorian public service or restraining public sector wages growth. Figures released last week showed that since 2014, when Labor took office, public sector wages only in Queensland had grown faster than those in Victoria. The NSW government has pledged to keep net debt under 15 per cent of state economic output. Many economists believe such a set target should be adopted by Victoria.



Uwe Dulleck, from the Crawford School of Public Policy in Canberra, cautioned that while spending cuts were necessary, they would hurt the economy in the short term. “Major repair can only be achieved with major cuts in infrastructure investments, which will have negative impact on the local economy, and a restructure of the public service (again, it has an impact on the local economy),” he said. “Thus, the balance between raising revenue and reducing expenditure is needed.” Apart from cuts, the economists largely agree there is scope for major tax reform with the number one item a shift from stamp duty on property sales to a broad-based land tax. Such a proposal was rejected by the Andrews government. Lisa Magnani, the head of Macquarie University’s economics department, said the next government should examine the state’s entire tax system, starting with its stamp duty system.



Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes “With one of the highest state debts in Australia, Victoria’s budget position is vulnerable to the negative effects of rising interest rates,” she said. “Victoria would benefit from a full review of its tax structure to possibly find new sources of revenues (particularly those with progressive features, such as taxes on high-income recipients and wealth owners).” Victoria University senior economist Janine Dixon said making the state more attractive to investors would go a long way to improving the budget. “Making Victoria an attractive place to invest would be a good start, and fits well with making sure Victoria’s considerable workforce, particularly in the outer suburbs, is well connected to employment opportunities. Addressing crime would also give potential investors more confidence,” she said.



While most economists believed budget cuts were a priority, some argued the new government should put its attention into other areas. Julie Toth, from the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia, said while budget repair was important in the long term, it was not the most urgent financial priority. She said it was more important that public services and infrastructure kept pace with Victoria’s growing population and that there was support for the state’s most disadvantaged and vulnerable residents. “Economic and social inclusion matters for everyone. We all feel the impact of ineffective safety nets and support services, directly and indirectly. This will become more urgent if unemployment rises, as is widely forecast over the next two to three years,” she said. Apart from spending cuts and tax reforms, the surveyed economists backed changes including a reduction in free services or universal concessions, introduction of road user charges and broadening of the payroll tax base.



There was also support for an overhaul of the Commonwealth Grants Commission GST allocation system which is the centre of a Productivity Commission report due by the end of the year. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: China on verge of eclipsing US power in Asia after Trump stumbles
World.content:
PoliticsFederalChina relations China on verge of eclipsing US power in Asia after Trump stumbles Matthew Knott November 22, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US President Donald Trump’s costly war against Iran has allowed China to come within a skerrick of overtaking the United States to become the most powerful country in Asia, a respected report card has found. The Lowy Institute’s latest Asia Power Index finds the US advantage over China, measured across 131 metrics, has plunged to its lowest level since the annual survey began in 2018, with the gap between the two nations’ military capabilities narrowing to its lowest level on record. The release of the report comes after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in a historic trilateral summit last week. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a rare trilateral meeting last week. Getty Russia remains ahead of Australia in fifth place in the index and behind only the US, China, India and Japan as middle powers struggle to exert influence in a region dominated by great power rivalry.



The warp-force speed of artificial intelligence developments was under the spotlight at APEC last week in Shenzhen, where Xi and Trump agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence. This Tuesday, five days after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese directly implored Xi, Trump and Putin to “make sure that AI is developed and deployed safely”, Foreign Minister Penny Wong will flag that Australia should have a role in forming AI safeguards as the frontline technology becomes a national security challenge. Citing reporting about the use of AI to attempt to sway elections in the US, Wong is expected to say: “We have long known actors beyond our shores seek to interfere in Australia’s democracy and in the lives of those who call Australia home. These tools make that interference faster, cheaper and harder to recognise.“ Wong emphasises that every advanced AI company operating in Australia - such as Anthropic - will have to build in security and safety protections. “We must do what we can to ensure that the race to develop frontier AI, concentrated in a handful of companies and countries, does not reward speed over prudence,” she will say, according to notes from an extract of her speech.



Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale is set to visit Canberra this week to strike a comprehensive treaty with Australia in the Albanese government’s latest attempt to push back China’s growing influence in the Pacific. “The conflict in the Middle East, following coordinated US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February, has fuelled perceptions of Washington’s waning interest in Asia,” authors Hunter Marston and Jack Sato argue in their report. The Trump administration’s decision to shift military resources from the Indo-Pacific to the Persian Gulf to support its war effort highlighted its lack of focus on Asia, the authors state. US strikes on Iran have depleted American missile stocks and weakened its military capabilities, and the US military has conducted fewer joint exercises and defence dialogues with its primary regional allies over the past year, including Australia, Japan, and South Korea.



Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Trump’s War Barbie is terrible at the one thing he’s supposed to be good at Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist The US received a comprehensive power score, measured across a range of areas from military capability to economic strength and cultural influence, of 78.9, just 5.3 points ahead of China. “This narrowing divide owes more to Washington’s missteps than to any major advances on Beijing’s part,” the authors state, arguing the decline demonstrated “how quickly a superpower can erode its credibility”. However, they credit Xi for continuing to expand China’s maritime warfare capabilities, noting Beijing is increasingly willing to use its naval power to challenge the territorial claims of smaller countries such as the Philippines and test Washington’s willingness to honour its security commitments. US President Donald Trump speaks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney after posing for a “family photo” during the APEC summit. Getty



Despite the attention given to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for middle powers to work closer together to expand their clout, the report found they had only a middling year in Asia, including Australia. The “middle power moment remains largely rhetorical, unmatched by the kind of action that would signal a reorientation of regional power”, the authors write. Expert respondents to the survey praised Albanese’s ability to

advance Australia’s economic interests, including his successful regional visits to secure fuel and fertiliser supplies during the Iran war. But they rated him less effective at advancing Australia’s diplomatic interests in Asia.

World.title: ‘Terrible to witness’: Man killed in second CBD stabbing attack
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘Terrible to witness’: Man killed in second CBD stabbing attack James Costa and Shelby Brooks Updated November 22, 2026 — 10:07pm ,first published 1:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Five teenagers have been arrested over a fatal stabbing in Melbourne’s CBD on Saturday night, which came hours after another stabbing only blocks away. Police said a 21-year-old Narre Warren man was killed on La Trobe Street near Elizabeth Street about 8.40pm on Saturday in a knife attack. Emergency services were called to the scene and took the man to hospital, where he died a short time later. Police pictured on Sunday in La Trobe Street, where a 21-year-old Narre Warren man was fatally stabbed on Saturday night. Luis Enrique Ascui A video posted to social media and seen by this masthead showed blood on the side of a parked white car, and a man collapsed in the bike lane between the road and the footpath. “It would have been terrible for members of the public to witness, and we have a significant number of witnesses for this event,” Superintendent Laura McCarthy said at a press conference on Sunday.



A 19-year-old man from Croydon, an 18-year-old man from Mooroolbark and a 17-year-old boy from the Maroondah area were arrested nearby before 12.30am in relation to the alleged attack. Related Article Crime Man critical after random stabbing attack in Bourke Street Mall On Sunday morning, a stolen Mazda 6 linked to the stabbing was recovered in Croydon, McCarthy said. The two occupants, an 18-year-old Mooroolbark man and a 17-year-old boy from the Yarra Ranges area were arrested and will also be interviewed by homicide squad detectives. The Mazda is understood to have been stolen from a Blackburn address overnight between November 10 and November 11.



Police are yet to lay any charges over the death. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the death of the young man was “a stain on this great state”. Police block entry to the scene of the La Trobe Street stabbing on Saturday night. @benwaterworth62/X “We can have a team committed to ending the crime crisis in this state, to investing in Victoria Police, in strengthening our bail laws and our sentencing laws this side of Christmas,” she said. Premier Ben Carroll condemned the attacks on Sunday, and pointed to government funding for the Salvation Army services and Flinders Street Health aimed at helping prevent crime.



“I want to make sure that every Victorian knows that I’m sickened by these crimes, and I’ll do everything I can in my power to prevent them,” he said. Related Article Tribute ‘I have completely broken down’: Wife’s grief after delivery driver’s death Earlier on Saturday, a 24-year-old man suffered non-life-threatening injuries after he was stabbed once in the chest about 2.30pm outside the H&M store, near the corner of Bourke and Elizabeth streets. Superintendent Laura McCarthy said it was believed the incident occurred after the man had failed to comply with the demands of the alleged attacker to hand over his phone. A 31-year-old man of no fixed address was on Sunday evening charged with attempted armed robbery, intentionally causing serious injury and intentionally causing injury in relation to the incident. He was remanded in custody to appear before Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on November 23.



The 21-year-old man died after he was stabbed on La Trobe St. Luis Enrique Ascui A third man was stabbed on Saturday night in Melbourne’s north, outside a fast-food restaurant. The 33-year-old suffered stab wounds about 8.40pm following an altercation with another man and two women on Pascoe Vale Road in Broadmeadows. Police said the victim drove himself to Upfield railway station, where he sought assistance from protective service officers on duty. The man was taken to hospital with serious injuries. It is believed the parties were known to each other; however, no arrests have been made.



Lord Mayor Nick Reece told 3AW the number of random stabbing attacks within the CBD over the past 12 months was “a big, big concern”. “It’s not just a law and order issue,” Reece said. “In [some of the random attacks], the common thread was somebody with an acute mental health issue, who frankly was not safe to themselves or to the community out on the streets. So we need to look at what we can do around the crisis in the mental health system,” he said. Police outside the GPO building after a man was stabbed on Saturday afternoon. Shelby Brooks “Maybe we need to go back to asylums, maybe not like they were in the old days ... [but] I think this policy of de-institutionalisation that commenced in the 1990s has not worked.” McCarthy said she believed the city was safe, but understood community concern.



“We do our very best as police to ensure that is safe through Operation Harmony, which we’ve had over 2500 patrols,” she said on Sunday. “I do take comfort, though, that our intelligence tells us that knife crime has decreased by 13 per cent, and that we have seized 10,000 or more knives.” Related Article Crime Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court Reece said there had been a rise in rough sleeping throughout the CBD over the past six months, climbing from about 80 people to 173. However, he said this was probably a seasonal change due to the warmer weather. Earlier this month, food delivery rider Feng Jianming, 47, was killed in the CBD after he and another rider were allegedly stabbed by a man they caught tampering with their bikes. Feng’s death has rocked Melbourne’s Chinese and business communities, prompting something of a reckoning. A vigil in his honour quickly turned into a protest voicing general feelings of unsafety in the CBD.



Reece said at the time that people were rightfully angry but that Melbourne was still a safe city “relative to other cities around the world ... but when you have an incident like [Feng’s stabbing] … it’s just a reminder that we need to do more”. Roberto Urbano, 51, was arrested in Footscray over that stabbing and has been charged with murder. In August, a 27-year-old man was charged after he allegedly assaulted a child and stabbed the boy’s mother with a pair of scissors in the CBD outside Victoria Police headquarters. “This really rarely occurs in the CBD in Melbourne. It’s an issue that doesn’t come up every day,” Inspector Dale Huntington said on Saturday afternoon. “We really want to encourage people to come in and enjoy the city,” he said, noting the area was popular with Christmas shoppers.

World.title: 'Nobody wants to close a pool' - councils struggle with proposed rates cap
World.content:
The mayor of Lower Hutt mayor says no decision has been made on whether public pools will have to close, as they work to balance the government's proposed rates cap.

Hutt City Council is weighing its options - including potentially closures to public pools, libraries, and community hubs - as it tries to keep rates affordable while providing public services.

Lower Hutt Mayor Fauono Ken Laban said they were facing difficult options.

"Nobody wants to close a pool, nobody wants to close a library, nobody wants to close a community hub, and nobody wants to spend less on roads and on rubbish," he said.

"But the reality is we need to find ways to reduce our costs and reduce our expenditure."

Lower Hutt Mayor Fauono Ken Laban. Photo/RNZ/Supplied

Laban said the pools were important public assets.

"We all have children and grandchildren that are in those pools, we all want to see children in our communities be active and learn to swim, but at the same time we've really got to be conscious of all of us trying to live within our means," he said.

"That's the dilemma that all councils are facing in this current rates capping environment."

Hutt City Council was tossing up three options as part of its draft long term plan:

4 percent in 2027/28, 4 percent in 2028/29 and 4 percent from 2029/30, where council would keep its three indoor pools, close all of its summer pools, and lower the number of hubs from eight to five, with the Naenae, Eastbourne and Petone sites sold.

7 percent in 2027/28, 5.1 percent in 2028/29 and 4 percent from 2029/30, where council would keep its three indoor pools and the Wainuiomata pool, but would no longer operate McKenzie Baths or Eastbourne Pool. This option would also see all eight communities keeping a hub or library, but with fewer days open and services. Meanwhile, the Petone Britannia Street site and the Eastbourne hub building would be sold, with Eastbourne services moving to the community hall. Petone hub services would continue to be operating from the Jackson Street site.

8 percent in 2027/28, 6 percent in 2028/29 and 4 percent from 2029/30, with the same pool changes as the 7 percent option. All eight hub sites would stay, with fewer opening days and services.

Public Service Association national secretary Duane Leo said the council had few options left.

"The reality is, councils are at the point now where they can't cut any more fat. They're down to the bone," he said.

"If rates-capping legislation comes in under the incoming government, we can expect to see more and more cuts just like this. You can expect to see pools closing, library hours cut down, playgrounds not being maintained."

Leo said pools in particular were a critical part of any community.

"They're lots of fun of course, but they are also essential hubs for exercise and teaching water safety," he said.

Caretaker minister for local government Simon Watts said under the legislation, councils would be expected to keep annual rates increases within a target range of two to four percent.

"For too long, ratepayers have been hit with steep and unexpected rates increases at a time many New Zealanders are already feeling the squeeze," he said.

"How local government prioritises its expenditure is a matter for them."

World.title: Large proportion of Teslas fail warrants due to steering and suspension issues
World.content:
Steering and suspension issues are the main reason Teslas are failing warrants of fitness, accounting for almost a third of all failures.

After receiving 156 complaints alleging suspension failure in Tesla vehicles, the US Department of Transportation opened a preliminary investigation.

Data obtained by First Up from the New Zealand Transport Agency shows steering and suspension is the main reason Teslas failed warrants of fitness.

In comparison, suspension failures for Nissan EVs were eight percent and BYD vehicles had a failure rate of 6 percent.

Jeff Smit - the founder of the EV & Hybrid Network in Australia, who has a workshop in Sydney specialising in EVs and hybrids - said there was no particular issue with Tesla's suspension when compared to other makes or models.

But he said the data did show that Teslas were not serviced as frequently as others.

On its website, Tesla said it designed every vehicle with the goal of eliminating the need for service.

Nissan and BYD say their vehicles must be serviced every 20,000 kilometers, or every 12 months.

Smit also observed that Tesla drivers tended to drive their vehicles more aggressively.

NZTA data also revealed a difference in warrant of fitness fail rates, depending on whether the inspection is carried out by Tesla itself or by another provider.

Tesla failed 15 percent of its own cars, compared to a 31 percent fail rate by VTNZ.

In a statement, VTNZ said different manufacturers had specific tolerances and requirements for their steering and suspension components.

NZTA said it was aware of Tesla's higher-than average WOF fail rate for steering and suspension, but it did not have concerns over the design of Tesla's steering or suspension systems.

In a statement, head of vehicle regulation Geoff Williamson said the higher-than average WOF failure rate was primarily associated with a well-known suspension wear issue affecting some Teslas and the company had a warranty replacement programme for these cars.

He said NZTA had not received formal complaints specifically relating to Tesla's steering and suspension design, and was monitoring international investigations, recall activity and complaint data to identify issues that may affect the New Zealand fleet and whether any regulatory response is required.

World.title: How a weak NZ dollar could help and hurt you
World.content:
Audio player for " Is it time to get my money out of AI? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2737523%2Fhow-a-weak-nz-dollar-could-help-and-hurt-you

Is it time to get my money out of AI? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

A weak New Zealand dollar might be hard on anyone shopping from international websites for Christmas presents or putting fuel in their cars but could be helping us in other ways, ASB says.

Over the past 20 years, the average value of the dollar has been about US70c.

On Friday, it was worth US54c.

ASB senior economist Chris Tennent-Brown said the impact would be felt differently across the economy. Households and New Zealanders travelling internationally would feel the pinch, but exporters, tourism operators and investors could benefit.

Tennent-Brown said the dollar was historically low against most major currencies except the Japanese yen. That was because our interest rates have got out of step with most other countries'.

"We've got very high inflation, which is something that many western economies are dealing with, but we're coming at that problem from a very low interest rate setting, and I'd still say our interest rates are quite low on a historical basis.

"If we compare it to across the Tasman, Australia's official cash rate is a couple of percent higher than ours, and normally New Zealand needs to have a bit of a premium over other countries, so we're below Aussie, we're below the US in terms of an official cash rate, that impacts wholesale rates and that does weigh on the New Zealand dollar."

The focus on interest rates would continue for some time, he said.

"I think interest rates will be important over the next couple of years, and some of that will be the Reserve Bank returning our official cash rate and our interest rates towards more normal levels - or neutral when we put some economic jargon in there about where the official cash rate should be - and likewise some of the countries that have been pretty aggressive on tightening over the past year, Australia is a good example, will perhaps be easing interest rates next year whilst we're still trying to get them back to more normal levels, so that will all impact the exchange rate over the year ahead."

How the dollar moved had different effects on various parts of the economy.

"For households buying imported goods, or Kiwis spending money overseas, it can mean higher prices and less bang for buck. But for exporters earning offshore, tourism businesses and some investors with international exposure there can be meaningful upside," he said.

Oil and refined products like diesel, petrol and aviation fuel are priced globally in US dollars, meaning a weaker NZ dollar compounds already high international fuel costs. The impact is ultimately felt at the petrol pump, in airline ticket prices, and in the cost of transporting people and goods.

But it made New Zealand a more appealing tourism destination and could also encourage New Zealanders to holiday at home, too.

"That could provide a double boost for parts of the tourism and hospitality sector over summer, with more international visitors coming and more Kiwi choosing to spend their holiday dollars at home. Some of us may even remember the 1980s tourism campaign - 'don't leave town until you've seen the country'. It's true, and it worked," Tennent-Brown said.

The weak dollar also boosted key exports such as dairy and meat.

"It's painful every time we buy something that has an international price, and petrol's the obvious one, but it is supporting the rural recovery with things like the Fonterra milk price update … reflecting how the weak New Zealand dollar flows through to improved incomes at the farm gate, but it has some impacts on the rest of the economy.

"The rural income story is definitely a beneficiary of the weak New Zealand dollar ... it's a twin-edged sword though, because things like fertilizer prices, investing in plant and machinery is clearly going up, just as the New Zealand dollar goes down."

He said there could also be a silver lining for those with money invested offshore, including through KiwiSaver. A weaker NZ dollar can provide a currency tailwind for international investors.

"Every investment manager will have an approach to FX management. ASB maintains a deliberate mix of hedged and unhedged international assets. Keeping a portion of global equities unhedged provides a natural buffer during global market downturns, as the NZD historically tends to fall during periods of economic stress, lifting the value of overseas shares."

World.title: A wave of funerals: The NZ student who went home to a wiped-out village
World.content:
He could have watched the disaster unfold from NZ - instead, he went home to Nepal to help. The extraordinary story of one man's connection to his home country and its people.

Audio player for " A wave of funerals: The NZ student who went home to a wiped-out village " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/community/2737522%2Fa-wave-of-funerals-the-nz-student-who-went-home-to-a-wiped-out-village

A wave of funerals: The NZ student who went home to a wiped-out village The Detail Download MP3 22m

Thousands of kilometres from his PhD studies in Christchurch, Sunil Tamang's heart remains with his people in Nepal.

He has just returned from helping communities devastated by the deadly flash floods - more than a decade after doing the same following the earthquakes there.

His own village was among the worst hit.

He admits to The Detail that it was a harrowing and heartbreaking trek back to his home country, which began five days after the flash floods hit on 26 August, and finished just a couple of weeks ago.

"We lost so many people... almost 400 people that I personally knew, and so every day was a funeral ritual," he says.

"So for 49 days I was just attending one funeral after another, and sometimes in a day...10 to 15 funeral rituals.

"Sometimes it was for an individual, sometimes a group. Sometimes it's communal with... 52 people. So, I was on a wave of funeral rituals.

"It's a very roller coaster time because all of a sudden you feel happy to see all the surviving people... you kind of feel 'oh, they survived', but then as you talk to them you also realise that so many people that you know are not going to come back."

In Nepal, more than 1400 people were killed, while more than 5200 remain missing.

In Tibet, 43 people died, with more than 500 on the missing list. Some victims were swept 250 kilometres into neighbouring India.

"Our village is completely obliterated, completely destroyed, now completely a floodplain - just a barren rock. Nothing exists there. Just from my home village, we lost 181 locals - mostly close relatives and friends... no one survived... during this disaster.

"When I saw my hometown... I didn't even realise that my eyes were full of tears and... my body was super cold and it was shivering, and then my friend gave me a hug, and then I realised... how bad it is."

Sunil's hometown, Syaphru Besi, in 2011 (L) and after the 2026 floods (R). Supplied

Tsunami-like walls of water destroyed the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border and struck dozens of settlements along a 72 km stretch of the Trishuli River on the morning of 26 August.

But nearly three months on, rebuilding has not been straightforward. Some of the houses Tamang rebuilt after the 2015 earthquakes can not be fixed this time round.

"We lost houses then, but we still had the land, so we could go back and somehow managed to rebuild. But now we don't have the land.

"And in some areas, it is completely unsafe. There is no possibility to rebuild there. That is the reality now, at least in my part of the village - I don't think that's possible."

So where do the surviving communities go?

"I think there is a need for the government to figure out some kind of solution with very, very close consultation with the local community.

"It's not just about losing your people, but you are also losing a place that holds so much to you... and being an indigenous community, this is really, really important."

He says about US$5 billion is required for the reconstruction recovery, but "we don't have that money - that's almost 10 percent of GDP for Nepal".

"We have got a lot of sympathies and support - emotional support - from international communities, but we also need to materialise this... with real help on the ground."

Tamang, who is studying glaciers as part of his PhD, believes the latest flash floods are linked - either "directly or indirectly" - to climate change.

"We can't directly link this disaster to climate change, but then we all know that the Himalayas have been warming twice the global average temperature.

"With global climate change this kind of disaster will happen more and more often, and we cannot completely ignore this."

He hopes tourists will return to the area, saying that "mountain tourism is a big part of their livelihood, and it's also a big force for reconstruction recovery".

"Yes, tourism does play a really, really important role... yes, we are suffering, and we are grieving, but Nepal is safe to come and visit.

"So, I do urge the international community and tourists to come back to this beautiful country. And yeah, people are still very friendly, and they're kind, so please, please do come and support us in this time of great crisis."

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: Children's safety compromised by ratio confusion, says early childhood teachers
World.content:
Early childhood teachers say children's safety is compromised by confusion about the teacher to child ratios that govern their sector.

They say some early learning services misunderstand the rules and leave groups of children with too few teachers while staff take breaks.

They warned the problem causes stress for teachers and is not safe for children.

The ratios set out the minimum number of adults required for different ages and numbers of children - broadly one teacher to every five under-twos and every 10 children over that age.

Zane McCarthy from teacher union the NZEI Te Riu Roa said teachers often struggled to keep within the ratio.

"I have worked in a centre where we had two teachers in an over-twos environment and 20 children and there was not cover for things such as nappy changes," he said.

"While one teacher was changing nappies the other would have to be basically straddling the door between inside and outside in order to keep an eye on 19 other children."

Early Childhood Education teacher Zane McCarthy supplied

McCarthy said he was not sure if that way of working was legal, but it was definitely not best-practice or safe.

He said government agencies needed to be clearer.

"From my knowledge there hasn't been clear direction in the legislation on how it actually is put in practice and because of that employers are finding those grey areas and wiggle room and the impact is on tamariki and on staff," he said.

A teacher who spoke to RNZ on condition of anonymity said parents did not understand what happened inside early childhood services once the doors were shut.

She said the working ratio of teachers to children was often not what parents were led to believe.

She said some centres she had worked in included teachers in the ratio calculation even when they were taking a lunch break, and in some centres teachers were required to stay on the premises during their break.

"This is the best centre I have worked in, and I have worked in quite a few, and there still isn't any cover for breaks," she said.

The teacher said the regulations should be much more explicit, but services also needed more funding so they could hire sufficient teachers.

She said teachers should only be counted in ratio when they were able to respond immediately to the children they were responsible for.

The regulations say ratios must be maintained at all times and if staff take breaks, someone else has to step in.

The Education Review Office is responsible for reviewing early learning centres.

It confirmed that adults on breaks or involved in duties away from children were not counted for ratio purposes.

"Adults cannot be counted in ratio while undertaking food preparation or serving, carrying out administrative or maintenance duties, taking a lunch break or rest break, or during non-contact time," it said.

But it told RNZ teachers were counted if they were changing nappies or helping children in the bathroom.

"This takes place in the licensed area, so it is included in ratio considerations," it said.

"The adult-to-child ratio is a minimum requirement that licensed early learning services must meet throughout the time children are present. However, meeting the minimum adult to child ratio does not necessarily mean adequate supervision of all children. Ratio and supervision have to be looked at together to ensure children's safety at all times."

Early years advocate Susan Bates said teachers who left a room to change nappies or perform other duties were not able to respond quickly to help children.

She said they should not be counted in the ratios.

Bates said a survey of 400 teachers in a social media group she ran indicated only 40 percent of services were maintaining ratios at all times.

The rest might have enough teachers under the roof, but in some rooms they were under ratio.

"A lot of teachers believed it wasn't necessary to have one teacher to six children, they could be with 25 children outside for instance, as long as they had enough teachers under the roof so to speak," she said.

"This has left a lot of teachers over the years getting more and more anxious and upset with what they're expected to do."

Bates said it was not fair on the children or the teachers.

"Teachers are distraught basically. They've been telling me for a long time that they just cannot care for children under these circumstances," she said.

"It's getting harder and harder to do, more and more children with more and more behavioural problems under less and less supervision is really putting too much stress on everybody," she said.

Te Rito Maioha Early Childhood New Zealand represents several hundred early education services. General manager Nikki Parsons said the ratios were complex and there was definitely misunderstanding.

Te Rito Maioha Early Childhood New Zealand general manager Nikki Parsons. supplied

She said the rules did allow centres to count the total number of staff and children at a centre rather than room by room but that needed to change.

"If you've got 10 under-two with two staff members, one of them goes to change a nappy, they're leaving one staff member then with nine children so in theory you're meeting the regulatory requirements but you're not meeting quality care for our tamariki at all," she said.

Parson said the ratios were drawn up in 1960 and were well overdue for a review because many more children attended early learning and for more hours.

"When they [the ratios] first came in they were just there for three hours a day, now they're in there for up to 10 hours a day. You have infants and toddlers in there right up to five or six-year-old children. Traditionally it was only three and four-year-olds. They haven't adjusted to the needs of the communities and whanau," she said.

Parsons said there should be a one to four ratio for under-threes, and one to eight for children aged 3-5-years.

World.title: More than a third struggling to put food on the table in Waikato
World.content:
Waikato produces nearly a fifth of the country's food, yet more than a third of its people are struggling to put kai on the table.

The recently released Hunger Report by the New Zealand Food Network found 36 percent of people in Waikato were more likely to experience food insecurity, a crisis that is entrenched and shows no sign of easing.

Colonial New Zealand was supposed to be the land of milk and honey but independent researcher Dr Kimberly Jackson said people just couldn't earn enough to get everything they needed.

"The idea was that no one was going to be poor here, no one would go hungry because with hard work ... this was the place where it would all pay off for you and you would be able to, you know, have this abundant life.

"There's definitely this need for these band-aid crisis responses on the ground, but when you're getting up to 40 percent in a place surrounded by food production, as we have here in Kirikiriroa, all the food banks in the world aren't going to be able to solve that problem."

Jackson said people shouldn't need charity.

"That's the point about looking around us and seeing all of this food being produced and then people going hungry. You know it's a policy choice.

"We've got the wrong idea about the nature of these problems. They're not a problem of individual compassion as a charity giver. There are problems that are structurally baked into the system that make it harder and harder for people to actually survive."

Charity Vinnies Hamilton's general manager, Mike Rolton, was baffled by food insecurity in Waikato.

This "social supermarket" - a unique type of food bank - opened in Hamilton earlier in 2026. RNZ / Rachel Moore

"We're big dairy farmers, we're big producers of product and yet we've got the highest food insecurity and also high unemployment.

"That doesn't make sense in the Waikato, which is a really wealthy region."

The charity feeds almost 50,000 people a year.

Poverty researcher Dr Rebekah Graham agreed with Rolton.

"It is heartbreaking for everyone involved to be producing this high-quality, amazing food that New Zealand produces. It all goes offshore because that is where the money is and then we sort of left importing very low-quality cheap goods to feed people here."

She did her PhD on this topic nearly 10 years ago, but it has only got worse.

"To see it go backwards like this is just heartbreaking because it's so hard on these families. It's so hard on these kids. It's horrendous for a family trying to figure out who gets fed, who doesn't get fed."

In the year to June, food and fibre exports made a record $65.2 billion.

Independent researcher Kimberly Jackson believed it was time to have a conversation about that.

"There is a kind of ethical and political decision that could be made around ... exporting nutritious foods while people in our own backyard cannot afford those foods," she said.

World.title: Just one stop for thousands of Aucklanders on City Rail Link
World.content:
Thousands of people are hopping just one city-centre stop on Auckland's new City Rail Link, new data shows.

Two months after it opened, overall passenger numbers on the network have surpassed pre-Covid levels already, with huge increases in people travelling in from some west Auckland stations.

Weekend numbers were especially high, running at double the same period in 2019, when public transport usage in Auckland hit its previous high-water mark, and triple what they were this time last year.

Auckland Transport said the network was on track to meet its unofficial target of 21 million train trips within this financial year, which ends on 30 June.

Ridership had increased across the whole network, but included thousands of people using the new Te Waihorotiu and Karanga-a-Hape stations to get around within the central city.

Bespoke preliminary data supplied to RNZ by Auckland Transport showed more than 3000 people were travelling between just the three city stations each weekday, and that rose to nearly 4500 a day on weekends.

There was a slight uphill bias, with about five uphill journeys for every four downhill.

Shelly - a resident living near Karanga-a-Hape Station - said she had not thought about that pattern, but it rang true.

"I'd probably walk there because it's easier downhill… and then I get [the train] back."

The city rail link had been "life-changing", she said.

"It's absolutely just turned Auckland into a normal big city."

Even Auckland Transport general manager of rail services Mark Lambert confessed to getting in on Auckland's new life-hack.

"It's probably something I didn't think about prior, but certainly I can speak from my own experience of using the network, I quite often board at Waitematā and take the train up to the city."

Auckland Transport's Mark Lambert has found himself using the train to hop up the hill. Jason Dorday / Stuff

The inner-city trips were a "stand-out" for him from the early data, he said.

"The more people use the public transport network to improve their daily lives, to get to different destinations, to try new things out, hopefully that will - if it hasn't already - translate into more regular and longer-term use of the network as well."

Across the entire train network, weekday passengers had jumped about 60 percent in the first eight weeks the CRL had been open, compared to the same time period last year.

They were as high, if not higher, than before Covid, Lambert said.

"Getting back to pre-Covid levels is actually quite an achievement in itself, because travel patterns have changed for people," he said.

"A lot of people, as we know, work from home on one, two, three, even more days a week sometimes."

Weekend growth was even stronger - double what it was before Covid and nearly triple what it was this time last year.

Some of the biggest growth was coming from West Auckland stations, Lambert said.

"If you're coming from some of the more inner-west stations such as Kingsland or Grafton, the journey times have effectively halved in some cases, so that's obviously going to be a big benefit to people."

Even those travelling from stations further west, such as Henderson, had culled their journey times by 30 to 40 percent, he said.

The data supplied to RNZ bore this out.

Average weekday boardings from Henderson to the city had more than doubled (from 139 a day to 368) while Kingsland boardings to the city had quadrupled, from 122 to 507 trips a day.

Kingsland resident Simon said the train was the fastest way into the city now.

"Previously we'd either drive or bus or Uber - usually Uber for work."

Passengers head out of Karanga-a-Hape Station. RNZ / Nick Monro

The train took about five minutes to travel the two stops to Karanga-a-Hape Station, with a five-minute walk to work to complete the journey, he said.

"It's just a no-brainer, it's literally the fastest way in and out. It's also the cheapest."

He laughed when told that more people used the CRL to travel uphill than downhill within the CBD.

"That makes sense - humans are lazy."

Charlotte Ryan from the Karangahape Business Association said there had been at least a 35 percent increase in foot traffic on Karangahape Road since the CRL had opened.

"Of course it helps the businesses and the retail and everything like that, but I think it changes the energy of the street in a really positive way," she said.

"It makes it way more social, it makes it way more accessible - the more people we have on the street, the safer it is."

Charlotte Ryan says the new Karanga-a-Hape Station has improved the energy of the surrounding area. Lucy Xia

Trains across the network had been running on preliminary timetables for the first weeks of the CRL's operation.

From today, the number of services would increase, Lambert said.

That included boosting the frequency of trains on the East-West line from six per hour to eight, and extending the 15-minute frequency of services later into the evening.

Reliability and punctuality was also the highest it had been for many years, Lambert said.

World.title: Fonterra seeks permission to dump millions of litres of raw milk
World.content:
Fonterra has alarmed environmentalists with a proposal to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk in Canterbury - the equivalent of almost nine Olympic-sized swimming pools.

The dairy giant said the move was necessary to manage a potential surplus caused by production constraints across the South Island. The company would not be drawn on what the production constraints were.

Federated Farmers welcomed the proposal, calling it a sign of prudent risk management.

Fonterra's applications to vary the conditions of seven resource consents were filed with the Canterbury Regional Council on 2 October. They relate to wastewater discharges at its Clandeboye, Darfield and Studholme sites in Canterbury.

The variations were sought as a contingency response to surplus raw milk that Fonterra anticipated during the peak milk period in the 2027 and 2028 financial years, but, if granted, would apply for the duration of the original consents, which range from 2027 to 2045.

In its technical memorandum to the council, Fonterra said it anticipated "surplus raw milk will require disposal during the peak period of FY27 due to processing constraints that may occur across the South Island", and estimated the volume would be approximately 22,340m3 (22 million litres) over the current season.

A Fonterra spokesperson said the consent variations would allow the co-operative to dispose of milk when events "out of its control" prevented it being processed.

"We deal with a perishable product that needs to be processed within 24-36 hours," they said.

The spokesperson said Fonterra had similar provisions in other consents across the country.

The company had not needed to dispose of milk this season and was already through the peak processing season (late-October to mid-November), nor did it foresee having to dispose of milk next season, the spokesperson said.

"Work done across our network during winter this year has helped to ensure that we have enough capacity to efficiently process all our milk," they said.

If needed, Fonterra could shift processing to the North Island or adjust the products it made, the spokesperson said.

"With 24 manufacturing sites across the country, we have considerable flexibility to manage our farmers' milk. If those options were exhausted, we have contingency arrangements for the safe and appropriate disposal of milk, including on farm, where necessary," they said.

New Zealand's milk production set a new record in the 2025/2026 season, processing 2.02 billion kilograms of milksolids, a 4.5 per cent increase on the previous season, from 21.8 billion litres of milk.

DairyNZ's latest figures showed the South Island had higher average milksolid production per cow and per hectare compared to the North Island, while North and South Canterbury had the biggest average herd sizes and stocking rates in the country.

Infometrics puts the average number of cows in the Canterbury region at just over 970,000 in the year to May, an increase of 2.1 per cent over the year, double the nationwide increase of one per cent.

The Canterbury Regional Council has granted effluent consents allowing for up to 57,000 more cows since a temporary freeze on dairy conversions expired in January last year.

Fonterra's application stated the surplus raw milk would be incorporated into existing wastewater systems or applied directly to land. Either way, the milk would end up on farmland after being mixed into the wastewater streams and irrigated onto pasture, or loaded straight into tankers and spread onto or injected into soil.

Raw milk contained the same substances as the consented wastewater, including organic matter, fats, protein, nitrogen and phosphorus but at "significantly higher concentrations", the application stated.

The company advised any environmental effects were considered to be "no more than minor".

Milk dumping would also have "positive effects" by adding extra capacity for surplus milk and "allow beneficial re-use of nutrients and organic matter", contributing to soil fertility and supporting pasture and crop growth, the application said.

The variations were consistent with the regional council's objectives and policies, including the Canterbury Land and Water Regional Plan, and neither public nor limited notification of the consent variations were required, Fonterra argued.

The Environmental Law Initiative (ELI) called on the regional council to reject the application.

Senior researcher Anna Sintenie said the group was concerned by a "vast" change in activity from the original consents and the scale of the proposal.

"We're looking at beforehand discharging wastewater related to processing of trucks and plant facilities' wash down. What's been proposed here is a completely different substance of raw milk and the scale of that is huge," she said.

"Twenty-two million litres is more than four litres of milk for every person in New Zealand. That's an extraordinary volume of food to waste, especially with so many households experiencing cost-of-living pressures.

"It also comes at a significant environmental cost, including greenhouse gas emissions, heavy freshwater use and nutrient pollution."

The council should require Fonterra to submit new consent applications, which had higher notification and analysis requirements than variations, Sintenie said.

"Fonterra is trying to shoehorn a major discharge of raw milk into existing wastewater consents through a variation. In our view, that's not acceptable. A discharge of this kind should require a full, new consent application and proper public scrutiny," she said.

ELI was also concerned about regional council dairy conversion approvals that had green lit consents associated with tens of thousands of additional cows in the past year, Sintenie said.

"That raises a fundamental question: why is the region continuing to expand dairy production when Fonterra is seeking permission to dispose of surplus milk because production is likely to exceed its processing capacity?"

The environmental footprint of 22.3 million litres of milk included about 20,000 tonnes of emissions, approximately 6.5 billion litres of freshwater (mostly for irrigation and stock water) as well as many billions of litres more to dilute nitrate pollution, she said.

Sintenie said the application also requested the definition of wastewater be amended to include raw milk.

"By applying for this, it would open the door to that happening in these consents into the future. It's concerning that it could set a real precedent about how we think about incorporating this hugely valuable and nutrient-rich food product into wastewater," she said.

Canterbury regional council general manager of regulatory implementation Paul Hulse said the council became aware of Fonterra's processing constraints in late September.

He said the council "do not and cannot take business constraints into account" when assessing consent applications.

Hulse said it was not for the council to say whether the application should have been lodged as new consent rather than a variation.

"Fonterra is entitled to submit the applications in the form it considers appropriate. Our role as regulator is to determine whether the proposed changes fall within the scope of the existing consents," he said.

Asked what effect large amounts of raw milk could have on the environment, Hulse said the council's water and land science team would "assist consents planners in evaluating an assessment of environmental effects for the proposed activity".

Federated Farmers national dairy chair Karl Dean said he was not aware of similar attempts to allow milk dumping but welcomed the move, calling it "good, prudent business practice."

He said there were a number of scenarios that could require milk to be disposed of, such as following an earthquake.

"It was a matter of making sure the appropriate systems and risk mitigations are in place so that if something bad did happen, the options are there - even if they never get used - that those options are available," he said.

"I think what this highlights to me in doing some research is it's a bit concerning that some of the other milk processors don't have that ability in their consents."

"Obviously, I would expect the cooperative to be ... wanting to utilise every drop of milk which I'm sure they will. I think this is more of a case of making sure that good risk management is in place so that should the absolute worst happen, that there's allowance to do something."

Dean also supported Fonterra's attempt to have the definition of wastewater changed to include raw milk, which he said would be beneficial for the entire industry.

Federated Farmers understood most South Island production constraints had already been mitigated, with significant upgrades to several sites in the South Island over the last year.

"As a farmer, I haven't been impacted this year the same way I was impacted last year when there was some issues, so I'd say that those mitigations have obviously worked," he said.

In September, Fonterra announced it would spend $1 billion over three years on its South Island manufacturing network.

Greenpeace freshwater campaigner Rhiannon Mackie said dumping raw milk could have harmful environmental impacts.

"Canterbury has highly porous soil, which means it's really easy for fluids to get through the soil and into water tables like we see with the cow urine and synthetic fertiliser that causes nitrate contamination," [she said https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment/2243326/nitrate-levels-still-rising-in-most-canterbury-wells].

"In lakes and rivers in particular you can see increases in toxic algal blooms, which are already an issue in Canterbury, and have a really negative impact on the health of the freshwater ecosystems," she said.

"Not only are New Zealanders subsidizing the dairy industry through the pollution of drinking water and lakes and rivers, we're also paying huge amounts of money at the supermarket for dairy products and meanwhile Fonterra is talking about dumping these raw milk products because they've just got so much of it," she said.

According to Fonterra's "conservative assessment scenario", the co-operative would send the bulk of the surplus milk (60 per cent) to the Clandeboye site, near Temuka - an indicative volume of 13,404m3 (13 million litres per season or 600,000 litres per day) - although it noted actual volumes could vary depending on milk supply, processing capacity and operational requirements.

The next largest amount (37 per cent of the total) would go to Darfield in the Selwyn district - 500,000 litres per day - while three per cent (25,000 litres per day) would be disposed of at Studholme near Waimate.

A recent Journal of Dairy Research paper quantified dairy food loss in New Zealand for the first time, finding the industry routinely lost 1.8 per cent of dairy food on farm and 5.5 per cent at the processor.

The study said the loss was "not a sizable issue" but equated to the annual milk production of approximately 86,000 cows on farm and 264,000 cows at the processor.

Victoria University research fellow Dr Mike Joy said the even the routine dairy losses had a big impact.

"You can call that minor if you like, but that's equivalent to 350,000 cows worth of milk that's just discarded. To me, that's criminal, that's not minor, that's a massive impact," he said.

Research led by Joy in 2022 concluded each litre of milk produced required up to 11,110 litres of water to dilute nitrogen leached from Canterbury dairy farms.

He dismissed Fonterra's stance the effects of the dumping on the environment or to neighbours, residents and groundwater users would be "less than minor".

World.title: Wallabies still have a pulse despite nervous moments in win over Wales
World.content:
In Les Kiss's words, the Wallabies "earned their corn" with their gritty 29-26 Nations Championship win over Wales in Cardiff.

After ending a four-match losing streak, the Wallabies coach struck a relieved but proud figure when he and captain Harry Wilson fronted the post-match media conference.

It couldn't be described as a polished display on the field, nor was there a moment during the match where it seemed the Wallabies were dominating their opposition.

Each time they opened up an encouraging lead on the scoreboard, it never felt as though Wales was too far away from clawing its way back into the contest.

Wallabies defeat Wales The Wallabies hold on to defeat Wales 29-26 following a thrilling finish to their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

But winning breeds confidence, which had been in short supply for the Wallabies following losses to New Zealand (twice), England and Scotland.

"They had to work hard for it and I think tonight was a true Test match [and] they earned their corn and got what they deserved," Kiss said.

An improved defensive effort was among the positives in the Wallabies' performance.

While three of the four tries they conceded came from driving mauls off line-outs, they denied Wales more than once with their scramble defence deep inside the 22.

"When we do it [defence] well, it's a real point of difference for us," Wilson said.

"I thought our D-zone [inside 22] defence tonight was unbelievable."

The Wallabies' aerial game in attack also showed glimpses of its potential, with Max Jorgensen's second-half try an example of the pressure they can apply to opposition teams.

The line-out was strong (they enjoyed a clean sheet on their throw), highlighted by Josh Canham's clutch steal when Wales was camped inside the Wallabies' 22 during the first half.

Wallabies lock Josh Canham (right) enjoyed an excellent all-round performance. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

But the Wallabies let themselves down with poor discipline, especially inside their territory.

They conceded nine penalties in the opening 40 minutes, seven of which were on their side of the halfway line.

By full-time, the Wallabies had given 11 penalties away inside their half, with Wilson shown a yellow card in the 77th minute for one of those indiscretions.

If the Wallabies do the same against Ireland at Twickenham next weekend, they won't be shown any leniency.

Kiss admits the Wallabies' penalty count gave him "the shits".

"Discipline was a little bit disappointing, I must say … it kept them [Wales] in the game with field position and a few things like that," he said.

"So we're going to have to look at that as well."

Ikitau to the fore

Among individual performances, Carter Gordon looked assured at fly half.

The Wallabies were still pedestrian at times with ball in hand, however Gordon did enough to indicate he's the most suitable candidate to wear the number 10 jersey.

Wallabies fly half Carter Gordon looked solid against Wales. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Len Ikitau was deservedly named player of the match, again proving he's a world-class operator.

But the question remains whether he's better suited to inside or outside centre.

When the Wallabies pulled off their upset 42-38 win over the world champion Springboks in Perth in September, his performance at outside was superb until he left the field injured.

On that occasion, he was partnered in the centres by Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable for the Wallabies' Nations Championship campaign in Great Britain.

Ikitau played inside centre against Wales, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii admirably slotting in at 13.

Len Ikitau was outstanding in the Wallabies' win. (Getty Images/CameraSport: Ian Cook)

A permanent Ikitau-Paisami midfield combination may be the Wallabies' best option at next year's Rugby World Cup, although Suaalii's stocks at outside centre rose in Cardiff, even though he appears more comfortable on the wing.

For now, the Wallabies will turn their focus to the Ireland Test, which pits the two third-ranked teams from the respective Nations Championship groups against each other.

Their spirits will be buoyed by halting their losing streak, but Kiss knows the pressure of Test rugby never lets up.

"Test match footy doesn't hand you things easy," Kiss said.

World.title: Bellamy to end Storm coaching stint after 2027 NRL season
World.content:
Melbourne can officially begin planning for life after Craig Bellamy, after the veteran coach confirmed the longest tenure in NRL premiership history would end in 2027.

After years of speculation about his future, Bellamy will officially finish with the Storm next year at the end of his 25th season in charge of the club.

The 67-year-old's call to walk away comes after he was diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder this year.

Craig Bellamy's coaching CV NRL - Brisbane Broncos (2002): Two matches, one win, one loss

NRL - Melbourne Storm (2003-current): 630 matches, 433 wins, 195 losses, two draws

NRL premierships: 2012, 2017, 2020 (all with Storm)

State of Origin - New South Wales (2008-10): Nine matches, two wins, seven losses

But he still hopes to play some role around the club after 2027, with the five-time premiership-winning coach the most powerful figure in the Storm's history.

"I love this club and everything it represents, the people, our history and our fans," Bellamy said.

"I still have huge passion for the job, and I'm excited about what we can achieve together in 2027.

"While 2027 will be my final season as senior coach, I'm determined to make the most of the opportunity and give everything I can to our club and our players.

"I've always said I'll continue coaching while I believe I can make a positive contribution, and I feel I can still do that.

"I also feel the time is right to make 2027 my final year."

Cameron Munster is one of several big-name Storm stars who are off-contract at the end of the 2027 season. (Getty Images: Pete Dovgan/Speed Media/Icon Sportswire)

Bellamy's decision to officially call stumps comes after chief executive Justin Rodksi admitted on Friday the uncertain future had complicated contract talks with the club's biggest names.

Harry Grant, Cameron Munster and Stefano Utoikamanu are all off-contract at the end of 2027, with the Storm facing an uphill fight to retain all three.

Melbourne hasn't been able to provide clarity on who will coach the club in 2028, unable to officially move on appointing a successor until Bellamy had decided his future.

Billy Slater remains the biggest name linked with Melbourne after he walked away from the Queensland State of Origin job in August.

Billy Slater is the highest-profile name tipped to be Bellamy's successor for the Storm. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Slater does sit on Melbourne's part-time staff, but has so far suggested he does not want to coach in the NRL.

Bellamy also declared in August that Melbourne's next coach should come from within, with Marc Brentnall, Ryan Hinchliffe and Bellamy's son Aaron his full-time assistants.

Brad Arthur, Michael Maguire, Anthony Seibold and Jason Ryles are among coaches to have come out of Bellamy's system in Melbourne.

Arthur is currently coaching Leeds in the Super League, but has signalled a desire to return to the NRL, while Maguire is under pressure at the Broncos.

Ryles is on the verge of signing an extension at Parramatta, while Seibold is a free agent after being sacked by Manly last season.

"Craig is one of the greatest coaches in the history of rugby league, and we're proud of everything he has achieved in the game," Storm chairman Matthew Tripp said.

"We're also delighted he'll have one final season in charge in 2027.

"While we would obviously love to have Craig coaching our team forever, we understand how significant this decision is and are incredibly grateful that we will have another season with him leading our club."

AAP

World.title: Piastri third, snaps at McLaren team, in Vegas GP with 352 overtakes
World.content:
Oscar Piastri has produced his finest performance of the 2026 season, claiming a sensational podium in Las Vegas after starting 17th on the grid.

Max Verstappen proved why he is one of the finest Formula 1 drivers of any era, winning a thrilling grand prix that will rank as one of the best this season. There were 352 overtakes on track, with 35 of those passes for the lead of the race.

Piastri took a 10-place grid penalty for using a new internal combustion engine, and was driving a McLaren described by team CEO Zak Brown as a "sitting duck" on the long straights, due to the car's lack of top speed.

But Piastri picked his way through the field across an action-packed 50 laps, crossing the line third behind Verstappen and McLaren teammate Lando Norris.

Piastri, who is notoriously cool under pressure, had an uncharacteristic snap at his team when they stressed the importance of being careful with his teammate Norris.

With a few laps remaining, and both drivers battling in a tightly packed top-five, Piastri was told he needed to be careful if he was battling his teammate, but Piastri was having none of it.

"Stop telling me to f****** be careful," he snapped.

Piastri would overtake Norris a few laps later, but his world champion teammate re-took the position on lap 48 of 50.

Neither McLaren driver looked set to finish on the podium, but the Mercedes duo of George Russell (off track) and Kimi Antonelli (energy deployment issue) both fell down the order.

"They say Las Vegas is the entertainment capital of the world, and I think that was pretty entertaining," Piastri said post-race.

"Everyone was just in such a big pack; it was bizarre to be a part of."

Verstappen wins after 35 lead changes

In 2025, Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix when there were 17 overtakes on track during the entire race.

In 2026, he won when there were 35 overtakes on track, just for the lead.

Verstappen was at his masterful best on Sunday (AEDT), converting pole position into the 75th grand prix win of his career.

The long straights at the Las Vegas Strip circuit resulted this year with a very powerful slipstream, meaning the car behind at the end of the straight would be going much quicker.

Verstappen drove a near-perfect race, losing the lead at the end of the long back straight several times, only to then smartly deploy his electrical power to retake the lead just a few corners later.

George Russell, Kimi Antonelli and Lando Norris all overtook Verstappen for the lead at the end of the back straight at some point, only for the four-time world champion to snatch the lead straight back.

"Crazy. Really, really surreal and something I have never seen before in Formula 1 myself," Verstappen said post-race.

Verstappen was ever present in the lead, while several drivers battled to be the next challenger to the Dutchman's position.

Russell, who started second, was Verstappen's main threat throughout the race, but while running third behind his teammate Antonelli late in the race, locked his wheels and went off the track.

Antonelli was shaping up to be Verstappen's challenger on the final lap, but an energy deployment issue on the penultimate lap led to the new world champion falling behind Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri. Antonelli would finish fourth.

Isack Hadjar, Verstappen's teammate, looked destined to be a contender as well. However, his race came unstuck when his front wing collapsed, without contact, on lap 26 during a restart after a safety car.

Alpine duo Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto were fifth and sixth, a terrific result to help cement the team into sixth place in the constructors' championship, and give them an outside chance of finishing fifth.

Lewis Hamilton was seventh for Ferrari, while Carlos Sainz secured a vital eighth place for Williams.

Russell was ninth after his late mistake, while Ferrari's Charles Leclerc dropped to 10th following a 10-second penalty for colliding with teammate Hamilton.

Follow all the action of the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix on the live blog below.

World.title: Dawn Fraser fired up for 1956 Melbourne Olympics reunion
World.content:
Amid the reunions and celebrations, Dawn Fraser is drawing some inspiration from the 70th anniversary of the Melbourne Olympics.

Australia's most famous Olympian has come to Melbourne for a lunch on Sunday at the MCG to mark the November 22 opening ceremony date of the 1956 Games.

Fraser is 89 and had to miss a commemorative 1956 Olympics dinner in Melbourne a few weeks ago because of a health issue.

Fraser says she will go from table to table in her wheelchair to meet old friends and make new ones at the lunch, which coincides with the opening ceremony at the MCG 70 years ago.

Asked if she might be there for the 2032 Brisbane Olympics — Fraser was also a key figure at the Sydney 2000 Games — there is a reminder of what made her an all-time sporting great.

TV memories of the 1956 Olympics Watching the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games was many Australians' first experience of television.

"I would love to be there at '32, to support our athletes," Fraser told AAP.

"I think of my age — I just turned 89 — and, 'Oh well, that's so many years off.' But then when I look at some of the athletes who are coming to this testimonial, some of them are 95, 99.

"Then I'm thinking — excuse the expression — 'Shit! I can do that. If they can do it, I can do it.'"

Likewise, the 19-year-old from a hardscrabble Balmain upbringing had her eyes opened wide at the 1956 Olympics.

Until then, Fraser had only swum against other Australians.

"I never thought about it. [To me, the Olympics] was just another swimming event. But when I won my gold medal, I realised how big it was," Fraser said.

"It wasn't until after I won … competing against so many nations.

"To win a gold medal was something out of this world. You didn't think about it until a month later, that you were the best swimmer in the world."

Fraser won the 100-metre freestyle in Melbourne and was a member of the 4x100 women's freestyle relay team that also claimed gold.

Dawn Fraser (centre) began her Olympic reign in the 100m freestyle in Melbourne. She won her third straight gold in Tokyo in 1964. (Getty Images: Central Press/Hulton Archive)

She went on to become the first of only four swimmers who have won gold in the same individual event at three-successive Olympics. Somewhere in there, she became "Our Dawn".

Two days after the reunion, the Sport Australia Hall Of Fame annual dinner will feature the Dawn Award. It goes to an individual, team or organisation that shows courage, breaks new ground and changes sport for the better.

But as far as Fraser is concerned, she is just one athlete at the reunion.

"I'm an athlete among athletes, and I'm very proud to be among the athletes who I met and competed against in 1956," she said.

Just as the Melbourne Games dramatically changed Fraser's life, it also was a landmark for Australian sport. Only 11 years after World War Two, Australia was still an international backwater.

It has been 70 years today since Ron Clarke lit the Olympic cauldron at the MCG to kick off the Games in 1956. (Getty Images)

"Here we were, a small country, having an Olympic event that meant so much to a lot of sportsmen and women in our country … and throughout the world," Fraser said.

"We were holding the biggest sporting event ever in Olympic history.

"It was the start of not only my swimming career but for a lot of other sportsmen and women in Australia — the start of their international careers.

"It was a big stepping stone for all of us because we didn't realise we were competing against the best athletes in the world."

And so to 2032, where Fraser hopes Australia can raise the bar again.

"I want them to make it as successful as all the other Olympic Games — if not a little bit better. It's very hard to do that, but Sydney, I thought the same thing," she said.

"Sydney outshone Melbourne and I'm sure Brisbane will outshine Sydney."

AAP

World.title: Alcaraz digs deep to beat Shelton and reach ATP Finals decider
World.content:
Seven-times grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz battled back from a set down to beat American Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-1) in their ATP Finals semifinal to charge into ​Sunday's showcase for the ‌second consecutive year.

Alcaraz, beaten by Shelton in the US Open quarterfinals on the Spaniard's return from a four-month injury break, stretched his winning run to 13 matches after ‌back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris.

He will face Alexander Zverev, who beat Daniil Medvedev of Russia in the other semifinal.

"I was a ​little bit frustrated at ‌the beginning because I didn't start the match the way I wanted to," said Alcaraz, unbeaten on indoor courts this season.

"Just happy that I came back in the second set playing such great tennis, step by step, ​focused ‌on all my things and ended up playing good tennis. The third set was even closer."

Shelton, making his second consecutive appearance in the ⁠season finale, grabbed an early break to ‌race to a 3-0 lead.

Alcaraz, ‌whose fitness had come under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy ‌strapping on his left leg following Wednesday's win over Medvedev, had his thigh wrapped heavily against Shelton.

He upped his game and ‌started ​moving the American around ⁠more, engaging him in longer rallies. He earned two break points at 4-2 but could not convert either, with Shelton's booming serve getting him out of trouble.

The world number four fired a second-serve ace ⁠on his first set point to move ahead but Alcaraz went 5-3 up in the second before ‌serving out the ‌second set.

The pair traded blows in the third set ​before Alcaraz eased through the tie-break, sealing the win with a return winner.

Zverev beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (0), 6-4 in the second semi-final at the elite season-ending event for the year’s top eight players.

In their only meeting this year, Alcaraz beat Zverev in the Australian Open semifinals. The Spaniard also holds a 7-6 edge in career meetings.

"We had a practice before the tournament started. It was unbelievable. We played one set for one and a half hours. So I hope it’s going to be similar tomorrow," Zverev said.

"I hope both of us are going to be at our best and hopefully it’s a really entertaining match for everybody."

Reuters/AP

World.title: England thrash All Blacks after Moody faces haka with team
World.content:
England has roared to a record victory over New Zealand at Twickenham in the Nations Championship, after emotional scenes before the game involving former skipper Lewis Moody, who has Motor Neurone Disease (MND).
