The English beat the All Blacks 37-12 to the delight of home fans, inflicting New Zealand's second-straight defeat after last week's loss to Wales.

Moody, who played 71 Tests for England between 2001 and 2011 and was part of the team's 2003 Rugby World Cup win, came onto the ground to a huge ovation and took his place with the team to face the NZ pre-match haka.

After the haka, various England players came to embrace Moody, who announced his MND diagnosis last year.

"Lewis is such an inspirational man, he ⁠was an inspirational player and, given his ‌diagnosis, the players jumped at ‌the opportunity to support him," current England captain Maro Itoje said.

"I think he and his family gave us that ‌extra lift today. He came to spend some time with us yesterday. He presented us our shirts for today's game.

"He addressed us ‌and there's no doubt that his ⁠presence, him joining us for the haka, him spending time with us, gave us an extra lift."

Itoje, though, played down the impact of how England responded to the haka.

"The most important thing is how you start ⁠the game against New Zealand," he said.

"You can do whatever you want. There are teams historically who've done different ‌things, different formations.

"It's ‌important, but the most important thing is how you start ​the game. I wouldn't pay too much attention to whatever anyone does to respond to the haka."

Ben Earl (second from right) scored one of England's five tries in their record win over NZ. (Getty Images: RFU/Steve Bardens)

The English ran in five tries against NZ, but Itoje was determined that his side must keep improving.

After four victories in a row over Fiji, Argentina, Australia and Japan, England were braced for a much sterner test against the All Blacks, who were hurting from a shock loss to Wales.

But ​England demolished NZ, ‌racing into an early lead and ultimately winning at a canter to record back-to-back victories over the All Blacks for the first time since 2003.

"I thought we took a step forward ‌today," Itoje told reporters.

"I thought we took advantage of the opportunity we ⁠had, but … we don't want this to be our ceiling, ‌we don't want this to be as good as it ‌gets for England.

"We want to push, we want to get better. We have an amazing opportunity next week, however the chips fall to do that."

In other matches in the Nations Championship, Ireland beat world champions South Africa 20-17 in Dublin, Scotland overwhelmed Japan 67-5, and Fiji defeated Italy 21-16 in Udine.

South Africa's losing bonus point meant they topped the Southern Hemisphere standings, and will play in next week's final.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Wallabies snap four-match losing streak with tense win over Wales
World.content:
The Wallabies have snapped a four-match losing run with a tense 29-26 win over Wales in their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

The result gives the Wallabies an injection of confidence and relieves some of the pressure on coach Les Kiss, although Wales did its best to deny the visitors in the shadows of full-time.

Wales scored a try through reserve hooker Ryan Elias in the 79th minute of the match, cutting the Wallabies' lead to three points.

Following the re-start, the home side launched an attacking movement from deep inside their 22, knowing it was the final play of the match.

But it came to nothing, allowing the Wallabies to celebrate victory after defeats to All Blacks (twice), England and Scotland.

The Wallabies claimed the James Bevan Trophy after defeating Wales. (Getty Images: Nations Chammpionship/Jan Kruger)

The Wallabies had entered the match low on morale, but their hopes were boosted when they established a 12-0 lead in the first half on the back of tries to Taniela Tupou and Brandon Paenga-Amosa.

But poor discipline proved costly, with the Wallabies giving away nine penalties to four, including seven inside their half.

Taniela Tupou opened the Wallabies' scoring with a first-half try. (Getty Images: Dan Istitene)

From one of those penalties, Wales scored its first converted try via captain Dewi Lake to reduce the Wallabies' lead to 12-7 at the half-time break.

The two sides traded tries early in the second half before Wales hit the front.

Wales hit the lead following Blair Murray's converted try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Jan Kruger)

Fullback Blair Murray's converted try gave Wales a 21-19 lead, but the Wallabies struck back with Len Ikitau scoring a five-pointer and Carter Gordon adding the extras in the 65th minute.

Leading 26-21, the Wallabies extended their advantage through Gordon's penalty goal with six minutes remaining in the match.

Wales refused to roll over, however, setting up a grandstand finish with Elias's late five-pointer.

The Wallabies finished third on the Southern Hemisphere standings in the Nations Championship.

They play Ireland at Twickenham next Saturday, AEDT, as part of the Nations Championship's Finals Weekend.

Wales, fifth in the Northern Hemisphere standings, faces Japan on Sunday, AEDT.

South Africa and France will face off in the Nations Championship grand final at Twickenham on Monday, AEDT.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Lehmann denies knowledge of sandpaper plot despite Bancroft statement
World.content:
Former Australian cricket coach Darren Lehmann has once again denied knowledge of a plan to use sandpaper in the Cape Town Test against South Africa in 2018, revealing the fallout left him in a "dark place".

Speaking on ABC Radio before Australia's T20 against England at the MCG, Lehmann apologised for his role in the team's culture at the time, admitting that the team's attempts to find reverse swing during the tour "went too far".

Lehmann said he had not signed a Non Disclosure Agreement with Cricket Australia and therefore was permitted to talk about the subject freely.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

"I haven't changed my views from what happened in 2018," he said.

"It was a dark time, and we got a lot of things wrong, but my version still stays the same. It was just a bad time. We all made mistakes."

Lehmann said he could not remember being a part of a conversation where David Warner raised the prospect of using sandpaper on the ball, as Cameron Bancroft detailed in his statement earlier this week.

"I can't remember being present in that conversation," he said.

"But again, it is eight and a half years ago; you'll have to ask those people. That's the issue, I have my version, and that's where I stand."

Darren Lehmann said he felt 'empathy' towards Cameron Bancroft after his statement. (Reuters)

Bancroft's statement mentioned Lehmann speaking to squad member Peter Handscomb via a walkie talkie asking him to tell Bancroft to remove the sandpaper from the field.

However, Lehmann stated that he only knew sandpaper was on the field after seeing vision of Bancroft hiding it on the TV screen.

Lehmann denied intentionally not asking about how the players were tampering with the ball during the 2018 tour.

"With reverse swing, you throw it into the dirt, you rough up one side of the ball, you might pick at it; that's been happening for 100 years, "he said.

"For me, I didn't know, but you're always ball tampering to try and get the reverse swing happening, but you never go to that extent.

"In 2018, it went too far, and I'm [responsible] for that as the coach."

Lehmann hit back at suggestions he did not pay a price for his involvement in the saga as he detailed the mental toll it took at the time.

"People said I didn't lose anything. I actually lost the best job in the world, and I'm sorry for that, and I'm sorry for what happened. That's all I can say to the general public," he said.

"I went to a really dark place. I went to as dark a place as you can think about.

"It took me probably three to four years to actually get back to some sort of normality.

Lehmann described the job of being Australia's coach as 'the best job in the world'. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I'm not going back to that dark place. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back.

"There's things I remember and not remember. It is eight and a half years ago, it was a traumatic time.

"I don't want to go back to that dark place, and I hope no one does. I feel for everyone and their families."

When asked what he felt towards Bancroft in particular after his statement, Lehmann said "empathy", adding that he felt empathy for all the players and staff involved.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

He also took aim at reporters doorstopping the individuals involved and the general media coverage of the sandpaper saga.

"Some of the things that have been said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people. That's what I care about," he said.

"There's a lot of people being hurt at the moment and I think people have forgotten about that aspect.

"Yes, we made mistakes, we apologise as best we can and you try and move on.

"I'm not going back to that place … but it feels like everyone is pushing everyone to these bad places."

Lehmann denied knowledge of a specific conversation Khawaja detailed in his book in which he claimed a coach told the players to get the ball moving by any means possible.

Lehmann says he trusts Australian bowlers' accounts of the events in 2018 despite having no evidence to back them up. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"I don't understand that statement as such, because at the end of the day, I didn't get that statement," he said.

"I didn't get that question posed to me, so I can't comment for anyone else."

However, Lehmann admitted the environment surrounding the team at the time was centred around winning at all costs.

"You're always trying to get the ball moving anywhere, in any Test match, whether it's normal or reverse," he said.

"It was an ugly series, that's what I do know. A lot of people suffered and paid the price.

" I just remember how volatile that series was … and we certainly could've handled it better. "

Lehmann also could not recall whether there were any meetings where an individual stood up and voiced their concerns against the use of sandpaper.

"Everyone talks about meetings at the moment; there [were] a whole heap of different meetings," he said.

"There are conversations going on and some people are privy to them and some people are not. I'm not privy to every conversation or meeting.

"So a lot of different conversations happen all the time, different meetings, not altogether, that's how it is."

Lehmann said he had no evidence to back up the fierce denials from Australia's bowling quartet at the time — Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon — but said: "I trust the bowlers. Everyone is entitled to their own opinion."

Lehmann confirmed that he would attend Cricket Australia's independent forum for those involved on the 2018 South Africa tour to tell their version of events.

Australian captain Pat Cummins has also stated his intention to attend the forum, as have Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

Tech.title: Sheherazaad’s Khudgarzi is gorgeous, ‘genre-chaotic’ South Asian folk
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sheherazaad started making ripples in the music world a few years ago with her EP Qasr, which was produced by Grammy Award winner Arooj Aftab. Now she’s back with Khudgarzi, her reverb-drenched folk-noir debut LP that’s primarily sung in Urdu.

The instrumentation on Khudgarzi draws on traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, but also dabbles in Arabic folk traditions, as well as modern Western electronic music. Trip-hop flourishes and Spaghetti Western guitar brush up against tanbur and ghatam. Sheherazaad’s stunning voice sits atop dripping percussion and seasick drones singing about the plight of “The Selfish Woman.”

For Sheherazaad, the character of the selfish woman isn’t the villain, it’s a charge leveled at women who didn’t conform to societal norms, “eccentric women whose desire for agency was often met with an awful end.” Even if you can’t understand most of the lyrics, the atmosphere tells the story clearly enough. From the barely simmering anger of “Registaan” to the bleak repetition of “Qatil” and the fantastical yearning of “Zeher,” Khudgarzi is clearly the work of a woman exploring what it means to be a woman, the lasting legacy of colonialism, and the perpetual threats of a patriarchal society.

Khudgarzi is alternately a funeral dirge and a celebration of femininity. Sheherazaad owes a lot of the album’s ability to navigate these various themes and moods to her impressive production work, top-notch mixing by J. Valleau, and the cast of over 30 “genre-chaotic” virtuosic musicians including Ria Modak, Sarathy Korwar, Jay Chakravorty, Shunya, and Qasim Naqvi. The instrumentation never distracts, though. It’s not showy, and all emulsifies around Sheherazaad’s vocals in a shawl that feels equal parts comforting and oppressive.

Khudgarzi is available now on Bandcamp and most major streaming platforms, including YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, and Qobuz.

Tech.title: Protesters storm Meta offices in India
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Members of the opposition Congress party protested outside Meta’s offices in Delhi on Friday and appear to have entered the building in a video shared by CNN. Members of the party’s youth wing are demanding the company restore accounts of party leaders and warned of more protests to come. The Congress party has criticized Meta for censoring speech that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party disagree with, and has placed banners accusing Mark Zuckerberg of favoring BJP around the city.

While two accounts in question were restored Friday, Manu Jain, who oversees social media for the party’s youth wing, told Reuters that “thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.”

In February, India issued tighter rules around the removal of “unlawful” content, changing the timeline from 36 hours to just three. Modi and the Indian government have long been criticized for their restrictive policies around free speech and accused of stifling opposition viewpoints and attempting to bully the press.

Meta did not immediately return a request for comment.

Tech.title: Nintendo’s Switch 2 console is $50 off for Black Friday
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Those hoping to save some cash on a Nintendo Switch 2 can do so starting today, November 22nd, through Saturday, December 5th, giving you plenty of time to think about it after Cyber Monday has passed. For a limited time, Nintendo has knocked $50 off one of its two current console bundles, temporarily rolling back the $50 price increase that went into effect in early September.

It’s tough to predict which bundle will be most popular for your household. The Mario Kart World bundle runs $499.99 (previously $549.99) and includes the console, a digital copy of the aforementioned game, and three months of Nintendo Switch Online. Then there’s the Nintendo Switch Sports Resort bundle for $529.99 (price unchanged for Black Friday), which includes the more recent minigame-filled title instead. Both are currently available from Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Nintendo.

Nintendo has delivered hit after hit since the console launched in mid-2025. There are now plenty of excellent games to justify snagging a Switch 2, including, most recently, the stellar remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Plus, the newer console can play nearly all of the original Switch games, and it’s wirelessly compatible with the older system’s Joy-Con and Switch Pro controllers.

If you’re planning to get a Switch 2, below are some useful guides filled with accessory recommendations. From tempered glass screen protectors and protective cases to controllers, there are plenty of goodies that’ll help you take better care of your Switch 2 and get more enjoyment from it.

Tech.title: ‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Up a few concrete steps and through the front door of a 200-year-old row house in New York City, I follow a crowd of people into the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse. As we filter to our seats, ushers hand each person a black drawstring bag with a pair of wired headphones connected to a small Auracast receiver. Then, soon after the play begins, we’re instructed to put them on.

The headphones are an integral storytelling tool of Love Me — a one-man show from the minds of stand-up comedian and former Saturday Night Live writer Drew Michael and director Prashanth Venkataramanujam. It’s a show about love and the bid for connection, told in five chapters about different relationships in Michael’s life, bound by the threads of his hearing loss and self-discovery.

Related The tech world is sleeping on the most exciting Bluetooth feature in years

Love Me’s experimental sound design is possible thanks to Auracast, a technology based on Bluetooth that can broadcast a high-quality audio stream to any number of nearby devices. As the show follows Michael from childhood through adulthood, sound designer Daniel Kluger uses the headphones in combination with the theater speakers to create experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a traditional setup. Tinnitus ringing and hearing test tones play in the music between sections as subtle clues as the show builds to Michael’s epiphany about his hearing loss. Kluger also explores the world through varying levels of sonic clarity. Sound playing through the theater’s speakers is sometimes intentionally muffled, which is then further dulled by the headphones, giving the audience a sense of what Michael is hearing in those moments.

But one sound that stays clear and pristine is Michael’s inner monologue, heard in the headphones throughout the show. The inner monologue consists of both prerecorded tracks and the live feed from Michael’s microphone on stage as he talks back and forth with himself. “Any time you’re in my head — anything in the headphones is coming through clearly,” Michael tells me after the show. “[We’re] trying to also highlight that the appeal of the inner world is such that it’s the highest fidelity space for this person. It’s more comfortable.”

The different sound sources and treatments of the sound can lead to intentionally confusing scenes for the audience. During one, where Michael is doing a stand-up set at a comedy club, three sounds compete for attention: The theater speakers play the crowd’s reactions (including a heckler whose voice is sometimes muffled and sometimes clear); his prerecorded inner monologue reacting to the crowd plays in the headphones; and on stage, Michael is performing the set, with his mic muffled so our focus is on his inner monologue. It’s one of the definitive moments where the audience feels the constant concentration necessary to parse what’s happening when sounds aren’t clear and become overwhelming.

Before the show begins, there are instructions on the screen to make sure the provided headphones are connected and working properly. Photo: John Higgins / The Verge Soon after the show starts, the audience is instructed to put on their headphones and wear them for most of the show. Photo: Curtis Brown

But the biggest impact comes during a climactic scene the sound design has been building toward, a realization that also incorporates the visuals of a series of Michael’s audiograms over the years. “I had this massive breakthrough about the whole history of what I’ve been doing — the cognitive labor, the invisible to myself labor that was affecting every single minute of my life,” Michael says. “That was a huge moment.”

That’s when the audience is instructed to remove the headphones we’ve been wearing for nearly the entire show. As Michael comes to the recognition of his relationship with his hearing loss and the clarity of mind that gives him, what we’ve become used to for the entire show’s experience — the headphones — are now gone, as is that literal weight from our heads. It’s an emotional moment, one that I’ve thought about multiple times since seeing the show.

It also leads into the final act, where Michael begins to understand his own Deaf identity. “The deafness is not the culprit, it’s the denial of it.” he tells me. “My hearing currently has never been worse, but I’ve never been more self-affirmed or self-actualized or felt happier in myself. It’s a misconception, I think, about deafness as a tragedy, deafness as a deficit, deafness as a burden, deafness as something that plagues a person.”

The ability of Auracast to broadcast an audio stream that any number of headphones can connect to is what made Love Me a possibility. Any Auracast headphones can connect to the audience broadcast — I brought along the Nothing Pro 1 to test the ability and connected to the audience broadcast channel in seconds — but I used the provided Auri receiver and Austrian Audio headset for the performance. The show’s sound was designed with those in mind, and I didn’t want the differing isolation of the Nothing headphones to affect the intent of the experience.

Audience members can use the provided headphones or connect their hearing aids or cochlear implants to the Auracast stream. Photo: John Higgins / The Verge iPads are also available for those who want to have captions during the show. Photo: Curtis Brown

Love Me is presented in partnership with Deaf West Theatre, which supports Deaf-centered storytelling in theatrical productions. In addition to the audience Auracast feed, there’s one for users of hearing aids and cochlear implants that’s designed for compliance with those devices, and iPads with captions are also available. During the performance, Michael connects to his own broadcast channel with Auracast-enabled Phonak Eon Sphere hearing aids. “We talked about using in-ear monitors, but if I use an in-ear monitor, then I don’t have amplification from my environment, so then I lose contact with the audience,” Michael says. “These function as two things: They’re hearing aids and also in-ear monitors.”

Love Me relies on the Auracast technology to tell its story, but it isn’t a story about hearing technology. The technology is there to tell the story of connection and discovery of identity. “I think right now … there are two things that are at odds — the hearing aid and audiological tech side of deafness and then the cultural identity side of deafness,” Michael says. Technological improvements, like cochlear implants and hearing aids, are cited as one of the reasons schools for the deaf have been on the decline, which leads to kids being mainstreamed (put into regular public schools) and losing out on Deaf history and culture. “I’m not against the tech,” Michael says, “I just think tech and Deaf identity should be a marriage rather than a divide.”

And that collaboration is why Love Me works as well as it does. The Auracast technology is there both for accessibility — in the same way it’s already used in other performances, lectures, or announcement systems — and to uplift the show’s story of love, acceptance, and acknowledgement of one’s own Deaf identity. It’s an inventive use of the technology that carries with it a powerful message.

Tech.title: How Tamagotchis got us hooked on digital pets
Tech.content:
If you were are a kid in the late 1990s, there’s a near-100 percent chance you either had a Tamagotchi or knew someone who did. The tiny digital pets came out of nowhere and became an overnight sensation, as millions of kids signed up to parent a crying, hungry, constantly dirty creature. Until they went to school, anyway, at which point their parents were given some new responsibilities they neither asked for nor wanted.

On this episode of Version History, we dig deep into the story of the Tamagotchi. That story has its 30th anniversary this week, even though the real craze only lasted a few years. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Mia Sato and Victoria Song to discuss the origins of the Tamagotchi, the product’s many iterations, its incredible engagement tactics, and whether any of us could tolerate the Tama experience three decades later. (We… could not.)

Tech.title: Your questions about Apple HomeView’s audio, answered
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker. So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. Have more? I’ll answer them in the comments.

Clockwise from left: HomeView, HomePod (second-gen), Sonos One, HomePod Mini 2. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

How does the HomeView sound compared to the HomePod Mini, Sonos One, and HomePod?

The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. Those are much better speakers. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling.

You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView:

The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.)

The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell.

Can you pair two HomeViews for stereo sound?

Two HomeViews can’t be paired for stereo sound, as the HomePod Minis can. I use a stereo pair in my office, and they pack a decent punch in the small space.

No. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms.

If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. The HomeView’s real benefit is the screen. I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! With a HomePod, you rely on Siri voice control or your Apple device to select content.

Handoff on HomeView works with audio and video and requires holding the phone near the bottom of the screen. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Can you AirPlay music/podcasts to the HomeView, and does audio handoff work?

You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. One addition with the HomeView: You can now hand off video.

Some video apps, including YouTube TV, can use handoff even without an app on the HomeView. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

In testing, handoff worked for Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Pocket Casts, YouTube Music, FaceTime, and phone calls — although phone calls sometimes dropped. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser.

One word of caution: Handoff is aggressive. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content.

Can you set a default speaker for the HomeView?

HomeViews can AirPlay audio to HomePods, Apple TVs, and other AirPlay-enabled speakers or devices. Photo: Hunter McRae for The Verge

HomeView doesn’t let you set a default speaker or group to use instead of its built-in speaker. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly.

For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. If it’s been a while since you opened the app, it pops up the option to choose the last-used speakers.

Spotify has no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving — only I’m not driving; I’m in my kitchen!

Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker.

So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music.

Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Like second-class citizens.

Does Spotify work on the HomeView?

Audio and video CarPlay apps appear on the HomeView app drawer when your phone is on the same Wi-Fi network, and you have a profile on the device. Photo: Hunter McRae for The Verge

Spotify works on the HomeView, but with limitations that apply to all non-native and third-party apps: they only show up when your phone is connected to the HomeView via your profile, so only you can use them.

Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform. This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).

In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi. It also results in slower performance and a laggy, inconsistent experience compared to the native apps.

I tried several apps: Pocket Casts, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, Spotify, and Audible. They all appeared in my HomeView app drawer, and I could access them, choose content via streamlined interfaces, and then play audio on the HomeView or AirPlay from it to any speakers.

But CarPlay apps don’t work as well as the built-in audio apps — Music, Podcasts, and Safari. They take longer to load and respond more slowly. You also can’t type a search query in any of them, as you can in the native apps, because they don’t have a search field or keyboard. Instead, you have to scroll through content to find what you want or use Siri voice search.

Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”

There’s no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving; only I’m not driving — I’m in my kitchen! This shows how much of a CarPlay port the apps are; they haven’t been updated to account for the fact that this device is stationary and in your home. Case in point, when I first pulled up the Apple TV app (the only CarPlay video app currently supported), a warning popped up telling me to make sure I was stationary before watching any video.

Playing audio through CarPlay apps is also buggy. It didn’t always bring up the music control screen, so I had to use my iPhone to control it. Plus, the Audible app often refused to load at all and didn’t work with Siri voice search. Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”

CarPlay support feels like a stopgap, and Apple needs to work with developers to refine the software and add HomeView-specific controls for a better, more integrated experience.

A smart display has several functions beyond being a smart speaker. One feature I like on the HomeView is its guided cooking experience. Photo: Hunter McRae for The Verge

Should you buy a HomeView as a smart speaker?

Much of the confusion around the HomeView stems from treating it like a smart speaker when it’s really a smart display. I get it; I’ve spent the last decade frustrated by smart displays from Google and Amazon that promise a lot but rarely do it all well.

If you don’t care about the other features of a smart display and just want a smart speaker, then the reason to buy a HomeView over a HomePod is if you have a use for it as a touchscreen music controller. This lets anyone in the household easily browse and control what’s playing. Bear in mind, though, Apple Music (with a subscription) is the only app anyone can use to play music on the HomeView, as CarPlay apps require a user profile.

If you want a smart speaker primarily to play music and are happy using your voice or phone to control it, go for a HomePod. If you use Spotify or other third-party music services, consider an Echo Dot or Google Home smart speaker; both let you set a default speaker and a default music provider — such as Spotify.

If you already own HomePods and use Apple Music, the HomeView’s touchscreen will fit in nicely as a simple way to control audio. Just don’t buy one expecting it to fully replace a dedicated smart speaker.

Tech.title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.

How it’s going

Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.

The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.

Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.

In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotakuthat the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.

All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”

The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want?

ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solidon the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list.

What happens next

The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.

Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.

At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.

But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which lots of people are doing) or your computer (which lots of people are also doing), do it carefully. And make lots of backups.

By the way

If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund.

You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on Waveshare , which has a big selection and pretty good prices.

Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called ESP-Claw . It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler.

Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi … to hack a Raspberry Pi.
